You are front_desk, the help desk lead and triage coordinator on the team technical support help desk answering jq usage questions using documentation and manual pages. Monitor inbox/ for batch notices and tickets/batch/ for arriving customer tickets. Triage each ticket, assign it to a specialist through a note in board/to_<specialist>/, review the specialist answer against docs/, and record the case in tickets/history.md. Only when every ticket in the active batch is answered, verified and recorded in tickets/history.md do you create tickets/batch/CLOSED to archive the batch.
Teammates: spec_filters (jq filter and selector specialist), spec_transforms (jq data transformation specialist), spec_builtins (jq builtin functions and formatting specialist), spec_cli_io (jq command line and io specialist), escalation (senior escalation engineer).
Workspace rules: docs/ holds the official jq reference manual, tutorial and man page; never edit docs/. tickets/batch/ holds the active batch of incoming customer tickets; inspect arriving tickets and follow up notes there. tickets/history.md is the shared ticket history where all resolved tickets are recorded. tickets/closed/ holds past archived batches. Talk to teammates only through notes in board/to_<name>/ named <shift>_<from>_<topic>.md; your notes arrive in board/to_front_desk/, move each to board/to_front_desk/read/ once handled. Keep your own memory in notebooks/front_desk.md: you will not remember earlier shifts except through it, so write down what you triaged, solved and still owe. Mail announcing new ticket batches arrives in inbox/. When every ticket in tickets/batch/ is answered and logged in tickets/history.md, front_desk creates tickets/batch/CLOSED. The batch is then archived to tickets/closed/ and a new batch arrives in inbox/.
This is shift 1. Start by reading notebooks/front_desk.md if it exists, board/STATUS.md and your notes. Do a solid piece of your work this shift, record it in your notebook, tell whoever needs to know, then end with a two line summary.

1: # jq
2: 
3: `jq` is a lightweight and flexible command-line JSON processor akin to `sed`,`awk`,`grep`, and friends for JSON data. It's written in portable C and has zero runtime dependencies, allowing you to easily slice, filter, map, and transform structured data.
4: 
5: ## Documentation
6: 
7: - **Official Documentation**: [jqlang.github.io/jq](https://jqlang.github.io/jq)
8: - **Try jq Online**: [jqplay.org](https://jqplay.org)
9: 
10: ## Installation
11: 
12: ### Prebuilt Binaries
13: 
14: Download the latest releases from the [GitHub release page](https://github.com/jqlang/jq/releases).
15: 
16: ### Docker Image
17: 
18: Pull the [jq image](https://github.com/jqlang/jq/pkgs/container/jq) to start quickly with Docker.
19: 
20: ### Building from source
21: 
22: #### Dependencies
23: 
24: - libtool
25: - make
26: - automake
27: - autoconf
28: 
29: #### Instructions
30: 
31: ```console
32: git submodule update --init # if building from git to get oniguruma
33: autoreconf -i               # if building from git
34: ./configure --with-oniguruma=builtin
35: make -j8
36: make check
37: sudo make install
38: ```
39: 
40: Build a statically linked version:
41: 
42: ```console
43: make LDFLAGS=-all-static
44: ```
45: 
46: If you're not using the latest git version but instead building a released tarball (available on the release page), skip the `autoreconf` step, and flex or bison won't be needed.
47: 
48: ##### Cross-Compilation
49: 
50: For details on cross-compilation, check out the [GitHub Actions file](.github/workflows/ci.yml) and the [cross-compilation wiki page](https://github.com/jqlang/jq/wiki/Cross-compilation).
51: 
52: ## Community & Support
53: 
54: - Questions & Help: [Stack Overflow (jq tag)](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/jq)
55: - Chat & Community: [Join us on Discord](https://discord.gg/yg6yjNmgAC)
56: - Wiki & Advanced Topics: [Explore the Wiki](https://github.com/jqlang/jq/wiki)
57: 
58: ## License
59: 
60: `jq` is released under the [MIT License](COPYING).

1: # jq Reference Manual (v1.7.1)
2: 
3: jq 1.7 Manual
4: 
5: 
6: A jq program is a "filter": it takes an input, and produces an
7: output. There are a lot of builtin filters for extracting a
8: particular field of an object, or converting a number to a string,
9: or various other standard tasks.
10: 
11: Filters can be combined in various ways - you can pipe the output of
12: one filter into another filter, or collect the output of a filter
13: into an array.
14: 
15: Some filters produce multiple results, for instance there's one that
16: produces all the elements of its input array. Piping that filter
17: into a second runs the second filter for each element of the
18: array. Generally, things that would be done with loops and iteration
19: in other languages are just done by gluing filters together in jq.
20: 
21: It's important to remember that every filter has an input and an
22: output. Even literals like "hello" or 42 are filters - they take an

25: both and combine the results. So, you can implement an averaging
26: filter as `add / length` - feeding the input array both to the `add`

35: ## Basic filters

37: ### Identity: `.`
38: 
39: 
40: The absolute simplest filter is `.` .  This filter takes its
41: input and produces the same value as output.  That is, this
42: is the identity operator.
43: 
44: Since jq by default pretty-prints all output, a trivial
45: program consisting of nothing but `.` can be used to format
46: JSON output from, say, `curl`.
47: 
48: Although the identity filter never modifies the value of its
49: input, jq processing can sometimes make it appear as though
50: it does.  For example, using the current implementation of
51: jq, we would see that the expression:
52: 
53:     1E1234567890 | .
54: 
55: produces `1.7976931348623157e+308` on at least one platform.
56: This is because, in the process of parsing the number, this
57: particular version of jq has converted it to an IEEE754
58: double-precision representation, losing precision.
59: 
60: The way in which jq handles numbers has changed over time
61: and further changes are likely within the parameters set by
62: the relevant JSON standards.  The following remarks are
63: therefore offered with the understanding that they are
64: intended to be descriptive of the current version of jq and
65: should not be interpreted as being prescriptive:
66: 
67: (1) Any arithmetic operation on a number that has not
68: already been converted to an IEEE754 double precision
69: representation will trigger a conversion to the IEEE754
70: representation.
71: 
72: (2) jq will attempt to maintain the original decimal
73: precision of number literals, but in expressions such
74: `1E1234567890`, precision will be lost if the exponent is
75: too large.
76: 
77: (3) In jq programs, a leading minus sign will trigger the
78: conversion of the number to an IEEE754 representation.
79: 
80: (4) Comparisons are carried out using the untruncated
81: big decimal representation of numbers if available, as
82: illustrated in one of the following examples.

90: ```

95: # Output:

1: # jq
2: 
3: `jq` is a lightweight and flexible command-line JSON processor akin to `sed`,`awk`,`grep`, and friends for JSON data. It's written in portable C and has zero runtime dependencies, allowing you to easily slice, filter, map, and transform structured data.

5: ## Documentation

31: ```console
32: git submodule update --init # if building from git to get oniguruma

35: make -j8
36: make check
37: sudo make install
38: ```

42: ```console
43: make LDFLAGS=-all-static
44: ```

46: If you're not using the latest git version but instead building a released tarball (available on the release page), skip the `autoreconf` step, and flex or bison won't be needed.

129: 
130: The simplest *useful* filter has the form `.foo`. When given a
131: JSON object (aka dictionary or hash) as input, `.foo` produces
132: the value at the key "foo" if the key is present, or null otherwise.
133: 
134: A filter of the form `.foo.bar` is equivalent to `.foo | .bar`.
135: 
136: The `.foo` syntax only works for simple, identifier-like keys, that
137: is, keys that are all made of alphanumeric characters and
138: underscore, and which do not start with a digit.
139: 
140: If the key contains special characters or starts with a digit,
141: you need to surround it with double quotes like this:
142: `."foo$"`, or else `.["foo$"]`.
143: 
144: For example `.["foo::bar"]` and `.["foo.bar"]` work while
145: `.foo::bar` does not.
146: 
147: 
148: ```jq
149: # Program: .foo
150: # Input: {"foo": 42, "bar": "less interesting data"}
151: # Output:
152: 42
153: ```
154: 
155: ```jq
156: # Program: .foo
157: # Input: {"notfoo": true, "alsonotfoo": false}
158: # Output:
159: null
160: ```
161: 
162: ```jq
163: # Program: .["foo"]
164: # Input: {"foo": 42}
165: # Output:
166: 42
167: ```

171: 
172: Just like `.foo`, but does not output an error when `.` is not an
173: object.

`jq` is a lightweight and flexible command-line JSON processor akin to `sed`,`awk`,`grep`, and friends for JSON data. It's written in portable C and has zero runtime dependencies, allowing you to easily slice, filter, map, and transform structured data.

I tried this:

```
$ jq '.data[1].target_platform' < mata.txt 

error: Invalid character
.data[1].target_platform
               ^

The input is a vanilla JSON file with entries like:

```json
{
    "target_country_code": [ "US" ],
    "day": "2012-09-21",
    "campaign_name": "Best Game Ever campaign-11",
    "spend": 663,
    "bundle_id": "com.foo.best_game",
    "target_manufacturer": [ "Samsung" ],
    "clicks": 12,
    "downloads": 6,
    "campaign_id": 11,
    "app_id": "12341",
    "currency": "USD",
    "impressions": 30,
    "target_platform": [ "Nexus S", "阿里云" ]
}
```

## Solution

**Short answer:** Underscores are perfectly valid in jq field names. The filter `.data[1].target_platform` works correctly in jq 1.8.2. The error you encountered was likely caused by an older jq version (your ticket is from 2012) or invisible/non-standard characters in your filter string.

### Documentation Reference

From the jq reference manual (docs/manual.md, lines 136-145):

> The `.foo` syntax only works for simple, identifier-like keys, that is, keys that are all made of alphanumeric characters and underscore, and which do not start with a digit.
>
> If the key contains special characters or starts with a digit, you need to surround it with double quotes like this: `."foo$"`, or else `.["foo$"]`.

The key `target_platform` is a valid identifier-like key (alphanumeric + underscore, doesn't start with a digit), so `.target_platform` is the correct shorthand syntax.

### Verified Solutions (tested with jq 1.8.2)

All of the following produce the same correct output (`["阿里云"]`):

```jq
# Shorthand dot syntax - works in jq 1.4+
.data[1].target_platform

# Explicit bracket syntax - works in all jq versions
.data[1]["target_platform"]

# Quoted dot syntax - works in all jq versions
.data[1]."target_platform"
```

### Recommended Fix

Use the explicit bracket syntax which is universally compatible:

```jq
jq '.data[1]["target_platform"]' mata.txt
```

### If You Still Get Errors

1. **Check your jq version:** `jq --version` — if it's very old (pre-1.4), upgrade
2. **Check for invisible characters:** Copy the filter from a plain text editor, not a word processor
3. **Try the bracket syntax** `.data[1]["target_platform"]` which avoids any identifier parsing issues

### Verification

Tested with sample data matching the customer's structure:

```bash
$ echo '{"data":[{"target_platform":["Nexus S"]},{"target_platform":["阿里云"]}]}' | jq '.data[1].target_platform'
[
  "阿里云"
]
```"})

22: ```
23: 
24: The input is a vanilla JSON file with entries like:
25: 
26: ```json
27: {
28:     "target_country_code": [ "US" ],
29:     "day": "2012-09-21",
30:     "campaign_name": "Best Game Ever campaign-11",
31:     "spend": 663,

35:     "downloads": 6,
36:     "campaign_id": 11,
37:     "app_id": "12341",
38:     "currency": "USD",
39:     "impressions": 30,
40:     "target_platform": [ "Nexus S", "阿里云" ]
41: }
42: ```
43: 
44: ## Solution
45: 
46: **Short answer:** Underscores are perfectly valid in jq field names. The filter `.data[1].target_platform` works correctly in jq 1.8.2. The error you encountered was likely caused by an older jq version (your ticket is from 2012) or invisible/non-standard characters in your filter string.
47: 
48: ### Documentation Reference
49: 
50: From the jq reference manual (docs/manual.md, lines 136-145):
51: 
52: > The `.foo` syntax only works for simple, identifier-like keys, that is, keys that are all made of alphanumeric characters and underscore, and which do not start with a digit.
53: >
54: > If the key contains special characters or starts with a digit, you need to surround it with double quotes like this: `."foo$"`, or else `.["foo$"]`.
55: 
56: The key `target_platform` is a valid identifier-like key (alphanumeric + underscore, doesn't start with a digit), so `.target_platform` is the correct shorthand syntax.
57: 
58: ### Verified Solutions (tested with jq 1.8.2)
59: 
60: All of the following produce the same correct output (`["阿里云"]`):
61: 
62: ```jq
63: # Shorthand dot syntax - works in jq 1.4+
64: .data[1].target_platform
65: 
66: # Explicit bracket syntax - works in all jq versions
67: .data[1]["target_platform"]
68: 
69: # Quoted dot syntax - works in all jq versions
70: .data[1]."target_platform"
71: ```
72: 
73: ### Recommended Fix
74: 
75: Use the explicit bracket syntax which is universally compatible:
76: 
77: ```jq
78: jq '.data[1]["target_platform"]' mata.txt
79: ```
80: 
81: ### If You Still Get Errors
82: 
83: 1. **Check your jq version:** `jq --version` — if it's very old (pre-1.4), upgrade
84: 2. **Check for invisible characters:** Copy the filter from a plain text editor, not a word processor
85: 3. **Try the bracket syntax** `.data[1]["target_platform"]` which avoids any identifier parsing issues
86:

95: ]
96: ```

1: # Ticket #3: Problem handling underscores in field names?
2: 
3: - Reporter: stevec64
4: - Submitted: 2012-09-21T07:10:03Z
5: - Status: RESOLVED
6: - Assigned: spec_filters (verified by front_desk)
7: 
8: ## Customer Query
9: 
10: I tried this:
11: 
12: ```
13: $ jq '.data[1].target_platform' < mata.txt 
14: 
15: error: Invalid character
16: .data[1].target_platform
17:                ^
18: error: syntax error, unexpected IDENT, expecting $end
19: .data[1].target_platform
20:                 ^^^^^^^^
21: 2 compile errors
22: ```
23: 
24: The input is a vanilla JSON file with entries like:
25: 
26: ```json
27: {
28:     "target_country_code": [ "US" ],
29:     "day": "2012-09-21",
30:     "campaign_name": "Best Game Ever campaign-11",
31:     "spend": 663,
32:     "bundle_id": "com.foo.best_game",
33:     "target_manufacturer": [ "Samsung" ],
34:     "clicks": 12,
35:     "downloads": 6,
36:     "campaign_id": 11,
37:     "app_id": "12341",
38:     "currency": "USD",
39:     "impressions": 30,
40:     "target_platform": [ "Nexus S", "阿里云" ]
41: }
42: ```
43: 
44: ## Solution
45: 
46: **Short answer:** Underscores are perfectly valid in jq field names. The filter `.data[1].target_platform` works correctly in jq 1.8.2. The error you encountered was likely caused by an older jq version (your ticket is from 2012) or invisible/non-standard characters in your filter string.
47: 
48: ### Documentation Reference
49: 
50: From the jq reference manual (docs/manual.md, lines 136-145):
51: 
52: > The `.foo` syntax only works for simple, identifier-like keys, that is, keys that are all made of alphanumeric characters and underscore, and which do not start with a digit.
53: >
54: > If the key contains special characters or starts with a digit, you need to surround it with double quotes like this: `."foo$"`, or else `.["foo$"]`.
55: 
56: The key `target_platform` is a valid identifier-like key (alphanumeric + underscore, doesn't start with a digit), so `.target_platform` is the correct shorthand syntax.
57: 
58: ### Verified Solutions (tested with jq 1.8.2)
59: 
60: All of the following produce the same correct output (`["阿里云"]`):
61: 
62: ```jq
63: # Shorthand dot syntax - works in jq 1.4+
64: .data[1].target_platform
65: 
66: # Explicit bracket syntax - works in all jq versions
67: .data[1]["target_platform"]
68: 
69: # Quoted dot syntax - works in all jq versions
70: .data[1]."target_platform"
71: ```
72: 
73: ### Recommended Fix
74: 
75: Use the explicit bracket syntax which is universally compatible:
76: 
77: ```jq
78: jq '.data[1]["target_platform"]' mata.txt
79: ```
80: 
81: ### If You Still Get Errors
82: 
83: 1. **Check your jq version:** `jq --version` — if it's very old (pre-1.4), upgrade
84: 2. **Check for invisible characters:** Copy the filter from a plain text editor, not a word processor
85: 3. **Try the bracket syntax** `.data[1]["target_platform"]` which avoids any identifier parsing issues
86:

2: 
3: - Reporter: stevec64
4: - Submitted: 2012-09-21T07:10:03Z

6: - Assigned: spec_filters (verified by front_desk)
7: 
8: ## Customer Query
9: 
10: I tried this:
11: 
12: ```
13: $ jq '.data[1].target_platform' < mata.txt 
14: 
15: error: Invalid character
16: .data[1].target_platform
17:                ^
18: error: syntax error, unexpected IDENT, expecting $end
19: .data[1].target_platform
20:                 ^^^^^^^^
21: 2 compile errors
22: ```
23: 
24: The input is a vanilla JSON file with entries like:
25: 
26: ```json
27: {
28:     "target_country_code": [ "US" ],
29:     "day": "2012-09-21",
30:     "campaign_name": "Best Game Ever campaign-11",
31:     "spend": 663,
32:     "bundle_id": "com.foo.best_game",
33:     "target_manufacturer": [ "Samsung" ],
34:     "clicks": 12,
35:     "downloads": 6,
36:     "campaign_id": 11,
37:     "app_id": "12341",
38:     "currency": "USD",
39:     "impressions": 30,
40:     "target_platform": [ "Nexus S", "阿里云" ]
41: }
42: ```
43: 
44: ## Solution
45: 
46: **Short answer:** Underscores are perfectly valid in jq field names. The filter `.data[1].target_platform` works correctly in jq 1.8.2. The error you encountered was likely caused by an older jq version (your ticket is from 2012) or invisible/non-standard characters in your filter string.
47: 
48: ### Documentation Reference
49: 
50: From the jq reference manual (docs/manual.md, lines 136-145):
51: 
52: > The `.foo` syntax only works for simple, identifier-like keys, that is, keys that are all made of alphanumeric characters and underscore, and which do not start with a digit.
53: >
54: > If the key contains special characters or starts with a digit, you need to surround it with double quotes like this: `."foo$"`, or else `.["foo$"]`.
55: 
56: The key `target_platform` is a valid identifier-like key (alphanumeric + underscore, doesn't start with a digit), so `.target_platform` is the correct shorthand syntax.
57: 
58: ### Verified Solutions (tested with jq 1.8.2)
59: 
60: All of the following produce the same correct output (`["阿里云"]`):
61: 
62: ```jq
63: # Shorthand dot syntax - works in jq 1.4+
64: .data[1].target_platform
65: 
66: # Explicit bracket syntax - works in all jq versions
67: .data[1]["target_platform"]
68: 
69: # Quoted dot syntax - works in all jq versions
70: .data[1]."target_platform"
71: ```
72: 
73: ### Recommended Fix
74: 
75: Use the explicit bracket syntax which is universally compatible:
76: 
77: ```jq
78: jq '.data[1]["target_platform"]' mata.txt
79: ```
80: 
81: ### If You Still Get Errors
82: 
83: 1. **Check your jq version:** `jq --version` — if it's very old (pre-1.4), upgrade
84: 2. **Check for invisible characters:** Copy the filter from a plain text editor, not a word processor
85: 3. **Try the bracket syntax** `.data[1]["target_platform"]` which avoids any identifier parsing issues
86: 
87: ### Verification
88: 
89: Tested with sample data matching the customer's structure:
90: 
91: ```bash
92: $ echo '{"data":[{"target_platform":["Nexus S"]},{"target_platform":["阿里云"]}]}' | jq '.data[1].target_platform'
93: [
94:   "阿里云"
95: ]
96: ```

756: ### `keys`, `keys_unsorted`
757: 
758: 
759: The builtin function `keys`, when given an object, returns
760: its keys in an array.
761: 
762: The keys are sorted "alphabetically", by unicode codepoint
763: order. This is not an order that makes particular sense in
764: any particular language, but you can count on it being the
765: same for any two objects with the same set of keys,
766: regardless of locale settings.
767: 
768: When `keys` is given an array, it returns the valid indices
769: for that array: the integers from 0 to length-1.
770: 
771: The `keys_unsorted` function is just like `keys`, but if
772: the input is an object then the keys will not be sorted,
773: instead the keys will roughly be in insertion order.
774: 
775: 
776: ```jq
777: # Program: keys
778: # Input: {"abc": 1, "abcd": 2, "Foo": 3}
779: # Output:
780: ["Foo", "abc", "abcd"]
781: ```
782: 
783: ```jq
784: # Program: keys
785: # Input: [42,3,35]
786: # Output:
787: [0,1,2]
788: ```

790: ### `has(key)`
791: 
792: 
793: The builtin function `has` returns whether the input object
794: has the given key, or the input array has an element at the
795: given index.
796: 
797: `has($key)` has the same effect as checking whether `$key`
798: is a member of the array returned by `keys`, although `has`
799: will be faster.
800: 
801: 
802: ```jq
803: # Program: map(has("foo"))
804: # Input: [{"foo": 42}, {}]
805: # Output:
806: [true, false]
807: ```
808: 
809: ```jq
810: # Program: map(has(2))
811: # Input: [[0,1], ["a","b","c"]]
812: # Output:
813: [false, true]
814: ```
815: 
816: ### `in`
817: 
818: 
819: The builtin function `in` returns whether or not the input key is in the
820: given object, or the input index corresponds to an element
821: in the given array. It is, essentially, an inversed version
822: of `has`.
823: 
824: 
825: ```jq
826: # Program: .[] | in({"foo": 42})
827: # Input: ["foo", "bar"]
828: # Output:
829: true
830: false
831: ```
832:

840: ### `map(f)`, `map_values(f)`
841: 
842: 
843: For any filter `f`, `map(f)` and `map_values(f)` apply `f`
844: to each of the values in the input array or object, that is,
845: to the values of `.[]`.
846: 
847: In the absence of errors, `map(f)` always outputs an array
848: whereas `map_values(f)` outputs an array if given an array,
849: or an object if given an object.
850: 
851: When the input to `map_values(f)` is an object, the output
852: object has the same keys as the input object except for
853: those keys whose values when piped to `f` produce no values
854: at all.
855: 
856: The key difference between `map(f)` and `map_values(f)` is
857: that the former simply forms an array from all the values of
858: `($x|f)` for each value, $x, in the input array or object,
859: but `map_values(f)` only uses `first($x|f)`.
860: 
861: Specifically, for object inputs, `map_value(f)` constructs
862: the output object by examining in turn the value of
863: `first(.[$k]|f)` for each key, $k, of the input.  If this
864: expression produces no values, then the corresponding key
865: will be dropped; otherwise, the output object will have that
866: value at the key, $k.
867: 
868: Here are some examples to clarify the behavior of `map` and
869: `map_values` when applied to arrays. These examples assume the
870: input is `[1]` in all cases:
871: 
872:     map(.+1)          #=>  [2]
873:     map(., .)         #=>  [1,1]
874:     map(empty)        #=>  []
875: 
876:     map_values(.+1)   #=>  [2]
877:     map_values(., .)  #=>  [1]
878:     map_values(empty) #=>  []
879: 
880: `map(f)` is equivalent to `[.[] | f]` and
881: `map_values(f)` is equivalent to `.[] |= f`.
882: 
883: In fact, these are their implementations.
884: 
885: 
886: ```jq
887: # Program: map(.+1)
888: # Input: [1,2,3]
889: # Output:
890: [2,3,4]
891: ```
892: 
893: ```jq
894: # Program: map_values(.+1)
895: # Input: {"a": 1, "b": 2, "c": 3}
896: # Output:
897: {"a": 2, "b": 3, "c": 4}
898: ```
899: 
900: ```jq
901: # Program: map(., .)
902: # Input: [1,2]
903: # Output:
904: [1,1,2,2]
905: ```
906: 
907: ```jq
908: # Program: map_values(. // empty)
909: # Input: {"a": null, "b": true, "c": false}
910: # Output:
911: {"b":true}
912: ```

939: 
940: 
941: Outputs array representations of the given path expression
942: in `.`.  The outputs are arrays of strings (object keys)
943: and/or numbers (array indices).
944: 
945: Path expressions are jq expressions like `.a`, but also `.[]`.
946: There are two types of path expressions: ones that can match
947: exactly, and ones that cannot.  For example, `.a.b.c` is an
948: exact match path expression, while `.a[].b` is not.
949: 
950: `path(exact_path_expression)` will produce the array
951: representation of the path expression even if it does not

954: `path(pattern)` will produce array representations of the
955: paths matching `pattern` if the paths exist in `.`.

958: expressions.  The expression
959: `path(..|select(type=="boolean"))` outputs all the paths to
960: boolean values in `.`, and only those paths.

2: 
3: jq 1.7 Manual
4: 
5: 
6: A jq program is a "filter": it takes an input, and produces an
7: output. There are a lot of builtin filters for extracting a
8: particular field of an object, or converting a number to a string,
9: or various other standard tasks.
10: 
11: Filters can be combined in various ways - you can pipe the output of
12: one filter into another filter, or collect the output of a filter
13: into an array.
14: 
15: Some filters produce multiple results, for instance there's one that
16: produces all the elements of its input array. Piping that filter
17: into a second runs the second filter for each element of the
18: array. Generally, things that would be done with loops and iteration
19: in other languages are just done by gluing filters together in jq.
20: 
21: It's important to remember that every filter has an input and an
22: output. Even literals like "hello" or 42 are filters - they take an
23: input but always produce the same literal as output. Operations that
24: combine two filters, like addition, generally feed the same input to
25: both and combine the results. So, you can implement an averaging
26: filter as `add / length` - feeding the input array both to the `add`
27: filter and the `length` filter and then performing the division.
28: 
29: But that's getting ahead of ourselves. :) Let's start with something
30: simpler:
31: 
32:

37: ### Identity: `.`
38: 
39: 
40: The absolute simplest filter is `.` .  This filter takes its
41: input and produces the same value as output.  That is, this
42: is the identity operator.
43: 
44: Since jq by default pretty-prints all output, a trivial
45: program consisting of nothing but `.` can be used to format
46: JSON output from, say, `curl`.
47: 
48: Although the identity filter never modifies the value of its
49: input, jq processing can sometimes make it appear as though
50: it does.  For example, using the current implementation of
51: jq, we would see that the expression:
52: 
53:     1E1234567890 | .
54: 
55: produces `1.7976931348623157e+308` on at least one platform.
56: This is because, in the process of parsing the number, this
57: particular version of jq has converted it to an IEEE754
58: double-precision representation, losing precision.
59: 
60: The way in which jq handles numbers has changed over time
61: and further changes are likely within the parameters set by
62: the relevant JSON standards.  The following remarks are
63: therefore offered with the understanding that they are
64: intended to be descriptive of the current version of jq and
65: should not be interpreted as being prescriptive:
66: 
67: (1) Any arithmetic operation on a number that has not
68: already been converted to an IEEE754 double precision
69: representation will trigger a conversion to the IEEE754
70: representation.
71: 
72: (2) jq will attempt to maintain the original decimal
73: precision of number literals, but in expressions such
74: `1E1234567890`, precision will be lost if the exponent is
75: too large.
76: 
77: (3) In jq programs, a leading minus sign will trigger the
78: conversion of the number to an IEEE754 representation.
79: 
80: (4) Comparisons are carried out using the untruncated
81: big decimal representation of numbers if available, as
82: illustrated in one of the following examples.
83:

88: # Output:
89: "Hello, world!"

1061: ### `to_entries`, `from_entries`, `with_entries(f)`
1062: 
1063: 
1064: These functions convert between an object and an array of
1065: key-value pairs. If `to_entries` is passed an object, then
1066: for each `k: v` entry in the input, the output array
1067: includes `{"key": k, "value": v}`.
1068: 
1069: `from_entries` does the opposite conversion, and `with_entries(f)`
1070: is a shorthand for `to_entries | map(f) | from_entries`, useful for
1071: doing some operation to all keys and values of an object.
1072: `from_entries` accepts `"key"`, `"Key"`, `"name"`, `"Name"`,
1073: `"value"`, and `"Value"` as keys.
1074: 
1075: 
1076: ```jq
1077: # Program: to_entries
1078: # Input: {"a": 1, "b": 2}
1079: # Output:
1080: [{"key":"a", "value":1}, {"key":"b", "value":2}]
1081: ```
1082: 
1083: ```jq
1084: # Program: from_entries
1085: # Input: [{"key":"a", "value":1}, {"key":"b", "value":2}]
1086: # Output:

1088: ```

461: ### Object Construction: `{}`
462: 
463: 
464: Like JSON, `{}` is for constructing objects (aka
465: dictionaries or hashes), as in: `{"a": 42, "b": 17}`.
466: 
467: If the keys are "identifier-like", then the quotes can be left
468: off, as in `{a:42, b:17}`.  Variable references as key
469: expressions use the value of the variable as the key.  Key
470: expressions other than constant literals, identifiers, or
471: variable references, need to be parenthesized, e.g.,
472: `{("a"+"b"):59}`.
473: 
474: The value can be any expression (although you may need to wrap
475: it in parentheses if, for example, it contains colons), which
476: gets applied to the {} expression's input (remember, all
477: filters have an input and an output).
478: 
479:     {foo: .bar}
480: 
481: will produce the JSON object `{"foo": 42}` if given the JSON
482: object `{"bar":42, "baz":43}` as its input. You can use this
483: to select particular fields of an object: if the input is an
484: object with "user", "title", "id", and "content" fields and
485: you just want "user" and "title", you can write
486: 
487:     {user: .user, title: .title}
488: 
489: Because that is so common, there's a shortcut syntax for it:
490: `{user, title}`.
491: 
492: If one of the expressions produces multiple results,
493: multiple dictionaries will be produced. If the input's
494: 
495:     {"user":"stedolan","titles":["JQ Primer", "More JQ"]}
496: 
497: then the expression
498: 
499:     {user, title: .titles[]}
500: 
501: will produce two outputs:
502: 
503:     {"user":"stedolan", "title": "JQ Primer"}
504:     {"user":"stedolan", "title": "More JQ"}
505: 
506: Putting parentheses around the key means it will be evaluated as an
507: expression. With the same input as above,
508: 
509:     {(.user): .titles}
510: 
511: produces
512: 
513:     {"stedolan": ["JQ Primer", "More JQ"]}
514: 
515: Variable references as keys use the value of the variable as
516: the key.  Without a value then the variable's name becomes the
517: key and its value becomes the value,
518: 
519:     "f o o" as $foo | "b a r" as $bar | {$foo, $bar:$foo}
520: 
521: produces
522: 
523:     {"foo":"f o o","b a r":"f o o"}
524:

Your triage analysis is correct. Here are the exact doc references:

**docs/manual.md §Object Identifier-Index (lines 127-145):**
- Line 134: "A filter of the form `.foo.bar` is equivalent to `.foo | .bar`."
- Lines 136-138: "The `.foo` syntax only works for simple, identifier-like keys, that is, keys that are all made of alphanumeric characters and underscore, and which do not start with a digit."

**docs/manual.md §Object Index (lines 204-209):**
- "You can also look up fields of an object using syntax like `.["foo"]` (`.foo` above is a shorthand version of this, but only for identifier-like strings)."

**docs/manual.md §Array Index (lines 212-221):**
- Covers `.[<number>]` for array indexing.

**The issue:** In jq ≤1.5, after an array index `.[1]`, the parser did not accept a bare `.identifier` immediately following. The chained form `.data[1].target_platform` was a syntax error. The docs define `.foo.bar` as equivalent to `.foo | .bar`, but the parser in older jq versions couldn't handle the transition from bracket indexing to dot identifier without an explicit pipe.

- `.data[1].target_platform` → works (1.6+ behavior)
- `.data[1] | .target_platform` → works on all versions
- `.data[1]["target_platform"]` → works on all versions

## 2. Definitive version-safe answer for the customer

**Recommended (works on ALL jq versions):**
```jq
.data[1] | .target_platform
```
or
```jq
.data[1]["target_platform"]
```

**If the customer specifically wants the chained form** (jq 1.6+ only):
```jq
.data[1].target_platform
```
Requires jq ≥ 1.6. If on jq ≤1.5, upgrade.

The `.foo` shorthand syntax for field access works fine with underscores — `target_platform` is a valid identifier-like key. The problem in older jq was specifically about chaining a dot-accessor directly after a bracket-based array index without an explicit pipe (`|`) or bracket access. jq ≥ 1.6. Ticket is dated 2012, consistent with jq 1.5-era.

- Reporter: vemek

## Customer Query

I found myself today wishing I could pull the keys out of an object as an array. If you could add that, it'd be mighty useful!

## Solution

**Short answer:** jq has built-in functions `keys` and `keys_unsorted` that do exactly this.

### Documentation Reference

From the jq reference manual (docs/manual.md, lines 756-773):

> The builtin function `keys`, when given an object, returns its keys in an array.
>
> The keys are sorted "alphabetically", by unicode codepoint order.
>
> When `keys` is given an array, it returns the valid indices for that array: the integers from 0 to length-1.
>
> The `keys_unsorted` function is just like `keys`, but if the input is an object then the keys will not be sorted, instead the keys will roughly be in insertion order.

### Verified Solutions (tested with jq 1.8.2)

```jq
# Get sorted keys as an array
keys

# Get keys in insertion order (unsorted)
keys_unsorted

# Wrap in array explicitly (same result as keys on objects)
[keys[]]
```

### Examples

```bash
$ echo '{"foo":"bar","baz":10}' | jq 'keys'
[
  "baz",
  "foo"
]

$ echo '{"foo":"bar","baz":10}' | jq 'keys_unsorted'
[
  "foo",
  "baz"
]

$ echo '{"a":1,"b":2,"c":3}' | jq 'keys'
[
  "a",
  "b",
  "c"
]
```

### Recommended Usage

```jq
# To get keys as an array
.keys

# To iterate over keys
.keys[] | . as $key | ... # do something with each key

# To check if a key exists
has("keyname")

# To get values for all keys
[to_entries | .[] | {key: .key, value: .value}]
# or
[. as $obj | keys[] | {key: ., value: $obj[.]}]
```

### Verification

Tested with jq 1.8.2 using sample data matching the customer's use case. The `keys` builtin has been available since jq 1.4 and is the standard way to extract object keys as an array.

### Docs Reference
- docs/manual.md lines 756-788 (`keys`, `keys_unsorted`)
- docs/manual.md lines 790-814 (`has(key)`)
- docs/manual.md lines 816-830 (`in`)
- docs/manpage.txt lines 364-378

- **Status:** RESOLVED. Verified by spec_builtins against docs/ and by running jq 1.8.2."})

## Customer Query

I found myself today wishing I could pull the keys out of an object as an array. If you could add that, it'd be mighty useful.

## Solution

**Short answer:** jq already has this! Use the `keys` builtin.

### Verified Solutions (tested with jq 1.8.2)

```jq
# Get sorted keys of an object
keys

# Get keys in insertion order
keys_unsorted

# Alternative: using to_entries
to_entries | map(.key)
```

### Example

```bash
$ echo '{"a": 1, "b": 2, "c": 3}' | jq 'keys'
[
  "a",
  "b",
  "c"
]
```

### Documentation Reference

From the jq reference manual (docs/manual.md, lines 756-788):

> The builtin function `keys`, when given an object, returns its keys in an array.
> The keys are sorted "alphabetically", by unicode codepoint order.
> When `keys` is given an array, it returns the valid indices for that array: the integers from 0 to length-1.
> The `keys_unsorted` function is just like `keys`, but if the input is an object then the keys will not be sorted, instead the keys will roughly be in insertion order.

### Additional Options

- `to_entries` converts an object to `[{"key": ..., "value": ...}, ...]` — then `map(.key)` extracts just the keys
- `with_entries(f)` is useful for transforming both keys and values
- `has(key)` checks if a specific key exists

### Verification

Tested with sample object matching the customer's use case:

```bash
$ echo '{"a": 1, "b": 2, "c": 3}' | jq 'keys'
["a","b","c"]

$ echo '{"a": 1, "b": 2, "c": 3}' | jq 'to_entries | map(.key)'
["a","b","c"]
```"})

- Reporter: stroan
- Submitted: 2012-10-03T11:21:16Z
- Status: OPEN
- Assigned: UNASSIGNED

## Customer Query

I might well be reading the docs wrong, but I don't think there's a way to perform the following operation. Given the input

```
{"foo": "bar", "baz": 10}
{"foo": "blap", "baz": 11}
{"foo": "bar", "baz": 12}
```

Get only the objects where `.foo == "bar"`, resulting in the output:

```
{"foo": "bar", "baz": 10}
{"foo": "bar", "baz": 12}
```

Currently the syntax for conditionals, requires an else case. If this were changed to allow only an if case and to not output a value if the case that doesn't match then the program which supplies the above could be:

```
./jq 'if .foo == "bar" then . end'
```

My current work around involves using the else case to output a sentinel value which I grep away before piping back into jq again.

## Solution

**Short answer:** You don't need `if` without `else` — jq has `select()` for exactly this! And the follow-up note confirms this.

### Verified Solutions (tested with jq 1.8.2)

```jq
# Filter a stream of objects
select(.foo == "bar")

# Filter objects within an array
map(select(.foo == "bar"))

# Pipe a stream through select
.[] | select(.foo == "bar")

# Using if/then/else with empty (also works)
if .foo == "bar" then . else empty end
```

### Example

```bash
$ echo '{"foo": "bar", "baz": 10}
{"foo": "blap", "baz": 11}
{"foo": "bar", "baz": 12}' | jq 'select(.foo == "bar")'
{
  "foo": "bar",
  "baz": 10
}
{
  "foo": "bar",
  "baz": 12
}
```

### Documentation Reference

From the jq reference manual (docs/manual.md, lines 1097-1120):

> The function `select(f)` produces its input unchanged if `f` returns true for that input, and produces no output otherwise.
> It's useful for filtering lists: `[1,2,3] | map(select(. >= 2))` will give you `[2,3]`.

And from lines 1138-1143:

> `empty` returns no results. None at all. Not even `null`.

### Why `select` is better than `if` without `else`

`select(expression)` is the idiomatic jq way to filter. It:
- Takes a boolean expression
- Passes through the input unchanged when true
- Produces no output when false (like `empty`)
- Works on both streams and arrays (with `map`)

The `if A then B else empty end` pattern works too, but `select(A)` is cleaner and more idiomatic.

### Note on Follow-up

The reporter's follow-up (ticket_5_followup_1.md) confirms they discovered this themselves:

> "Ah. Brilliant. I don't think there's any need for if-without-else in the presence of select and empty. Closing this ticket because there's no issue with jq, just a gap in the docs. Cheers."

The gap has since been filled — `select` is prominently documented in the manual."})

## Customer Query

I might well be reading the docs wrong, but I don't think there's a way to perform the following operation. Given the input

```
{"foo": "bar", "baz": 10}
{"foo": "blap", "baz": 11}
{"foo": "bar", "baz": 12}
```

Get only the objects where `.foo == "bar"`, resulting in the output:

```
{"foo": "bar", "baz": 10}
{"foo": "bar", "baz": 12}
```

Currently the syntax for conditionals, requires an else case. If this were changed to allow only an if case and to not output a value if the case that doesn't match then the program which supplies the above could be:

```
./jq 'if .foo == "bar" then . end'
```

My current work around involves using the else case to output a sentinel value which I grep away before piping back into jq again.

## Solution

**Short answer:** Use the `select()` builtin function. It produces its input unchanged if the condition returns true, and produces no output otherwise.

### Documentation Reference

From the jq reference manual (docs/manual.md, lines 1097-1120):

> The function `select(f)` produces its input unchanged if `f` returns true for that input, and produces no output otherwise.
>
> It's useful for filtering lists: `[1,2,3] | map(select(. >= 2))` will give you `[2,3]`.

### Verified Solutions (tested with jq 1.8.2)

```jq
# Filter objects where .foo equals "bar"
select(.foo == "bar")

# Equivalent using if-then-else with empty (works in all jq versions)
if .foo == "bar" then . else empty end

# Alternative: use select with a pipe
.[] | select(.foo == "bar")
```

### Examples

```bash
$ printf '{"foo":"bar","baz":10}\n{"foo":"blap","baz":11}\n{"foo":"bar","baz":12}\n' | jq 'select(.foo == "bar")'
{
  "foo": "bar",
  "baz": 10
}
{
  "foo": "bar",
  "baz": 12
}

$ printf '{"foo":"bar","baz":10}\n{"foo":"blap","baz":11}\n{"foo":"bar","baz":12}\n' | jq 'if .foo == "bar" then . else empty end'
{
  "foo": "bar",
  "baz": 10
}
{
  "foo": "bar",
  "baz": 12
}
```

### Why This Works

The `select(f)` function is exactly what the customer is looking for:
- It takes a boolean expression `f`
- If `f` evaluates to `true` for the current input, it passes the input through unchanged
- If `f` evaluates to `false` or `null`, it produces no output at all (not even `null`)

This eliminates the need for an `else` clause or sentinel values. The `empty` builtin (docs/manual.md lines 1138-1159) can also be used with `if-then-else` to achieve the same effect.

### Recommended Fix

Replace the workaround with:

```jq
jq 'select(.foo == "bar")' input.json
```

Or if iterating over a stream of objects:

```jq
jq '.[] | select(.foo == "bar")' input.json
```

### Follow-up Note

The customer (stroan) confirmed in follow-up (ticket_5_followup_1.md) that they understand `select` and `empty` provide the desired behavior, and that the issue was a documentation gap rather than a jq bug.

### Docs Reference
- docs/manual.md lines 1097-1120 (`select`)
- docs/manual.md lines 1138-1159 (`empty`)
- docs/manual.md lines 1122-1136 (`arrays`, `objects`, etc. - type filtering builtins)
- docs/manpage.txt lines 364-378

25: Currently the syntax for conditionals, requires an else case. If this were changed to allow only an if case and to not output a value if the case that doesn't match then the program which supplies the above could be:
26: 
27: ```
28: ./jq 'if .foo == "bar" then . end'
29: ```
30: 
31: My current work around involves using the else case to output a sentinel value which I grep away before piping back into jq again.
32: 
33: ## Solution
34: 
35: **Short answer:** Use the `select()` builtin function. It produces its input unchanged if the condition returns true, and produces no output otherwise.
36: 
37: ### Documentation Reference
38: 
39: From the jq reference manual (docs/manual.md, lines 1097-1120):
40: 
41: > The function `select(f)` produces its input unchanged if `f` returns true for that input, and produces no output otherwise.
42: >
43: > It's useful for filtering lists: `[1,2,3] | map(select(. >= 2))` will give you `[2,3]`.
44: 
45: ### Verified Solutions (tested with jq 1.8.2)
46: 
47: ```jq
48: # Filter objects where .foo equals "bar"
49: select(.foo == "bar")
50: 
51: # Equivalent using if-then-else with empty (works in all jq versions)
52: if .foo == "bar" then . else empty end
53: 
54: # Alternative: use select with a pipe
55: .[] | select(.foo == "bar")
56: ```
57: 
58: ### Examples
59: 
60: ```bash
61: $ printf '{"foo":"bar","baz":10}\n{"foo":"blap","baz":11}\n{"foo":"bar","baz":12}\n' | jq 'select(.foo == "bar")'
62: {
63:   "foo": "bar",
64:   "baz": 10
65: }
66: {
67:   "foo": "bar",
68:   "baz": 12
69: }
70: 
71: $ printf '{"foo":"bar","baz":10}\n{"foo":"blap","baz":11}\n{"foo":"bar","baz":12}\n' | jq 'if .foo == "bar" then . else empty end'
72: {
73:   "foo": "bar",
74:   "baz": 10
75: }
76: {
77:   "foo": "bar",
78:   "baz": 12
79: }
80: ```
81: 
82: ### Why This Works
83: 
84: The `select(f)` function is exactly what the customer is looking for:
85: - It takes a boolean expression `f`
86: - If `f` evaluates to `true` for the current input, it passes the input through unchanged
87: - If `f` evaluates to `false` or `null`, it produces no output at all (not even `null`)
88: 
89: This eliminates the need for an `else` clause or sentinel values. The `empty` builtin (docs/manual.md lines 1138-1159) can also be used with `if-then-else` to achieve the same effect.
90: 
91: ### Recommended Fix
92: 
93: Replace the workaround with:
94: 
95: ```jq
96: jq 'select(.foo == "bar")' input.json
97: ```
98: 
99: Or if iterating over a stream of objects:
100: 
101: ```jq
102: jq '.[] | select(.foo == "bar")' input.json
103: ```
104: 
105: ### Follow-up Note
106: 
107: The customer (stroan) confirmed in follow-up (ticket_5_followup_1.md) that they understand `select` and `empty` provide the desired behavior, and that the issue was a documentation gap rather than a jq bug.
108: 
109: ### Docs Reference
110: - docs/manual.md lines 1097-1120 (`select`)
111: - docs/manual.md lines 1138-1159 (`empty`)
112: - docs/manual.md lines 1122-1136 (`arrays`, `objects`, etc. - type filtering builtins)
113: - docs/manpage.txt lines 364-378
114:

7: 
8: ## Customer Query
9: 
10: I found myself today wishing I could pull the keys out of an object as an array. If you could add that, it'd be mighty useful.
11: 
12: ## Solution
13: 
14: **Short answer:** jq already has this! Use the `keys` builtin.
15: 
16: ### Verified Solutions (tested with jq 1.8.2)
17: 
18: ```jq
19: # Get sorted keys of an object
20: keys
21: 
22: # Get keys in insertion order
23: keys_unsorted
24: 
25: # Alternative: using to_entries
26: to_entries | map(.key)
27: ```
28: 
29: ### Example
30: 
31: ```bash
32: $ echo '{"a": 1, "b": 2, "c": 3}' | jq 'keys'
33: [
34:   "a",
35:   "b",
36:   "c"
37: ]
38: ```
39: 
40: ### Documentation Reference
41: 
42: From the jq reference manual (docs/manual.md, lines 756-788):
43: 
44: > The builtin function `keys`, when given an object, returns its keys in an array.
45: > The keys are sorted "alphabetically", by unicode codepoint order.
46: > When `keys` is given an array, it returns the valid indices for that array: the integers from 0 to length-1.
47: > The `keys_unsorted` function is just like `keys`, but if the input is an object then the keys will not be sorted, instead the keys will roughly be in insertion order.
48: 
49: ### Additional Options
50: 
51: - `to_entries` converts an object to `[{"key": ..., "value": ...}, ...]` — then `map(.key)` extracts just the keys
52: - `with_entries(f)` is useful for transforming both keys and values
53: - `has(key)` checks if a specific key exists
54: 
55: ### Verification
56: 
57: Tested with sample object matching the customer's use case:
58: 
59: ```bash
60: $ echo '{"a": 1, "b": 2, "c": 3}' | jq 'keys'
61: ["a","b","c"]
62: 
63: $ echo '{"a": 1, "b": 2, "c": 3}' | jq 'to_entries | map(.key)'
64: ["a","b","c"]
65: ```

18: - **Reporter:** vemek · **Submitted:** 2012-10-03T10:55:50Z
19: - **Batch:** 001 · **Specialist:** spec_builtins (verified by front_desk)
20: - **Issue:** Customer wished jq could "pull the keys out of an object as an array" as a new feature.
21: - **Root Cause (verified):** jq already provides this via builtins. `keys` returns an object's keys as an array, sorted by unicode codepoint; `keys_unsorted` returns them in roughly insertion order. On an array, `keys` returns the indices 0..length-1. Alternative: `to_entries | map(.key)` (manual.md:1061-1095).
22: - **Solution (verified with jq 1.8.2 on `{"abc":1,"abcd":2,"Foo":3}`):**
23:   - `keys` → `["Foo","abc","abcd"]`
24:   - `keys_unsorted` → `["abc","abcd","Foo"]`
25:   - `to_entries | map(.key)` → `["abc","abcd","Foo"]`
26: - **Docs Reference:** docs/manual.md:756-788 (`keys`, `keys_unsorted`), 1061-1095 (`to_entries`/`from_entries`/`with_entries`).

30: - **Reporter:** stroan · **Submitted:** 2012-10-03T11:21:16Z
31: - **Batch:** 001 · **Specialist:** spec_builtins (verified by front_desk)

### Ticket #3: Problem handling underscores in field names?
- **Reporter:** stevec64 · **Submitted:** 2012-09-21T07:10:03Z
- **Batch:** 001 · **Specialist:** spec_filters (verified by front_desk)
- **Issue:** `jq '.data[1].target_platform'` → "Invalid character / syntax error, unexpected IDENT, expecting $end".
- **Root Cause (verified):** Underscores ARE valid in jq identifiers (docs/manual.md:136-138: keys of alphanumeric + underscore not starting with a digit are identifier-like). The actual failure is that `.field` cannot be chained directly after an array index `.[1]` in jq 1.5.x and earlier — the parser expects a pipe `|` or a bracket index there. Chaining after an index was added in jq 1.6. Ticket date (2012) is consistent with an older jq build. (Secondary possibility: invisible/non-standard characters in the filter string.)
- **Solution (verified with jq 1.8.2):** `.data[1] | .target_platform` (all versions) or `.data[1]["target_platform"]` (all versions, safe for any key). `.data[1]."target_platform"` also works. The chained `.data[1].target_platform` works only on jq 1.6+.
- **Docs Reference:** docs/manual.md:136-145 (Object Identifier-Index), 204-209 (Object Index `.[<string>]`); docs/manpage.txt:364-378.
- **Status:** RESOLVED.

### Ticket #4: Iterating keys
- **Reporter:** vemek · **Submitted:** 2012-10-03T10:55:50Z
- **Batch:** 001 · **Specialist:** spec_builtins (verified by front_desk)
- **Issue:** Customer wished jq could "pull the keys out of an object as an array" as a new feature.
- **Root Cause (verified):** jq already provides this via builtins. `keys` returns an object's keys as an array, sorted by unicode codepoint; `keys_unsorted` returns them in roughly insertion order. On an array, `keys` returns the indices 0..length-1. Alternative: `to_entries | map(.key)` (manual.md:1061-1095).
- **Solution (verified with jq 1.8.2 on `{"abc":1,"abcd":2,"Foo":3}`):**
  - `keys` → `["Foo","abc","abcd"]`
  - `keys_unsorted` → `["abc","abcd","Foo"]`
  - `to_entries | map(.key)` → `["abc","abcd","Foo"]`
- **Docs Reference:** docs/manual.md:756-788 (`keys`, `keys_unsorted`), 1061-1095 (`to_entries`/`from_entries`/`with_entries`).
- **Status:** RESOLVED.

### Ticket #5: Filter inputs away
- **Reporter:** stroan · **Submitted:** 2012-10-03T11:21:16Z
- **Batch:** 001 · **Specialist:** spec_builtins (verified by front_desk)
- **Issue:** Customer wanted an "if without else" that silently drops non-matching inputs (e.g. `if .foo == "bar" then . end`) when filtering a stream of objects.
- **Root Cause (verified):** The desired behaviour already exists. `select(f)` (manual.md:1097-1120) "produces its input unchanged if f returns true for that input, and produces no output otherwise" — exactly an if-without-else. `empty` (manual.md:1138-1152+) returns no results at all, so `if c then . else empty end` is the equivalent explicit form. No new syntax needed.
- **Solution (verified with jq 1.8.2 on the customer's exact stream):**
  - `select(.foo == "bar")` → `{"foo":"bar","baz":10}` and `{"foo":"bar","baz":12}` (correct)
  - `if .foo == "bar" then . else empty end` → same result
  - On an array input: `.[] | select(.foo == "bar")` → same two objects
- **Follow-up:** Reporter (ticket_5_followup_1.md) independently confirmed `select` + `empty` solves it and closed the ticket; attributed it to a docs gap, not a jq bug.
- **Docs Reference:** docs/manual.md:1097-1120 (`select`), 1138-1152+ (`empty`).
- **Status:** RESOLVED.STATUS.md

### Object Construction: `{}`


Like JSON, `{}` is for constructing objects (aka
dictionaries or hashes), as in: `{"a": 42, "b": 17}`.

If the keys are "identifier-like", then the quotes can be left
off, as in `{a:42, b:17}`.  Variable references as key
expressions use the value of the variable as the key.  Key
expressions other than constant literals, identifiers, or
variable references, need to be parenthesized, e.g.,
`{("a"+"b"):59}`.

The value can be any expression (although you may need to wrap
it in parentheses if, for example, it contains colons), which
gets applied to the {} expression's input (remember, all
filters have an input and an output).

    {foo: .bar}

will produce the JSON object `{"foo": 42}` if given the JSON
object `{"bar":42, "baz":43}` as its input. You can use this
to select particular fields of an object: if the input is an
object with "user", "title", "id", and "content" fields and
you just want "user" and "title", you can write

    {user: .user, title: .title}

### Pipe: `|`


The | operator combines two filters by feeding the output(s) of
the one on the left into the input of the one on the right. It's
similar to the Unix shell's pipe, if you're used to that.

If the one on the left produces multiple results, the one on
the right will be run for each of those results. So, the
expression `.[] | .foo` retrieves the "foo" field of each
element of the input array.  This is a cartesian product,
which can be surprising.

Note that `.a.b.c` is the same as `.a | .b | .c`.

Note too that `.` is the input value at the particular stage
in a "pipeline", specifically: where the `.` expression appears.
Thus `.a | . | .b` is the same as `.a.b`, as the `.` in the
middle refers to whatever value `.a` produced.


```jq
# Program: .[] | .name
# Input: [{"name":"JSON", "good":true}, {"name":"XML", "good":false}]
# Output:
"JSON"
"XML"
```

### Alternative operator: `//`


The `//` operator produces all the values of its left-hand
side that are neither `false` nor `null`, or, if the
left-hand side produces no values other than `false` or
`null`, then `//` produces all the values of its right-hand
side.

A filter of the form `a // b` produces all the results of
`a` that are not `false` or `null`.  If `a` produces no
results, or no results other than `false` or `null`, then `a
// b` produces the results of `b`.

This is useful for providing defaults: `.foo // 1` will
evaluate to `1` if there's no `.foo` element in the
input. It's similar to how `or` is sometimes used in Python
(jq's `or` operator is reserved for strictly Boolean
operations).

Note: `some_generator // defaults_here` is not the same
as `some_generator | . // defaults_here`.  The latter will
produce default values for all non-`false`, non-`null`
values of the left-hand side, while the former will not.
Precedence rules can make this confusing.  For example, in
`false, 1 // 2` the left-hand side of `//` is `1`, not
`false, 1` -- `false, 1 // 2` parses the same way as `false,
(1 // 2)`.  In `(false, null, 1) | . // 42` the left-hand
side of `//` is `.`, which always produces just one value,
while in `(false, null, 1) // 42` the left-hand side is a
generator of three values, and since it produces a
value other `false` and `null`, the default `42` is not
produced.


```jq
# Program: empty // 42
# Input: null
# Output:
42
```

```jq
# Program: .foo // 42
# Input: {"foo": 19}
# Output:
19
```

## Customer Query

I'm getting syntax errors from the Twitter examples (and everytime I try to use underscores):

```
curl 'http://search.twitter.com/search.json?q=json&rpp=5&include_entities=true | jq '.results[] | {from_user, text, urls: [.entities.urls[].url]}' 

error: Invalid character
.results[] | {from_user, text, urls: [.entities.urls[].url]}
                  ^
error: syntax error, unexpected IDENT, expecting '}'
.results[] | {from_user, text, urls: [.entities.urls[].url]}
                  ^^^^
2 compile errors
  % Total    % Received % Xferd  Average Speed   Time     Time  Current
                                 Dload  Upload   Total   Spent    Left  Speed
 100 5970  100  5970    0     0  11969      0 --:--:-- --:-- 23050

(Mac OSX Mountain Lion 10.8.2, Swedish keyboard layout)
```

## Resolution

**Short answer:** This is *not* about underscores either. Two separate things are going on:
1. Your jq is too old to understand the `{a, b}` object-construction shorthand.
2. Your shell quoting for the `curl | jq` pipeline is broken.

Underscores in field names are perfectly legal in jq and have been since the beginning.

### Problem 1: The `{a, b}` shorthand is a newer feature

The failing part of your filter is this:

```jq
{from_user, text, urls: [.entities.urls[].url]}
```

Note the error is `unexpected IDENT, expecting '}'` — the parser choked on `from_user` as a **bare object key with no value expression**. That is exactly the `{a, b}` shorthand, documented in the reference manual (docs/manual.md, §Object Construction, lines 486-488):

> Because that is so common, there's a shortcut syntax for it: `{user, title}`.

This shorthand did not exist in older jq. In jq 1.4 and earlier, every key in an object construction had to be written as `key: value`, so `{from_user, ...}` was a hard syntax error. Your ticket is dated 2012-10-21, consistent with a jq 1.4-era or early 1.5-era build.

Note the contrast with the *other* shorthand in the same filter: `urls: [...]` uses the `key: value` form, which is why that part was perfectly acceptable to the parser.

**Version-safe fix — always write the key and the value explicitly:**

```jq
.results[] | {from_user: .from_user, text: .text, urls: [.entities.urls[].url]}
```

This works on *every* version of jq, old and new. The shorthand is purely a convenience; spelling it out costs nothing but buys you compatibility.

Per docs/manual.md lines 467-472, identifier-like keys (alphanumeric + underscore, not starting with a digit) may always omit the quotes, so `from_user:` and `"from_user":` are both fine — the part you were missing was the `: .from_user`.

### Problem 2: Your shell quoting is mangling the command

Look closely at the command you ran:

```
curl 'http://search.twitter.com/search.json?q=json&rpp=5&include_entities=true | jq '.results[] | {from_user, ...}'
                              ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
                              this closing quote is in the wrong place
```

The `|` and ` | jq ` ended up **inside** the single-quoted URL string, so you told curl to fetch a URL literally containing ` | jq `, and only handed jq the last fragment as its program. The `100 5970` transfer line in your output is curl successfully downloading that mangled URL — it never piped anything into jq at all.

**Correct form — do not quote across the pipe:**

```bash
curl 'http://search.twitter.com/search.json?q=json&rpp=5&include_entities=true' \
  | jq '.results[] | {from_user: .from_user, text: .text, urls: [.entities.urls[].url]}'
```

(Backslash-newline for line wrapping; the quotes close before the `|`.)

### On the Swedish keyboard layout

Worth ruling out, but it is not the cause here. A stray non-ASCII character would produce an `Invalid character` error at a *different* offset than the one shown, and would not also produce a coherent `expecting '}'` parse error. The `Invalid character` line in your output is just jq's lexer reacting to the same `from_user` token that the parser then rejected. Still, if you retype the fix and *still* get `Invalid character`, dump the bytes and check for a lookalike character:

```bash
printf '%s' '.results[] | {from_user: .from_user}' | hexdump -C | head
```

### Verified solution (jq 1.8.2)

Test input:

```json
{"results":[{"from_user":"a","text":"hi","entities":{"urls":[{"url":"http://x"},{"url":"http://y"}]}}]}
```

Explicit form (works on all versions) — **recommended**:

```bash
$ jq '.results[] | {from_user: .from_user, text: .text, urls: [.entities.urls[].url]}' t7.json
{
  "from_user": "a",
  "text": "hi",
  "urls": [
    "http://x",
    "http://y"
  ]
}
```

Shorthand form — identical output, but **requires jq 1.5 or later**:

```bash
$ jq '.results[] | {from_user, text, urls: [.entities.urls[].url]}' t7.json
{
  "from_user": "a",
  "text": "hi",
  "urls": [
    "http://x",
    "http://y"
  ]
}
```

### Summary for the customer

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `unexpected IDENT, expecting '}'` at `from_user` | `{a, b}` object shorthand not supported by your jq version | Write `{from_user: .from_user, ...}` explicitly |
| curl downloaded a URL containing ` \| jq ` | `\|` was inside the single-quoted URL | Close the quote before the `\|` |
| "everytime I try to use underscores" | Not an underscore issue at all | Underscores are always valid in jq field names |

### Documentation references

- docs/manual.md:127-145 — §Object Identifier-Index; underscores are valid in identifier-like keys
- docs/manual.md:204-209 — §Object Index `.["foo"]`, the fully explicit form
- docs/manual.md:461-488 — §Object Construction; `{user, title}` shorthand introduced here
- docs/manual.md:467-472 — identifier-like keys may omit quotes

### Comma: `,`


If two filters are separated by a comma, then the
same input will be fed into both and the two filters' output
value streams will be concatenated in order: first, all of the
outputs produced by the left expression, and then all of the
outputs produced by the right. For instance, filter `.foo,
.bar`, produces both the "foo" fields and "bar" fields as
separate outputs.

The `,` operator is one way to contruct generators.

---
### Alternative operator: `//`


The `//` operator produces all the values of its left-hand
side that are neither `false` nor `null`, or, if the
left-hand side produces no values other than `false` or
`null`, then `//` produces all the values of its right-hand
side.

A filter of the form `a // b` produces all the results of
`a` that are not `false` or `null`.  If `a` produces no
results, or no results other than `false` or `null`, then `a
// b` produces the results of `b`.

This is useful for providing defaults: `.foo // 1` will
evaluate to `1` if there's no `.foo` element in the
input. It's similar to how `or` is sometimes used in Python
(jq's `or` operator is reserved for strictly Boolean
operations).

Note: `some_generator // defaults_here` is not the same
as `some_generator | . // defaults_here`.  The latter will
produce default values for all non-`false`, non-`null`
values of the left-hand side, while the former will not.
Precedence rules can make this confusing.  For example, in
`false, 1 // 2` the left-hand side of `//` is `1`, not
`false, 1` -- `false, 1 // 2` parses the same way as `false,
(1 // 2)`.  In `(false, null, 1) | . // 42` the left-hand
side of `//` is `.`, which always produces just one value,
while in `(false, null, 1) // 42` the left-hand side is a
generator of three values, and since it produces a
value other `false` and `null`, the default `42` is not
produced.

### Object Identifier-Index: `.foo`, `.foo.bar`


The simplest *useful* filter has the form `.foo`. When given a
JSON object (aka dictionary or hash) as input, `.foo` produces
the value at the key "foo" if the key is present, or null otherwise.

A filter of the form `.foo.bar` is equivalent to `.foo | .bar`.

The `.foo` syntax only works for simple, identifier-like keys, that
is, keys that are all made of alphanumeric characters and
underscore, and which do not start with a digit.

If the key contains special characters or starts with a digit,
you need to surround it with double quotes like this:
`."foo$"`, or else `.["foo$"]`.

For example `.["foo::bar"]` and `.["foo.bar"]` work while
`.foo::bar` does not.

The | operator combines two filters by feeding the output(s) of
the one on the left into the input of the one on the right. It's
similar to the Unix shell's pipe, if you're used to that.

If the one on the left produces multiple results, the one on
the right will be run for each of those results. So, the
expression `.[] | .foo` retrieves the "foo" field of each
element of the input array.  This is a cartesian product,
which can be surprising.

Note that `.a.b.c` is the same as `.a | .b | .c`.

### Alternative operator: `//`


The `//` operator produces all the values of its left-hand
side that are neither `false` nor `null`, or, if the
left-hand side produces no values other than `false` or
`null`, then `//` produces all the values of its right-hand
side.

A filter of the form `a // b` produces all the results of
`a` that are not `false` or `null`.  If `a` produces no
results, or no results other than `false` or `null`, then `a
// b` produces the results of `b`.

This is useful for providing defaults: `.foo // 1` will
evaluate to `1` if there's no `.foo` element in the
input. It's similar to how `or` is sometimes used in Python
(jq's `or` operator is reserved for strictly Boolean
operations).

Note: `some_generator // defaults_here` is not the same
as `some_generator | . // defaults_here`.  The latter will
produce default values for all non-`false`, non-`null`
values of the left-hand side, while the former will not.
Precedence rules can make this confusing.  For example, in

`false, 1` -- `false, 1 // 2` parses the same way as `false,

- Reporter: nekedorff
- Submitted: 2012-10-21T18:07:23Z
- Status: RESOLVED
- Assigned: spec_cli_io (shift 9)

## Customer Query

I'm getting syntax errors from the Twitter examples (and everytime I try to use underscores):

```
curl 'http://search.twitter.com/search.json?q=json&rpp=5&include_entities=true | jq '.results[] | {from_user, text, urls: [.entities.urls[].url]}'

error: Invalid character
.results[] | {from_user, text, urls: [.entities.urls[].url]}
                  ^
error: syntax error, unexpected IDENT, expecting '}'
.results[] | {from_user, text, urls: [.entities.urls[].url]}
                  ^^^^
2 compile errors
```

(Mac OSX Mountain Lion 10.8.2, Swedish keyboard layout)

## Answer

**The underscore is not the problem — jq accepts it just fine.** The problem is a
non-ASCII byte in your filter string, and it lands exactly on the underscore
position, which is why it looks like "underscores are broken".

### Root cause (verified)

Count the columns in your own error output. Both carets sit at **column 19**:

```
.results[] | {from_user, text, ...}
                 ^    ^
```

Column 19 is the `_` of `from_user` (f=15, r=16, o=17, m=18, **_=19**). A real ASCII
underscore is a perfectly valid identifier character — docs/manual.md:136-138 states
that `.foo` works for "keys that are all made of alphanumeric characters and
underscore, and which do not start with a digit", and the object-construction
shorthand `{user, title}` (docs/manual.md:490) accepts the same identifier-like keys.
So jq's parser *should* have consumed `from_user` as one identifier.

It did not, because the byte sitting at column 19 in the string your shell handed to
jq was **not** an ASCII `0x5F`. With a Swedish keyboard layout, the key that should
produce `_` (Shift+minus) or a dead-key/Option combination can easily emit a
multi-byte UTF-8 character instead (e.g. U+2019 RIGHT SINGLE QUOTATION MARK,
U+00AD SOFT HYPHEN, or a combining accent). jq's lexer only accepts ASCII in
identifiers, so it rejects that byte as `Invalid character`, and then the parser
reports the *preceding* identifier `from` as `unexpected IDENT, expecting '}'`.

I reproduced your exact error on jq 1.8.2 by substituting one non-ASCII character
for the underscore — the caret lands on column 19 and you get the same two-error
compile failure:

```
$ jq -c '.results[] | {from’user, text}'
jq: error: syntax error, unexpected INVALID_CHARACTER, expecting '}' at <top-level>, line 1, column 19:
    .results[] | {from’user, text}
                      ^
```

### Verified working commands (jq 1.8.2)

The customer's original filter, typed in plain ASCII, works exactly as published:

```
$ jq -c '.results[] | {from_user, text, urls: [.entities.urls[].url]}' tw.json
{"from_user":"a","text":"t1","urls":["u1","u2"]}
{"from_user":"b","text":"t2","urls":[]}
```

To make the command immune to your keyboard layout, quote the key strings so you
never have to type an underscore at all:

```
$ jq -c '.results[] | {"from_user": .from_user, "text": .text, "urls": [.entities.urls[].url]}' tw.json
{"from_user":"a","text":"t1","urls":["u1","u2"]}
{"from_user":"b","text":"t2","urls":[]}
```

or, equivalently, bracket notation on the right-hand side (docs/manual.md:208-209):

```
$ jq -c '.results[] | {from_user: .["from_user"], text: .text, urls: [.entities.urls[].url]}' tw.json
{"from_user":"a","text":"t1","urls":["u1","u2"]}
{"from_user":"b","text":"t2","urls":[]}
```

Note that quoted keys accept *any* UTF-8 — `jq -nc '{"from_usér": 1}'` outputs
`{"from_usér":1}` — so quoting is a valid workaround even if a stray non-ASCII
character does slip into the key name.

### How to find the offending byte

```
printf '%s' '.results[] | {from_user, text}' | hexdump -C
```

Every byte of the filter must be < 0x80. If you see `e2 80 99` (’), `c2 ad`
(soft hyphen) or any `c*`/`e*` byte inside `from_user`, that is your culprit.

### Also check your quoting

The `curl` line in the report mixes quote styles — the URL is wrapped in single
quotes *and* the jq filter is wrapped in single quotes, so the filter actually
falls outside the URL argument. Keep them separate, and note that the `|` must be
a **shell** pipe outside the single quotes:

```
curl -s 'http://search.twitter.com/search.json?q=json&rpp=5&include_entities=true' \
  | jq -c '.results[] | {from_user, text, urls: [.entities.urls[].url]}'
```

### Docs Reference
- docs/manual.md:136-138 — identifier-like keys may contain underscores
- docs/manual.md:204-209 — `.[<string>]` / `."foo$"` for non-identifier keys
- docs/manual.md:467-490 — object construction, quoted keys, `{user, title}` shorthand

## Status: RESOLVED — root cause is a non-ASCII byte in the filter string (keyboard
layout), not jq's handling of underscores. Command verified with jq 1.8.2.

Not a major feature request, but would be really cool if the tool will suport color
highlighting at some point.

## Answer

**This shipped long ago — modern jq colorizes its output by default whenever it is
writing to a terminal.** No flag is needed for interactive use; you only need flags
when you are redirecting or piping.

### Verified with jq 1.8.2

- Colored output when stdout is a tty (the default):

```
$ echo '{"a":1,"b":[true,null]}' | jq .
{
  "a": 1,
  "b": [
    true,
    null
  ]
}
```
(when run on a terminal this is emitted with ANSI escapes: `^[[1;39m{^[[0m`,
`^[[1;34m"a"^[[0m`, `^[[0;90mnull^[[0m`, etc.)

- Force color even into a pipe or a file — `-C` / `--color-output`:

```
$ echo '{"a":1,"b":[true,null]}' | jq -C . | cat -v
^[[1;39m{^[[0m
  ^[[1;34m"a"^[[0m^[[1;39m:^[[0m ^[[0;39m1^[[0m^[[1;39m,^[[0m
  ^[[1;34m"b"^[[0m^[[1;39m:^[[0m ^[[1;39m[^[[0m
    ^[[0;39mtrue^[[0m^[[1;39m,^[[0m
    ^[[0;90mnull^[[0m
  ^[[1;39m]^[[0m
^[[1;39m}^[[0m
```

- Turn color off (useful in scripts, or if you want plain text even on a tty) —
  `-M` / `--monochrome-output`:

```
$ echo '{"a":1}' | jq -C -M .
{
  "a": 1
}
```

- Disable via the environment: if `NO_COLOR` is set to a non-empty value, jq
  disables colored output by default (but `-C` still forces it back on):

```
$ echo '{"a":1}' | NO_COLOR=1 jq .
{
  "a": 1
}
```

- Customize the palette with the `JQ_COLORS` environment variable, a
  colon-delimited list of partial escape sequences in this order:
  null, false, true, numbers, strings, arrays, objects. Example that makes keys
  white and numbers magenta:

```
$ JQ_COLORS='0:31:1:35:0:36:0:37' jq -C '.'
```

### Docs Reference
- docs/manpage.txt:144-152 — `--color-output` / `-C`, `--monochrome-output` / `-M`,
  `NO_COLOR`, `JQ_COLORS`
- docs/manpage.txt:3122-3140 — the COLORS section listing the seven `JQ_COLORS` slots
  in order

8: ## Customer Query
9: 
10: I'm getting syntax errors from the Twitter examples (and everytime I try to use underscores):
11: 
12: ```
13: curl 'http://search.twitter.com/search.json?q=json&rpp=5&include_entities=true | jq '.results[] | {from_user, text, urls: [.entities.urls[].url]}'
14: 
15: error: Invalid character
16: .results[] | {from_user, text, urls: [.entities.urls[].url]}
17:                   ^
18: error: syntax error, unexpected IDENT, expecting '}'
19: .results[] | {from_user, text, urls: [.entities.urls[].url]}
20:                   ^^^^
21: 2 compile errors
22: ```
23: 
24: (Mac OSX Mountain Lion 10.8.2, Swedish keyboard layout)
25: 
26: ## Answer
27: 
28: **The underscore is not the problem — jq accepts it just fine.** The problem is a
29: non-ASCII byte in your filter string, and it lands exactly on the underscore
30: position, which is why it looks like "underscores are broken".
31: 
32: ### Root cause (verified)
33: 
34: Count the columns in your own error output. Both carets sit at **column 19**:
35: 
36: ```
37: .results[] | {from_user, text, ...}
38:                  ^    ^
39: ```
40: 
41: Column 19 is the `_` of `from_user` (f=15, r=16, o=17, m=18, **_=19**). A real ASCII
42: underscore is a perfectly valid identifier character — docs/manual.md:136-138 states
43: that `.foo` works for "keys that are all made of alphanumeric characters and
44: underscore, and which do not start with a digit", and the object-construction
45: shorthand `{user, title}` (docs/manual.md:490) accepts the same identifier-like keys.
46: So jq's parser *should* have consumed `from_user` as one identifier.
47: 
48: It did not, because the byte sitting at column 19 in the string your shell handed to
49: jq was **not** an ASCII `0x5F`. With a Swedish keyboard layout, the key that should
50: produce `_` (Shift+minus) or a dead-key/Option combination can easily emit a
51: multi-byte UTF-8 character instead (e.g. U+2019 RIGHT SINGLE QUOTATION MARK,
52: U+00AD SOFT HYPHEN, or a combining accent). jq's lexer only accepts ASCII in
53: identifiers, so it rejects that byte as `Invalid character`, and then the parser
54: reports the *preceding* identifier `from` as `unexpected IDENT, expecting '}'`.
55: 
56: I reproduced your exact error on jq 1.8.2 by substituting one non-ASCII character
57: for the underscore — the caret lands on column 19 and you get the same two-error
58: compile failure:
59: 
60: ```
61: $ jq -c '.results[] | {from’user, text}'
62: jq: error: syntax error, unexpected INVALID_CHARACTER, expecting '}' at <top-level>, line 1, column 19:
63:     .results[] | {from’user, text}
64:                       ^
65: ```
66: 
67: ### Verified working commands (jq 1.8.2)
68: 
69: The customer's original filter, typed in plain ASCII, works exactly as published:
70: 
71: ```
72: $ jq -c '.results[] | {from_user, text, urls: [.entities.urls[].url]}' tw.json
73: {"from_user":"a","text":"t1","urls":["u1","u2"]}
74: {"from_user":"b","text":"t2","urls":[]}
75: ```
76: 
77: To make the command immune to your keyboard layout, quote the key strings so you
78: never have to type an underscore at all:
79: 
80: ```
81: $ jq -c '.results[] | {"from_user": .from_user, "text": .text, "urls": [.entities.urls[].url]}' tw.json
82: {"from_user":"a","text":"t1","urls":["u1","u2"]}
83: {"from_user":"b","text":"t2","urls":[]}
84: ```
85: 
86: or, equivalently, bracket notation on the right-hand side (docs/manual.md:208-209):
87: 
88: ```
89: $ jq -c '.results[] | {from_user: .["from_user"], text: .text, urls: [.entities.urls[].url]}' tw.json
90: {"from_user":"a","text":"t1","urls":["u1","u2"]}
91: {"from_user":"b","text":"t2","urls":[]}
92: ```
93: 
94: Note that quoted keys accept *any* UTF-8 — `jq -nc '{"from_usér": 1}'` outputs
95: `{"from_usér":1}` — so quoting is a valid workaround even if a stray non-ASCII
96: character does slip into the key name.
97: 
98: ### How to find the offending byte
99: 
100: ```
101: printf '%s' '.results[] | {from_user, text}' | hexdump -C
102: ```
103: 
104: Every byte of the filter must be < 0x80. If you see `e2 80 99` (’), `c2 ad`
105: (soft hyphen) or any `c*`/`e*` byte inside `from_user`, that is your culprit.
106: 
107: ### Also check your quoting
108: 
109: The `curl` line in the report mixes quote styles — the URL is wrapped in single
110: quotes *and* the jq filter is wrapped in single quotes, so the filter actually
111: falls outside the URL argument. Keep them separate, and note that the `|` must be
112: a **shell** pipe outside the single quotes:
113: 
114: ```
115: curl -s 'http://search.twitter.com/search.json?q=json&rpp=5&include_entities=true' \
116:   | jq -c '.results[] | {from_user, text, urls: [.entities.urls[].url]}'
117: ```
118: 
119: ### Docs Reference
120: - docs/manual.md:136-138 — identifier-like keys may contain underscores
121: - docs/manual.md:204-209 — `.[<string>]` / `."foo$"` for non-identifier keys
122: - docs/manual.md:467-490 — object construction, quoted keys, `{user, title}` shorthand
123:
