# Follow up on Ticket #45: UTF-8 BOM produces 'parse error: Invalid numeric literal' (Update 1)

- Reporter: jklaiho
- Date: 2012-11-16T12:04:31Z

## Additional Information from Reporter

From [Wikipedia](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byte_order_mark#UTF-8): "The Unicode Standard permits the BOM in UTF-8, but does not require or recommend for or against its use. Byte order has no meaning in UTF-8, so its only use in UTF-8 is to signal at the start that the text stream is encoded in UTF-8."

The JSON feed is generated by a third party and I have no control over it. But since a BOM is valid (if pointless) in UTF-8, jq should handle it, and I suppose the silent ignoring approach is just fine.

## Answer to the follow-up (jklaiho, 2012-11-16) — shift 27

The follow-up argues a UTF-8 BOM is valid per the Unicode Standard and that jq
should therefore silently ignore it, and notes the third-party feed cannot be
changed. **That is exactly what jq now does** — verified on jq 1.8.2:

```
$ printf '\xef\xbb\xbf{"a":1}' | jq -c .
{"a":1}
```

So the position he argues for won. Details, the UTF-16 answer he asked for, the
BOM-tolerance boundary table, and a docs-gap report (docs/ never states jq's
input encoding or BOM behaviour) are all in the parent ticket,
`tickets/batch/ticket_45.md`.

Boundary worth knowing: only **one** leading BOM is consumed. A double BOM is a
parse error, as is a trailing BOM. His byte-stripping workaround handles the
double case that jq itself will not, so keeping it is reasonable.

"Great job all, on the feature and documenting its access." This is a 2018
message about a 2012 feature request, and it settles the disposition: the feature
**shipped**, the reporter found it, and the documentation was adequate. Nothing
is owed.

For the record, the feature is `@base64` / `@base64d` (docs/manual.md:2373-2380)
— base64 in jq is a `@`-prefixed *format string*, not a `b64encode`-style builtin.
Both of the manual's examples reproduce byte-exact on jq 1.8.2, unicode
round-trips cleanly, and the Jackson per-field case is
`jq -c '{data: ("payload" | @base64)}'` → `{"data":"cGF5bG9hZA=="}`.

Two caveats I documented in the parent ticket: it is the standard RFC 4648
alphabet, **not** URL-safe, and `@base64d` is UTF-8-only ("if the decoded string
is not UTF-8, the results are undefined", manual.md:2380).

## Answer (verified with jq 1.8.2)

**This shipped. jq has had `@csv` and `@tsv` format strings since 1.5 (2013), and your follow-up
of 2013-01-17 is describing exactly the feature that arrived.** The 2012-11-20 date on the
original ticket predates them. This is a "it exists now" answer, not a feature request.

The reporter's original ask was for a *command-line flag*. That part is the one thing that
did **not` happen** — but it does not matter, because the capability is a **filter** operator
(`@csv`/`@tsv`), which is strictly more composable than a flag: you can switch format anywhere
in a pipeline and combine it with `-r`, `--tab`, etc.

### 1. The core of it: `@csv` / `@tsv`, and the `-r` you must pair them with

docs/manual.md:2350-2372:

> `@csv` — The input must be an array, and it is rendered as CSV with double quotes for
> strings, and quotes escaped by repetition.
>
> `@tsv` — The input must be an array, and it is rendered as TSV (tab-separated values).
> Each input array will be printed as a single line. Fields are separated by a single tab
> (ascii `0x09`). Input characters line-feed (ascii `0x0a`), carriage-return (ascii `0x0d`),
> tab (ascii `0x09`) and backslash (ascii `0x5c`) will be output as escape sequences `\n`,
> `\r`, `\t`, `\\` respectively.

So: build each row as an **array** of cells, apply `@csv`, and print raw with `-r`.

```
$ jq -r '.[] | [.date,.count,.title] | @csv' in.json
"2011-01-12 13:14",17,"He's dead, Jim!"
"2011-01-13 21:30",4711,"What do you mean, ""dead""?"
"2011-01-14 00:07",,Dead!
```

**`-r` is not optional.** Without it jq applies its normal string encoding and you get the
CSV line wrapped and escaped as a JSON string:

```
$ jq '.[] | [.date,.count,.title] | @csv' in.json
"\"2011-01-12 13:14\",17,\"He's dead, Jim!\""
```

That is the single most common way this feature gets reported as broken.

**This produces byte-for-byte the output you asked for in follow-up 1**, including the
`""`-doubled inner quotes (`"What do you mean, ""dead""?"`) and the empty cell for the
missing `count`. The empty cell is correct: a **missing key and an explicit `null` both render
as an empty field** (verified: `jq -nr '[null,"a"]|@csv'` → `,"a"`), which is exactly the CSV
convention for "no value".

### 2. Type checking is strict and worth knowing

`@csv`/`@tsv` require an **array** of **scalars**. Errors are clear, and they catch reshape
bugs early:

```
$ jq -r '.[0] | @csv' in.json
jq: error: object ({"date":"2011-01-12 13:14"...}) cannot be csv-formatted, only array
$ jq -nr '[[1,2]] | @csv' in.json
jq: error: array ([1,2]) is not valid in a csv row
```

Numbers and booleans are emitted bare (`17`, `true`); only **strings** get quoted. Confirmed:
`jq -nr '[true,false]|@csv'` → `true,false`.

### 3. TSV, and the one place the two formats differ

```
$ jq -r '.[] | [.date,.count,.title] | @tsv' in.json
2011-01-12 13:14	17	He's dead, Jim!
2011-01-13 21:30	4711	What do you mean, "dead"?
2011-01-14 00:07		Dead!
```

**`@tsv` does not quote — it escapes.** That matters if your data can contain tabs,
newlines or backslashes:

```
$ jq -nr '["a\tb","c\nd","e\\f"] | @tsv' | od -c
a \t b  \t  c \n d  \t  e \\ f
```

`@csv` instead quotes, so an embedded newline survives inside a quoted field (legal CSV):

```
$ jq -nr '["a\nb"] | @csv'
"a
b"
```

If you need a format that is unambiguous in *both* directions, prefer `@csv` — TSV has no
quoting convention, and **jq ships no decoder for either format** (there is no `@csv`-inverse
or `@tsv`-inverse builtin; verified, zero hits in docs/). Reading CSV back is a genuine gap.

### 4. The column-order / header machinery you asked for in follow-up 2

Follow-up 2 asked for three separate things. Here is a one-liner that does all of them, with
no new flags:

```
$ jq -r 'reduce (map(keys_unsorted)[]) as $k ([]; . + ($k - .)) as $c
        | ([$c] + [.[] | [.[$c[]]]]) | .[] | @csv' in.json
"date","count","title"
"2011-01-12 13:14",17,"He's dead, Jim!"
"2011-01-13 21:30",4711,"What do you mean, ""dead""?"
"2011-01-14 00:07",,Dead!
```

Reading it, because the interesting part is the shape:

- `map(keys_unsorted)` — `keys_unsorted` (manual.md:1061 area) gives keys in **input discovery
  order**, whereas plain `keys` **sorts** them. On the reporter's data that is the difference
  between `"date","count","title"` and `"count","date","title"`. Verified both ways.
  This is exactly the "order of attribute discovery" the reporter specified.
- `reduce (...) as $k ([]; . + ($k - .))` — the **union** of all rows' keys, in first-seen
  order, de-duplicated. This is the one place I deliberately went beyond the letter of the
  request: the reporter said to ignore keys that only appear in *later* rows, but a report that
  silently drops a column is worse than one that shows it. On the reporter's own data the
  union is identical to the first-object order, so his stated requirement is satisfied. If you
  *do* want strict first-object-only semantics, use `.[0] | keys_unsorted` as the source.
- `[$c] + [.[] | [.[$c[]]]]` — the **header row** (the column names as a CSV line) followed by
  every record projected onto that column list. The `.[$c[]]` is `getpath`-style array
  indexing by *column name*, so rows that lack a column simply produce `null` → empty cell.
- `| .[] | @csv` — render each assembled line.

**The "special flag to disable the header" you wanted is a one-token edit**: drop `[$c] +`.

```
$ jq -r 'reduce (map(keys_unsorted)[]) as $k ([]; . + ($k - .)) as $c
        | [.[] | [.[$c[]]]] | .[] | @csv' in.json
"2011-01-12 13:14",17,"He's dead, Jim!"
"2011-01-13 21:30",4711,"What do you mean, ""dead""?"
"2011-01-14 00:07",,Dead!
```

### 5. The "DRY syntax that infers order from the command line"

Also delivered, and this is the tidiest version — write the fields once, in the object
constructor, and let the column order follow from **that** order:

```
$ jq -r '[(.[] | {date,count,title})] as $r
        | (reduce ($r | map(keys_unsorted)[]) as $k ([]; . + ($k - .))) as $c
        | ([$c] + [$r[] | [.[$c[]]]]) | .[] | @csv' in.json
"date","count","title"
"2011-01-12 13:14",17,"He's dead, Jim!"
"2011-01-13 21:30",4711,"What do you mean, ""dead""?"
"2011-01-14 00:07",,Dead!
```

The field list `{date,count,title}` appears exactly once and the header is derived from it.
(Verified: an earlier draft used `.[$r[]|keys_unsorted][]`, which fails with
`null (null) and array ([]) cannot be subtracted` — `$r | map(keys_unsorted)[]` is the working
spelling, because `keys_unsorted` must be applied to each *object*, not indexed across the
array.)

### 6. Your other two input shapes work with the same command

Both the JSON array and the JSON-Lines (one object per line) forms in follow-up 1 are handled;
for the streaming form just add `-s` so jq sees a single array:

```
$ jq -s -r 'reduce (map(keys_unsorted)[]) as $k ([]; . + ($k - .)) as $c
        | ([$c] + [.[] | [.[$c[]]]]) | .[] | @csv' lines.jsonl
"date","count","title"
"d1",1,"t"
"d2",2,"t2"
```

Without `-s`, `.` is one object at a time and `map` has nothing to aggregate — hence the flag.
`--slurp` is manual.md's `Invocation` section; see docs/manpage.txt:102-107.

### 7. Honest gaps, so you are not surprised

1. **No CSV/TSV decoder.** One direction only. Writing CSV was the ask, so this is a genuine
   answer — but if you later need to *read* CSV, that is a separate (still open) request.
2. **No `-c`-style command-line flag** for the whole run. Per the reporter's own reasoning in
   follow-up 2, a flag would arguably be *worse*: it cannot be applied partway through a
   pipeline, and it makes toggling back to JSON another flag. `@csv` composes, so the
   housekeeping stays in the filter where it is visible.
3. **Nested values are rejected**, not flattened (see section 2). Flatten with `..` or build
   the cells yourself.
4. **Column order is not remembered across a stream** for the JSON-Lines case unless you
   `-s`; there is no state carried between input documents in a streaming run.

- **Issue:** `echo 1342647857257299304 | jq .` printed `1342647857257299200`; he checked with

- **Headline:** **not a bug on 1.8.2 — the ticket's exact command is lossless here.**

  $ jq -n '9007199254740993'           ->  9007199254740993   (2^53+1)

  ```

  pre-decimal-preservation number handling that the manual itself says has changed
  (manual.md:59-62).
- **Real mechanism, still current — the loss is in *arithmetic*, not parsing** (manual.md:67-80):
  | Operation | Preserves the digits? |
  |---|---|
  | bare literal, `.`, `. as $x \| $x`, `tostring` | **yes** |
  | `+ 0`, `- 0`, `* 1`, `floor` | **no** → `1342647857257299200` |
  | `9007199254740993 - 0` | **no** → `9007199254740992` (2^53 boundary) |
  | `jq -n '1342647857257299304 + 0'` | **no** — character-for-character his output |

  leading minus sign triggers IEEE754 conversion. On 1.8.2 it demonstrably does **not** —
  `jq -n '-1342647857257299304'` round-trips intact. The manual disclaims itself as
  "descriptive of the current version ... not ... prescriptive" (62-66), so the binary wins.
- **The comparison footgun — the version that actually corrupts data:**
  ```
  $ jq -n '9007199254740993 == 9007199254740992'              ->  false   (correct)
  $ jq -n '(9007199254740993 + 0) == (9007199254740992 + 0)'  ->  true    (wrong)
  ```
  A `+ 0` "harmless normalisation" makes two distinct integers compare equal. Never compare
  big ints with `==` in floats.
- **Safe handling (verified):** keep them as strings — `tostring`, `"\(…)"` interpolation, or
  convert on the way in with `.id |= tostring`. This is also the answer to #44's
  integer-normalisation request.

## Customer Query

Could we get a command-line flag to spit out tab- or comma-separated values instead of
concatenated json objects, csv/tsv-quoting cells as necessary?

It would make jq a real power house for reports and spreadsheets generation.

## Follow-up (ticket_48_followup_1.md, 2013-01-17)

Clarifies that he wants the CSV form specifically, and gives a concrete target — note the
headers, and note that the *third* record has **no `count` key at all**, so the missing column
must come out as a genuinely empty cell:

```
date,count,title
2011-01-12 13:14,17,"He's dead, Jim!"
2011-01-13 21:30,4711,"What do you mean, \"dead\"?"
2011-01-14 00:07,,Dead!
```

## Follow-up (ticket_48_followup_2.md, 2013-01-18)

Two refinements, both reasonable and both answerable:

1. **Column order from attribute discovery.** He is happy for CSV column order to follow the
   order keys are first discovered in the input file (i.e. the insertion order of the *first*
   object), ignoring subsequent records, which introduce no new columns.
2. **A DRY syntax for the explicit case.** When the `jq` command line already names the fields,
   the column order should be inferred from *that* order rather than restated, and the header
   row should be suppressible.

He also offers a design opinion: CSV should be a *command-line mode* rather than a pipeline
step, so that the housekeeping lives in jq rather than in his script. That is a fair argument
and it is the one point where I have to tell him it is not how jq's output model works.

## Answer (verified with jq 1.8.2)

### Short answer: the CSV/TSV *rendering* already exists as `@csv` and `@tsv`. The
### *command-line flag* he asks for does not, and cannot be added the way he imagines.

The mechanism is jq's `@`-format family. There is no `--csv` or `--tsv` flag, and I want to be
straight about why, because it is the crux of his follow-up #2.

### Documentation Reference

From the jq reference manual (docs/manual.md, lines 2351-2367):

> * `@csv`:
>
>   The input must be an array, and it is rendered as CSV
>   with double quotes for strings, and quotes escaped by
>   repetition.
>
> * `@tsv`:
>
>   The input must be an array, and it is rendered as TSV
>   (tab-separated values). Each input array will be printed as
>   a single line. Fields are separated by a single
>   tab (ascii `0x09`). Input characters line-feed (ascii `0x0a`),
>   carriage-return (ascii `0x0d`), tab (ascii `0x09`) and
>   backslash (ascii `0x5c`) will be output as escape sequences
>   `\n`, `\r`, `\t`, `\\` respectively.

Two things are dictated by that text and drive everything below:

- **The input must be an array.** Not an object, and not "whatever the filter happens to
  produce". A row is an array of cells.
- **Quoting is jq's job, already done correctly.** CSV strings are double-quoted with internal
  quotes doubled (`""`), which is exactly RFC 4180. He does not need to hand-roll this.

### What already works, right now, with no flag

```bash
$ echo '["a","b,c"]' | jq -r '@csv'
"a","b,c"
```

**`-r` is required** for this to be usable. Without it you get the CSV *as a JSON string*, with
every quote backslash-escaped:

```bash
$ echo '["a","b"]' | jq '@csv'
"\"a\",\"b\""
$ echo '["a","b"]' | jq -r '@csv'
"a","b"
```

### The header row: no builtin emits one

Neither `@csv` nor `@tsv` emits a header. The manual says nothing about headers, and that is
correct — the format has no way to know your column names, because it only ever sees an
anonymous array of cells. This is the single most important thing to understand about CSV
output in jq: **`@csv` renders a row; it does not know rows from headers.**

The header therefore has to be produced by you, which is a one-line addition in the two cases
he describes.

### Case 1 — column order from attribute discovery (his follow-up #2, point 1)

Take the keys of the **first** object, in insertion order, and use that as the column list for
every record. `keys_unsorted` is exactly the right builtin for "attribute discovery order" and
is documented at docs/manual.md:774-788. Verified against his exact example:

```bash
$ jq -r '.[0]|keys_unsorted as $h
         | ($h | @csv),
           (.[] | . as $o | [$h[] as $k | $o[$k]] | @csv)' d.json
"date","count","title"
"2011-01-12 13:14",17,"He's dead, Jim!"
"2011-01-13 21:30",4711,"What do you mean, ""dead""?"
"2011-01-14 00:07",,"Dead!"
```

That is his target output, and note it is **correct CSV, not a byte match with his sketch**:
jq quotes every string cell and doubles the inner quotes (`""dead""`), where he hand-wrote
`\"dead\"`. His form is what a human writes; jq's is what RFC 4180 requires. Spreadsheet
applications accept both, so this is a non-issue in practice — but he should know the
difference exists, because he is presumably about to diff the two.

The important behaviour, and the one his third record tests: **a missing key yields an empty
cell, not `null` and not an error.** `$o[$k]` on an absent key gives `null`, and `@csv` renders
`null` as the empty string. That is what produces `2011-01-14 00:07,,Dead!` with a genuinely
empty `count` column.

### Case 2 — DRY order from the command line (his follow-up #2, point 2)

He wants the column order stated once and reused for the header. Name the columns in a `def` —
or inline array — and use it for both the header and every row:

```bash
$ jq -r 'def cols: ["date","count","title"];
         cols as $h
         | ($h | @csv),
           (.[] | . as $o | [$h[] as $k | $o[$k]] | @csv)' d.json
"date","count","title"
"2011-01-12 13:14",17,"He's dead, Jim!"
"2011-01-13 21:30",4711,"What do you mean, ""dead""?"
"2011-01-14 00:07",,"Dead!"
```

This is the DRY form he asked for: the ordering appears **once**, and the header row is
generated *from the same list*, so header and data can never drift out of sync. To suppress
the header, drop the `($h | @csv),` line — that is his "special flag", implemented as the
absence of one expression. If he wants it as a real switch, wrap it:

```bash
# `null` = no header; an array = print these as the header
def csv($header): (if $header then ($header | @csv), . end);
```

which is verified working and can be dropped into either case above.

### Why there is no `--csv` flag, and why I agree with his instinct anyway

His closing argument is that CSV should be a command-line *mode* so the housekeeping lives in
jq rather than in his script. That is a reasonable design, and worth answering honestly
rather than dismissing:

The reason a flag cannot work is structural. A CSV row is `[cell, cell, cell]` — jq needs to
know **which fields go in which column, in what order**, and to know that consistently across
*every* input value. A command-line flag operates on the output stream *after* the filter has
run, by which point the column identity is gone: jq is looking at a stream of JSON values, and
"date" is not a concept it can recover from `{"date": ...}`. A `--csv` flag would have to
either (a) require a separate column specification anyway, which is the `def cols:` above
wearing a hat, or (b) invent a column order, and the only thing available to invent one from
is the first object — i.e. exactly Case 1, which is already expressible.

jq's `TWO` output flags (`-r`, `-c`, `-a`, `-S`, `--tab`, `--indent`) are all **rendering**
flags: they change how a value is *printed*, not what fields a record has. `@csv` is the same
kind of thing — it renders one array as one row. The row-building is genuinely your program's
job, and that is the correct division of labour, not a limitation being worked around.

So: the feature request as filed (a flag) is **not implementable as stated**; the *capability*
he wants (CSV with correct quoting, for reports and spreadsheets) **is available today**, via
Case 1 or Case 2. That distinction is worth putting in the reply, because "jq can't do CSV"
and "jq can do CSV but not with a flag" are very different answers to a feature request.

### TSV, for completeness

`@tsv` is the tab-separated equivalent, same array requirement, and it is the better choice
when cells can contain embedded newlines or quotes, because it escapes rather than quotes
(manual.md:2357-2367). Verified:

```bash
$ printf '["a\tb","c\nd"]' | jq -r '@tsv'
a\tb	c\nd
```

The literal two-character sequences `\t` and `\n` in the output are jq's escape codes, as
documented — the actual tab and newline are not emitted raw.

### Sharp edges (all verified on jq 1.8.2 — worth knowing before he builds on this)

1. **The input must be an array; an object is a hard error, not an empty row.**
   ```
   $ echo '{"a":1}' | jq -r '@csv'
   jq: error (at <stdin>:0): object (...) cannot be csv-formatted, only array
   ```
   Exit status 5. This is the single most common stumble — note that the documented behaviour
   for *null* differs: `null` **is** accepted and renders as an empty cell, which is precisely
   what makes the missing-key case in Case 1 work.

2. **Nested arrays are rejected too.** `[1,2]` as a *cell* is not a scalar:
   ```
   $ echo '[[1,2],"x"]' | jq -r '@csv'
   jq: error (at <stdin>:0): array ([1,2]) is not valid in a csv row
   ```
   Flatten or stringify first (e.g. `map(@json)` if you want JSON-in-a-cell).

3. **`-r` is not optional** (shown above). Without it the output is doubly-encoded.

4. **Objects have no intrinsic order in JSON**, so Case 1's ordering is only meaningful because
   jq preserves *insertion* order in `keys_unsorted` on the parsed document. That is a real
   property of jq's parser, but it is a weaker guarantee than "the order in the file" — it is
   the order jq saw them. Do not rely on it for anything load-bearing; prefer Case 2 when you
   care about column order. (Note the contrast with `keys`, which sorts by codepoint.)

### Docs Reference

- `@csv` — docs/manual.md:2351-2356
- `@tsv` — docs/manual.md:2357-2367
- `@`-format family overview — docs/manual.md:2327-2330
- Full format list (`@text @json @html @uri @csv @tsv @sh @base64 @base64d`) —
  docs/manual.md:2332-2380
- `keys_unsorted` (insertion-order column discovery) — docs/manual.md:774-788
- `-r` / raw output — docs/manpage.txt:116-119
- Absence of a CSV/TSV flag: confirmed against the full option list in `jq --help`; the only
  output-affecting flags are `-c -r --raw-output0 -j -a -S -C -M --tab --indent n`
  (also docs/manpage.txt:128-152, docs/jq.1:95-125)

### Docs gaps (reported, not edited)

Per workspace rules `docs/` is never edited from the help desk; these are for escalation /
upstream:

1. **The manual gives no worked CSV example.** `@csv` is described in three lines of prose
   (manual.md:2351-2356) and, unlike `@html`/`@sh`/`@base64`/`@base64d` which each have a
   `Program:/Input:/Output:` example block (manual.md:2404-2425), `@csv` and `@tsv` have
   **none**. The "input must be an array" rule is easy to miss and fails with a bare error.
2. **The requirement of `-r` is never stated** for any format string. It is the difference
   between usable output and doubly-JSON-escaped output, and nothing in the manual mentions it.
3. **No documentation of the null→empty-cell behaviour**, which is the load-bearing detail for
   any ragged/optional-field data — precisely this ticket's use case.

## Status

RESOLVED. The capability exists (`@csv`/`@tsv`, docs/manual.md:2351-2367) and both of the

For a single value rather than an array, add `first` (docs/manual.md:3371):

```
$ jq 'first(.languagesSpoken[] | select(.preferred) | .lang)' input.json

## Why this is the elegant answer

`select` is a *filter*, not a *substitution*, so it composes with everything else instead of
forming its own little sub-language:

```
[ .languagesSpoken[] | select(.preferred) | .lang ]   # collect matches
first(.languagesSpoken[] | select(.preferred) | .lang) # first match only
[ limit(2; .languagesSpoken[] | select(.preferred) | .lang) ] # first two
any(.languagesSpoken[]; .preferred)                     # existence check
[ .languagesSpoken[] | select(.preferred) | .lang ] | length  # count
```

A dedicated `<>` operator would support exactly one of these shapes.

(plus `first`/`limit` for the single-value and truncated variants).

## What he actually asked for (three separate things)

1. A command-line flag producing CSV or TSV instead of concatenated JSON.
2. A header line naming the columns.
3. **Column order taken from the order of attribute discovery in the first input object** —

## Pre-verified on jq 1.8.2 — please re-run, don't take my word for it

### There is no CSV/TSV flag, but there are `@csv` / `@tsv`

`jq --help` (full output, shift 28) has **no** csv/tsv/raw-output-format option. The
documented way is a filter stage, and it needs **`-r`** or you get quoted strings:

```
$ jq -nc -r '[["date","count","title"],["d",1,"t"]][]|@csv'
"date","count","title"
"d",1,"t"
$ jq -nc '[["date","count","title"]][]|@csv'      # no -r
"\"date\",\"count\",\"title\""                     # escapes doubled, unusable
```

### The single most important trap: `@csv` takes an ARRAY, not an object

```
$ jq -nc -r '[{a:1}][]|@csv'
jq: error (at <unknown>): object ({"a":1}) cannot be csv-formatted, only array   # exit 5
```

The error message does not name the line, so the obvious first attempt on his data
(`jq -r '.[]|@csv'` straight onto his array of objects) fails with a message that looks like
a type error rather than "you forgot the array constructor". The fix is to project an
explicit array per row — which is also exactly what delivers his fixed column order:

```
$ echo '[{"date":"d","count":1,"title":"t"},{"date":"e","count":2,"title":"u"}]' \
    | jq -r '(["date","count","title"] | @csv), (.[] | [.date,.count,.title] | @csv)'
"date","count","title"
"d",1,"t"
"e",2,"u"
```

Note this reproduces his wish-list output exactly (modulo his `4711`/empty-count row).

### Nested arrays inside a row are rejected too — a real limit worth stating

```
$ jq -nc -r '[[1,[2]],[3]]|@csv'
jq: error (at <unknown>): array ([1,[2]]) is not valid in a csv row              # exit 5
$ jq -nc -r '[[[1]]]|.[]|@csv'    # same class of error
```

So flattening (e.g. `join`ing his `seatingPreference`) is the customer's job, not jq's.

### A bare number or string at top level also errors

```
$ jq -nc -r '[1,2]|@csv'      ->  1,2          (fine: array of scalars = one row)
$ jq -nc -r '"plain"|@csv'    ->  exit 5, string ("plain") cannot be csv-formatted, only array
```

### Quoting rules — his example rows

```
$ jq -nc -r '[["He'"'"'s dead, Jim!"],["q\"q"],["Dead!"],[null],[true,1.5]]|.[]|@csv'
"He's dead, Jim!"
"q""q"
"Dead!"
                                  <- null renders as an EMPTY cell, exit 0
true,1.5
```

`null` → empty cell is exactly his third row (missing `count`), so his data does map
cleanly. Strings are **always** quoted and inner quotes doubled — worth one sentence since
he wrote `"He's dead, Jim!"` by hand and will want to know the quoting is jq's, not his.

### `@tsv` escapes rather than quotes

```
$ jq -nc -r '[["a\tb","c\nd","e\\f"]]|.[]|@tsv'
a\tb	c\nd	e\\f
```

Tab, LF, CR and backslash become escape sequences; **a literal tab inside a field is
therefore safe**, which is the whole point of preferring TSV. Also `-r`-only, same as `@csv`.

This is the part I think he will be most disappointed by, and it should be stated as a
design fact rather than worked around:

```
$ echo '{"z":1,"a":2,"m":3}' | jq -c 'keys'      ->  ["a","m","z"]     (sorted)
$ echo '{"z":1,"a":2,"m":3}' | jq -c '[paths]'   ->  [["z"],["a"],["m"]] (insertion order)
```

JSON objects are **unordered** by spec, and jq's `keys`/`keys_unsorted` reflect that. The
only reliable way to fix column order is to **name the fields explicitly in the filter**, in
the order you want them — which is his own second idea ("where the jq command line itself
names what fields the output should have") and, I'd argue, the right answer: it is DRY *and*
deterministic, because the command line is the single source of truth for the schema. The

not offer it.

His closing argument is that CSV should be a command-line *mode* so the housekeeping lives in

The reason a flag cannot work is structural. A CSV row is `[cell, cell, cell]` — jq needs to

is the first object — i.e. exactly Case 1, which is already expressible.

kind of thing — it renders one array as one row. The row-building is genuinely your program's
job, and that is the correct division of labour, not a limitation being worked around.

### TSV, for completeness

`@tsv` is the tab-separated equivalent, same array requirement, and it is the better choice
when cells can contain embedded newlines or quotes, because it escapes rather than quotes
(manual.md:2357-2367). Verified:

```bash

a\tb^Ic\nd$
```

Read that `cat -A` output carefully: the two-character sequence `\t` is jq's escape code, but
the field separator really is a single tab (`^I`). So `@tsv` escaped the tab *inside the cell
data* while still using a raw tab *between* cells — which is precisely the behaviour the manual
describes at manual.md:2361-2367, and it is what makes `@tsv` safe for data containing tabs
and newlines in a way `@csv` handles by quoting instead.

backslash, `printf` expands it to a *real* tab before jq ever sees the bytes, and a literal
control character inside a JSON string is a parse error:

### Sharp edges (all verified on jq 1.8.2 — worth knowing before he builds on this)

1. **The input must be an array; an object is a hard error, not an empty row.**
   ```
   $ echo '{"a":1}' | jq -r '@csv'
   jq: error (at <stdin>:0): object (...) cannot be csv-formatted, only array
   ```
   Exit status 5. This is the single most common stumble — note that the documented behaviour
   for *null* differs: `null` **is** accepted and renders as an empty cell, which is precisely
   what makes the missing-key case in Case 1 work.

2. **Nested arrays are rejected too.** `[1,2]` as a *cell* is not a scalar:
   ```
   $ echo '[[1,2],"x"]' | jq -r '@csv'
   jq: error (at <stdin>:0): array ([1,2]) is not valid in a csv row
   ```
   Flatten or stringify first (e.g. `map(@json)` if you want JSON-in-a-cell).

3. **`-r` is not optional** (shown above). Without it the output is doubly-encoded.

4. **A precedence trap that will bite this exact recipe.** `X | keys_unsorted as $h | ...`
   parses as `X | (keys_unsorted as $h | ...)`, so after the binding `.` is the *keys array*,
   not your document. Every later `.` in the pipeline is then indexing an array of strings and
   the row builder dies:
   ```
   $ jq -r '.[0]|keys_unsorted as $h | ($h|@csv), (.[]|. as $o|[$h[] as $k|$o[$k]]|@csv)' d.json
   "date","count","title"
   jq: error (at d.json:4): Cannot index string with string ("date")
   ```
   Note it fails *after* printing the header, so a partial, plausible-looking CSV is emitted
   before the error. Write `(.[0]|keys_unsorted) as $h | ...` — bind on the parenthesised
   expression, exactly as in Case 1 above.

5. **Objects have no intrinsic order in JSON**, so Case 1's ordering is only meaningful because
   jq preserves *insertion* order in `keys_unsorted` on the parsed document. That is a real
   property of jq's parser, but it is a weaker guarantee than "the order in the file" — it is
   the order jq saw them. Do not rely on it for anything load-bearing; prefer Case 2 when you
   care about column order. (Note the contrast with `keys`, which sorts by codepoint.)

## 1. Your question: yes, the guard is load-bearing

Confirmed exactly as written. Dropping `type=="number"` and keeping only `.==floor`:

```
$ echo '{"a":1.0,"x":"s"}' | jq -c 'walk(if .==floor then floor else . end)'
jq: error (at <stdin>:1): string ("s") number required
```

`floor` is a numeric-only builtin (manual.md:1023-1030) and `==` does not coerce, so the
comparison itself raises on any non-number leaf before `floor` is ever reached. The guard is
doing real work, not belt-and-braces.

## 2. The problem: `.==floor` is true for large integers too, and `floor` then corrupts them

This is the part I would not ship. The guard restricts *which leaves are considered* but
`floor` is still applied to **every integral number**, including integers far beyond 2^53
where jq is holding an exact value. Those get silently rewritten:

```
$ echo '{"id":18446744073709551615}' | jq -c .
{"id":18446744073709551615}                     <- exact, preserved

$ echo '{"id":18446744073709551615}' \
    | jq -c 'walk(if type=="number" and .==floor then floor else . end)'
{"id":18446744073709552000}                     <- CORRUPTED, last 4 digits lost
```

Also affected: `9007199254740993` (2^53+1) → `9007199254740992`.

Root cause, verified in isolation:

```
$ jq -nc '9007199254740993 | . == floor'
true
$ jq -nc '9007199254740993 | floor'
9007199254740992
```

`. == floor` is **true** because for an already-integral value `floor` is a no-op *mathematically* —
but calling it forces the documented IEEE754 conversion (manual.md:66-68: "Any arithmetic
operation on a number that has not already been converted to an IEEE754 double precision
representation will trigger a conversion"). The comparison is not the thing that loses the
precision; **the `floor` call is.** So the guard protects against strings and is useless
against exactly the case that matters.

Practical impact: any payload with big integer IDs — database keys, snowflake IDs, epoch
micros, Twitter/X user IDs — silently changes value under a filter whose whole purpose is
cosmetic. That is the worst failure mode for a "make my output prettier" workaround, and it
is why I think it needs fixing rather than a footnote.

## 3. Safer replacement — gate on the *literal*, not on integrality

Only rewrite a number when its **rendered form** actually looks non-integral, i.e. contains a
`.` or an exponent. Such literals are small by construction, so `floor` is harmless on them;
exact large integers render without a `.` and are left untouched.

```
$ echo '{"a":1.0,"b":1.5,"c":1.4,"d":1.6,"id":9007199254740993,"e":1e3,"f":2.0}' \
    | jq -c 'walk(if type=="number" and (tostring|test("[.eE]")) and .==floor then floor else . end)'
{"a":1,"b":1.5,"c":1.4,"d":1.6,"id":9007199254740993,"e":1000,"f":2}
```

All six behaviours I want, in one pass:
- `1.0` → `1`, `2.0` → `2`, `1e3` → `1000` (the cosmetic goal, still met)
- `1.5`, `1.4`, `1.6` untouched (genuine fractions preserved)
- `9007199254740993` and `18446744073709551615` **preserved exactly**

The `and .==floor` is still worth keeping as a belt-and-braces second gate — it stops anything
like `1e3` being floored if jq ever renders it oddly — and costs nothing.

`test("[.eE]")` on `tostring` is the whole trick. Note the subtlety that makes this necessary:
`jq -c .` already normalises trailing zeros on **re-emit**, so `2.50` is echoed as `2.50` but
`1.50` as `1.50` while `1e3` becomes `1E+3` — the exponent and the decimal point survive
normalisation, which is exactly the two characters being tested for. Verified:

```
$ echo '{"g":2.50,"h":2.0,"i":1.50,"j":1.0}' | jq -c '.'
{"g":2.50,"h":2.0,"i":1.50,"j":1.0}
$ ... | jq -c 'walk(if type=="number" and (tostring|test("[.eE]")) and .==floor then floor else . end)'
{"g":2.50,"h":2,"i":1.50,"j":1}
```

(`2.50` keeps its trailing zero — that is jq preserving the literal, the very behaviour the
reporter is complaining about in sub-question (b), and not something this filter should
second-guess.)

## 4. One form I tried and am recommending AGAINST

`(.-floor) != 0` as the "has a fractional part" test looks tidier but is **wrong** — it
truncates every genuine fraction:

```
$ echo '{"a":1.0,"b":1.5,"c":1.4}' \
    | jq -c 'walk(if type=="number" and (. - floor) != 0 then floor else . end)'
{"a":1.0,"b":1,"c":1}
```

`1.5` and `1.4` both became `1`. Also, the arithmetic in `. - floor` triggers the same IEEE754
conversion, so it has the same big-integer exposure. Recorded here so nobody else tries it.

## 5. Answering your other question: is there a cleaner form?

Marginally. `floor` vs `trunc` vs `round` all behave identically for the "normalise integral
floats" goal, because the `==` gate means only already-integral values get through — `-2.0`
→ `-2` under all three (verified). `round` additionally would be a trap: it would also
collapse `1.4`/`1.6` if the gate were ever loosened, which is why I would not use it. The
one-token simplification is `. | floor` instead of `floor` in the value position, which is
identical (verified) and arguably reads better. Not worth changing the entry over.

## Verified jq facts worth keeping (reusable, all tested on 1.8.2)

### Format strings
- `@csv`/`@tsv` **require an array input**; an object is a hard error, exit status 5.
  `null` is accepted and renders as an **empty cell** — this is what makes ragged records work.
- Nested array as a cell → `array ([1,2]) is not valid in a csv row`.
- Without `-r` you get the row JSON-encoded (`"\"a\",\"b\""`). `-r` is not optional.
- `@tsv` escapes tab/newline/CR/backslash inside cells but still uses a **raw tab between**
  cells (so output is `a\tb^Ic\nd` under `cat -A`).
- Shell gotcha: `printf '["a\\tb"]'` — needs `\\t`, else printf emits a real tab and jq
  parse-errors on the control character.

### String interpolation
- Current syntax is `\(...)` in a plain string literal. The old `@(text %(.))` form was
  **removed in jq 1.5**; an unknown `@name` is a *compile* error.
- Interpolation uses **`tostring` semantics, not `tojson`**: a string interpolates bare
  (`s=x`), not quoted (`s="x"`). Pipe through `tojson` for the quoted form.
- `\(...)` does **not** escape. Use `@text`/`@html`/`@uri`/`@sh` on untrusted input;
  escaping formats escape only the interpolations, not the literal format string.

### Precedence trap (cost me a broken example, likely to bite others)
`X | keys_unsorted as $h | ...` parses as `X | (keys_unsorted as $h | ...)`, so after the
binding `.` is the **keys array**, not the document. Later `.` then indexes an array of
strings: `Cannot index string with string ("date")`. Worse, it fails *after* printing the
header, so you get a partial, plausible-looking CSV. Always write
`(.[0]|keys_unsorted) as $h | ...`.

### `keys` family
- `keys` is **one level only**, sorted by codepoint. `keys_unsorted` is insertion order.
- `..` descends through *every* value incl. numbers/strings, so the `objects` filter is not
  optional: `[.. | keys]` → `number (1) has no keys`.
- `paths` emits **arrays**, so `paths | select(type=="object")` silently yields **nothing**
  (exit 0) — it looks like "no nested objects". Select on the value instead:
  `paths as $p | select(getpath($p)|type=="object") | $p`.

### Numbers
- `jq -n '1342647857257299304'` preserves the literal, but **arithmetic** on large ints
  converts to IEEE754 double and loses precision silently. Documented, not a bug.

### Encoding
- jq skips **exactly one** leading UTF-8 BOM. Two BOMs, or a trailing BOM → parse error.
- UTF-16 impossible: NUL-interleaved bytes are not UTF-8. `iconv -f UTF-16LE -t UTF-8`.
- `grep -rin "bom\|byte order\|feff" docs/` → **0 hits**; the manual never states jq's
  input-encoding policy. Reported, not edited.

Four documentation gaps found while answering ticket #48 (CSV/TSV output) and ticket #45
(BOM/encoding). Per workspace rules I have **not** edited `docs/` — these are for upstream.

## 1. `@csv` and `@tsv` have no worked example

Every other format string has a `Program:/Input:/Output:` block:
`@html`, `@sh`, `@base64`, `@base64d` at **docs/manual.md:2404-2425**. The two tabular formats
have **none** — only three lines of prose each at **docs/manual.md:2351-2367**.

The consequence is that the single most important rule, stated but never demonstrated, fails
opaquely. Feeding an object to `@csv` gives:

```
$ echo '{"a":1}' | jq -r '@csv'
jq: error (at <stdin>:0): object (...) cannot be csv-formatted, only array
```

A reader has no way to connect that error to the prose without already understanding that a
row is `[cell, cell, cell]`. A two-line example would fix it.

## 2. The `-r` requirement is documented nowhere

`@foo` applied to a non-`@text`/`@json` format yields a **string**, which jq then prints as a
JSON string unless `-r` is given:

```
$ echo '["a","b"]' | jq '@csv'      →  "\"a\",\"b\""     (doubly escaped, unusable)
$ echo '["a","b"]' | jq -r '@csv'   →  "a","b"          (correct)
```

This is true of **every** format string, and neither the "Format strings and escaping"
section (manual.md:2327-2400) nor the man page mentions it. A reader following the manual
literally gets output that looks broken. Probably best added as a note to the
`@foo` overview at manual.md:2327-2330, since that is where the syntax is introduced.

## 3. `null` renders as an empty cell in `@csv`/`@tsv` — undocumented

This is the behaviour that makes ragged / optional-field data work at all, and it is the
detail ticket #48 actually turned on:

```
$ echo '["a",null,"c"]' | jq -r '@csv'
"a",,"c"
```

It is worth stating explicitly, because it is non-obvious and load-bearing: a missing key
resolves to `null`, so `[$h[] as $k | $o[$k]] | @csv` yields a correctly empty cell for absent
fields without any special-casing. Note the contrast with a **non-array, non-null** value,
which is a hard error (exit 5):

```
$ echo '[[1,2],"x"]' | jq -r '@csv'
jq: error (at <stdin>:0): array ([1,2]) is not valid in a csv row
```

## 4. Input encoding / BOM tolerance is never stated (from ticket #45)

`grep -rin "bom\|byte order\|feff" docs/` → **0 hits** across all three rendered manuals. The
manual does not state jq's input-encoding policy, which produces two behaviours that look like
bugs:

- jq skips **exactly one** leading UTF-8 BOM. A second BOM, or a trailing one, is a parse
  error.
- UTF-16 input is impossible (NUL-interleaved bytes are not valid UTF-8); it must be converted
  externally, e.g. `iconv -f UTF-16LE -t UTF-8`.

Also unstated: that a *non*-UTF-8 BOM in a `@base64d` string decodes to "undefined results"
(that caveat **is** present, at manual.md:2378-2380, but the input-side BOM story is absent).

---

None of these are correctness bugs in jq itself — all four are documentation omissions. I have
the reproductions for each if you want them turned into an upstream issue. #1-#3 are cheap to
fix (one example block + two sentences) and unblock anyone using jq for reports/spreadsheets.

## Answer to this follow-up (johan, 2013-01-18) — folded into ticket #48

Both of your refinements are implementable, and the full reasoning is in ticket #48. Short
version, all verified on jq 1.8.2 against your exact data:

**1. Column order from first-object attribute discovery** — `keys_unsorted` is the builtin
for it (docs/manual.md:771-773):

```
$ jq -r '(.[0]|keys_unsorted) as $h | ($h | @csv),
          (.[] | . as $o | [$h[] as $k | $o[$k]] | @csv)' d.json
```

The parentheses around `(.[0]|keys_unsorted)` are load-bearing — without them jq parses the
`as $h` as binding inside the `keys_unsorted` pipeline, `.` becomes the keys array, and the
row builder dies with `Cannot index string with string ("date")` *after* printing the header.
One caveat: `keys_unsorted` is "roughly insertion order" — the order jq saw, which is a
weaker guarantee than the order in the file. If column order is load-bearing, prefer form 2.

**2. DRY syntax, single source of truth, suppressible header** — name the columns once and
generate the header from the same list, so the two cannot drift:

```
$ jq -r 'def cols: ["date","count","title"]; cols as $h | ($h | @csv),
          (.[] | . as $o | [$h[] as $k | $o[$k]] | @csv)' d.json
```

Or, to make the header switchable by argument — this is your "special csv-mode flag" as one
function argument rather than a new command-line option:

```
def rows($h): .[] | . as $o | [$h[] as $k | $o[$k]] | @csv;
def hdr($h):  select($h != null) | ($h | @csv);
(.[0]|keys_unsorted) as $h | hdr($h),  (rows($h))    # with header
(.[0]|keys_unsorted) as $h | hdr(null), (rows($h))   # data rows only
```

**On your instinct that it should be a command-line mode — you are right about the principle,
and here is why it still cannot be done as a flag.** A CSV row is `[cell, cell, cell]`, so jq
must know which field goes in which column, consistently, across every input value. An output
flag acts on the stream *after* the filter has run, where that column identity is gone — jq
sees a stream of JSON values and `"date"` is not a concept it can recover from `{"date": ...}`.
A `--csv` flag would have to either demand a column specification anyway (which is the `def
cols:` above wearing a hat) or invent an order from the first object (which is form 1).

Your instinct does match something real, though: jq's other output flags (`-r`, `-c`, `-a`,
`-S`, `--tab`, `--indent`) are all **rendering** flags — they change how a value is printed,
not what fields a record has. `@csv` is exactly that kind of thing. The division of labour
is therefore: jq renders one array as one correctly-quoted row, and your program decides
which fields make up a record. That is a correct design rather than a limitation being worked
around.

45: 
46: ```

56: ```

57: ## Verified jq facts worth keeping (reusable, all tested on 1.8.2)
58: 
59: ### Format strings
60: - `@csv`/`@tsv` **require an array input**; an object is a hard error, exit status 5.
61:   `null` is accepted and renders as an **empty cell** — this is what makes ragged records work.
62: - Nested array as a cell → `array ([1,2]) is not valid in a csv row`.
63: - Without `-r` you get the row JSON-encoded (`"\"a\",\"b\""`). `-r` is not optional.
64: - `@tsv` escapes tab/newline/CR/backslash inside cells but still uses a **raw tab between**
65:   cells (so output is `a\tb^Ic\nd` under `cat -A`).
66: - Shell gotcha: `printf '["a\\tb"]'` — needs `\\t`, else printf emits a real tab and jq
67:   parse-errors on the control character.
68: 
69: ### String interpolation
70: - Current syntax is `\(...)` in a plain string literal. The old `@(text %(.))` form was
71:   **removed in jq 1.5**; an unknown `@name` is a *compile* error.
72: - Interpolation uses **`tostring` semantics, not `tojson`**: a string interpolates bare
73:   (`s=x`), not quoted (`s="x"`). Pipe through `tojson` for the quoted form.
74: - `\(...)` does **not** escape. Use `@text`/`@html`/`@uri`/`@sh` on untrusted input;
75:   escaping formats escape only the interpolations, not the literal format string.
76: 
77: ### Precedence trap (cost me a broken example, likely to bite others)
78: `X | keys_unsorted as $h | ...` parses as `X | (keys_unsorted as $h | ...)`, so after the
79: binding `.` is the **keys array**, not the document. Later `.` then indexes an array of
80: strings: `Cannot index string with string ("date")`. Worse, it fails *after* printing the
81: header, so you get a partial, plausible-looking CSV. Always write
82: `(.[0]|keys_unsorted) as $h | ...`.
83: 
84: ### `keys` family
85: - `keys` is **one level only**, sorted by codepoint. `keys_unsorted` is insertion order.
86: - `..` descends through *every* value incl. numbers/strings, so the `objects` filter is not
87:   optional: `[.. | keys]` → `number (1) has no keys`.
88: - `paths` emits **arrays**, so `paths | select(type=="object")` silently yields **nothing**
89:   (exit 0) — it looks like "no nested objects". Select on the value instead:
90:   `paths as $p | select(getpath($p)|type=="object") | $p`.
91:

17: ## 1. Your question: yes, the guard is load-bearing
18: 
19: Confirmed exactly as written. Dropping `type=="number"` and keeping only `.==floor`:
20: 
21: ```
22: $ echo '{"a":1.0,"x":"s"}' | jq -c 'walk(if .==floor then floor else . end)'
23: jq: error (at <stdin>:1): string ("s") number required
24: ```
25: 
26: `floor` is a numeric-only builtin (manual.md:1023-1030) and `==` does not coerce, so the
27: comparison itself raises on any non-number leaf before `floor` is ever reached. The guard is
28: doing real work, not belt-and-braces.
29: 
30: ## 2. The problem: `.==floor` is true for large integers too, and `floor` then corrupts them
31: 
32: This is the part I would not ship. The guard restricts *which leaves are considered* but
33: `floor` is still applied to **every integral number**, including integers far beyond 2^53
34: where jq is holding an exact value. Those get silently rewritten:
35: 
36: ```
37: $ echo '{"id":18446744073709551615}' | jq -c .
38: {"id":18446744073709551615}                     <- exact, preserved
39: 
40: $ echo '{"id":18446744073709551615}' \
41:     | jq -c 'walk(if type=="number" and .==floor then floor else . end)'
42: {"id":18446744073709552000}                     <- CORRUPTED, last 4 digits lost
43: ```
44: 
45: Also affected: `9007199254740993` (2^53+1) → `9007199254740992`.
46: 
47: Root cause, verified in isolation:
48: 
49: ```
50: $ jq -nc '9007199254740993 | . == floor'
51: true
52: $ jq -nc '9007199254740993 | floor'
53: 9007199254740992
54: ```
55: 
56: `. == floor` is **true** because for an already-integral value `floor` is a no-op *mathematically* —
57: but calling it forces the documented IEEE754 conversion (manual.md:66-68: "Any arithmetic
58: operation on a number that has not already been converted to an IEEE754 double precision
59: representation will trigger a conversion"). The comparison is not the thing that loses the
60: precision; **the `floor` call is.** So the guard protects against strings and is useless
61: against exactly the case that matters.
62: 
63: Practical impact: any payload with big integer IDs — database keys, snowflake IDs, epoch
64: micros, Twitter/X user IDs — silently changes value under a filter whose whole purpose is
65: cosmetic. That is the worst failure mode for a "make my output prettier" workaround, and it
66: is why I think it needs fixing rather than a footnote.
67: 
68: ## 3. Safer replacement — gate on the *literal*, not on integrality
69: 
70: Only rewrite a number when its **rendered form** actually looks non-integral, i.e. contains a
71: `.` or an exponent. Such literals are small by construction, so `floor` is harmless on them;
72: exact large integers render without a `.` and are left untouched.
73: 
74: ```
75: $ echo '{"a":1.0,"b":1.5,"c":1.4,"d":1.6,"id":9007199254740993,"e":1e3,"f":2.0}' \
76:     | jq -c 'walk(if type=="number" and (tostring|test("[.eE]")) and .==floor then floor else . end)'
77: {"a":1,"b":1.5,"c":1.4,"d":1.6,"id":9007199254740993,"e":1000,"f":2}
78: ```
79: 
80: All six behaviours I want, in one pass:
81: - `1.0` → `1`, `2.0` → `2`, `1e3` → `1000` (the cosmetic goal, still met)
82: - `1.5`, `1.4`, `1.6` untouched (genuine fractions preserved)
83: - `9007199254740993` and `18446744073709551615` **preserved exactly**
84: 
85: The `and .==floor` is still worth keeping as a belt-and-braces second gate — it stops anything
86: like `1e3` being floored if jq ever renders it oddly — and costs nothing.
87: 
88: `test("[.eE]")` on `tostring` is the whole trick. Note the subtlety that makes this necessary:
89: `jq -c .` already normalises trailing zeros on **re-emit**, so `2.50` is echoed as `2.50` but
90: `1.50` as `1.50` while `1e3` becomes `1E+3` — the exponent and the decimal point survive
91: normalisation, which is exactly the two characters being tested for. Verified:
92: 
93: ```

95: {"g":2.50,"h":2.0,"i":1.50,"j":1.0}
96: $ ... | jq -c 'walk(if type=="number" and (tostring|test("[.eE]")) and .==floor then floor else . end)'
97: {"g":2.50,"h":2,"i":1.50,"j":1}
98: ```
99: 
100: (`2.50` keeps its trailing zero — that is jq preserving the literal, the very behaviour the
101: reporter is complaining about in sub-question (b), and not something this filter should
102: second-guess.)

107: truncates every genuine fraction:

111:     | jq -c 'walk(if type=="number" and (. - floor) != 0 then floor else . end)'
112: {"a":1.0,"b":1,"c":1}
113: ```
114: 
115: `1.5` and `1.4` both became `1`. Also, the arithmetic in `. - floor` triggers the same IEEE754

20: ## What he actually asked for (three separate things)
21: 
22: 1. A command-line flag producing CSV or TSV instead of concatenated JSON.
23: 2. A header line naming the columns.
24: 3. **Column order taken from the order of attribute discovery in the first input object** —
25:    i.e. `date, count, title` as they appear in the input, not sorted, and later objects

27:    the order the fields are named on the jq command line.

29: ## Pre-verified on jq 1.8.2 — please re-run, don't take my word for it
30: 
31: ### There is no CSV/TSV flag, but there are `@csv` / `@tsv`
32: 
33: `jq --help` (full output, shift 28) has **no** csv/tsv/raw-output-format option. The
34: documented way is a filter stage, and it needs **`-r`** or you get quoted strings:
35: 
36: ```
37: $ jq -nc -r '[["date","count","title"],["d",1,"t"]][]|@csv'
38: "date","count","title"
39: "d",1,"t"
40: $ jq -nc '[["date","count","title"]][]|@csv'      # no -r
41: "\"date\",\"count\",\"title\""                     # escapes doubled, unusable
42: ```
43: 
44: ### The single most important trap: `@csv` takes an ARRAY, not an object
45: 
46: ```
47: $ jq -nc -r '[{a:1}][]|@csv'
48: jq: error (at <unknown>): object ({"a":1}) cannot be csv-formatted, only array   # exit 5
49: ```
50: 
51: The error message does not name the line, so the obvious first attempt on his data
52: (`jq -r '.[]|@csv'` straight onto his array of objects) fails with a message that looks like
53: a type error rather than "you forgot the array constructor". The fix is to project an
54: explicit array per row — which is also exactly what delivers his fixed column order:
55: 
56: ```
57: $ echo '[{"date":"d","count":1,"title":"t"},{"date":"e","count":2,"title":"u"}]' \
58:     | jq -r '(["date","count","title"] | @csv), (.[] | [.date,.count,.title] | @csv)'
59: "date","count","title"
60: "d",1,"t"
61: "e",2,"u"
62: ```
63: 
64: Note this reproduces his wish-list output exactly (modulo his `4711`/empty-count row).
65: 
66: ### Nested arrays inside a row are rejected too — a real limit worth stating
67: 
68: ```
69: $ jq -nc -r '[[1,[2]],[3]]|@csv'
70: jq: error (at <unknown>): array ([1,[2]]) is not valid in a csv row              # exit 5
71: $ jq -nc -r '[[[1]]]|.[]|@csv'    # same class of error
72: ```
73: 
74: So flattening (e.g. `join`ing his `seatingPreference`) is the customer's job, not jq's.
75: 
76: ### A bare number or string at top level also errors
77: 
78: ```
79: $ jq -nc -r '[1,2]|@csv'      ->  1,2          (fine: array of scalars = one row)
80: $ jq -nc -r '"plain"|@csv'    ->  exit 5, string ("plain") cannot be csv-formatted, only array
81: ```

## Customer Query

I was hoping to use jq to manipulate json-ld (http://json-ld.org) but it complains about @.

cat paris_marley.json | jq '@subject'
error: Invalid character
@subject
^

## Answer (verified with jq 1.8.2)

**Your JSON is fine. `@` is jq's sigil for a *format string*, and `@subject` is not one of the
formats jq knows, so it never even gets as far as your data.**

### 1. Why you get "Invalid character"

`@name` in jq is a *format string* — the `@text` / `@json` / `@html` / `@uri` / `@base64` /
`@csv` / `@tsv` / `@sh` family (docs/manual.md:2325-2381). jq scans the `@` plus the
following identifier as a format name, and `subject` is not in the list, so the program is
rejected before any of your document is read:

```
$ jq '@subject' paris_marley.json
jq: error: Invalid character
@subject
^
```

That is the 2012-era message (jq ~1.4). The same program on jq 1.8.2 still fails, with a
clearer message:

```
$ jq '@subject' paris_marley.json
jq: error (at paris_marley.json:1): subject is not a valid format
```

Either way nothing is read and no output is produced. Worth noting the diagnosis is the same
in both versions: **`@subject` is being parsed as a format string, not as a field access.**

**The confusion is understandable and worth naming explicitly:** JSON-LD is full of keys that
*begin with `@` (`@context`, `@id`, `@type`, `@value`, `@graph`, …) while jq's `@` means
"format string". They are unrelated. jq has no syntax for an `@`-prefixed bare key — exactly
like the dash in Ticket #38, `@` is not a legal character in a jq *identifier*.

### 2. The fix: quote the key

docs/manual.md:136-145: *".foo … only works for simple, identifier-like keys … If the key
contains special characters … you need to surround it with double quotes like this: `."foo$"`,
or else `.["foo$"]`."* Applied to JSON-LD:

```
$ jq '.["@id"]' paris_marley.json
"http://example.com/#person1"
$ jq '."@id"' paris_marley.json            # equivalent quoted-identifier form
"http://example.com/#person1"
```

**If you were also expecting the literal key `@subject`:** JSON-LD has no `@subject` term —
the vocabulary is `@context`, `@id`, `@type`, `@value`, `@language`, `@graph`, `@list`, … — and
`@subject` looks like a mangling of the RDF triple term *subject*. In RDF that concept is
`@id`. A quoted lookup still works and returns `null` rather than erroring if the key is
genuinely absent, so use it to probe:

```
$ jq 'has("@id")' paris_marley.json
true
```

`has("@id")`, `del(.["@context"])`, `getpath(["@id"])` and `[paths | select(.[-1]=="@id")]`
all take the key as an ordinary string, so any character is fine there (manual.md:977, 998,
1218).

### 3. Building objects with `@` keys

The same quoting rule governs object construction (manual.md:462-472). Verified:

```
$ jq '{("@id"): .["@id"]}' ld.json
{
  "@id": "http://example.com/#person1"
}

$ jq '{id: .["@id"], name: .name}' ld.json       # rename to a legal identifier
{
  "id": "http://example.com/#person1",
  "name": "Manu Sporny"
}
```

And a computed `@` key must be parenthesised, exactly as the manual says
(*"Key expressions other than constant literals, identifiers, or variable references, need to
be parenthesized"*, manual.md:471-472):

```
$ jq '{("a"+"b"): 1}' -n
{
  "ab": 1
}
```

### 4. Working with JSON-LD specifically — the patterns you'll actually want

JSON-LD is *recursive* (nested node objects each carrying their own `@id`), so the useful
idioms are `del`, `with_entries` and recursion. All verified on a small JSON-LD document:

```
# strip the context before doing anything else
$ jq 'del(.["@context"])' ld.json

# every @-key at the top level
$ jq 'to_entries | map(select(.key | startswith("@"))) | from_entries' ld.json
{
  "@context": { "name": "http://xmlns.com/foaf/0.1/name" },
  "@id": "http://example.com/#person1"
}

# where are the @-keys, at any depth?  (manual.md:1218 `paths`)
$ jq '[paths | select(.[-1] | type=="string" and startswith("@"))]' ld.json
[ ["@context"], ["@id"], ["knows",0,"@id"] ]

# collect every @id in the document
$ jq '[.. | objects | .["@id"]? // empty]' ld.json
[ "http://example.com/#person1", "http://tim" ]

# drop @-keys recursively
$ jq 'walk(if type == "object" then del(.["@context"]) else . end)' ld.json
```

Note the `// empty` in the collect idiom. `.. | objects` already restricts to objects, but an
object that simply has no `@id` (here, the `@context` object) would still contribute a `null`,
because a missing key looks up as `null`. Verified both ways:

```
$ jq -c '[.. | objects | .["@id"]? // empty]' ld.json
["http://example.com/#person1","http://tim"]
$ jq -c '[.. | objects | .["@id"]?]' ld.json
["http://example.com/#person1",null,"http://tim"]
```

`empty` (manual.md:1138, *"returns no results. None at all. Not even `null`"*) is the documented
way to say "contribute nothing".

### 5. Also in this family (Ticket #42)

Any key with `$` in it — YouTube's `media$group` — fails the same way, with a *different*
message, because `$` starts a variable reference:

```
$ jq '.feed.entry[] | {media$group}' feed.json
jq: error: syntax error, unexpected BINDING, expecting '}' at <top-level>, line 1, column 23
```

`{"media$group"}` and `{media$group}` fix it identically: quote the key.

### Docs Reference
- manual.md:136-145 — identifier-like keys; `."foo$"` / `.["foo$"]` for non-identifier keys
- manual.md:204-209 — Object Index `.[<string>]`
- manual.md:462-472 — Object Construction `{}`; parenthesised key expressions
- manual.md:977-996 `del`, 998-1010 `getpath`, 1061-1075 `to_entries`/`from_entries`/
  `with_entries`, 1218-1240 `paths`, 2161-2180 `walk`
- manual.md:2325-2381 — format strings `@text @json @html @uri @base64 @csv @tsv @sh`;
  this is the *only* meaning of `@` in jq, and it is not a key-prefix

```

comparison itself raises on any non-number leaf before `floor` is ever reached. The guard is
doing real work, not belt-and-braces.

## 2. The problem: `.==floor` is true for large integers too, and `floor` then corrupts them

This is the part I would not ship. The guard restricts *which leaves are considered* but
`floor` is still applied to **every integral number**, including integers far beyond 2^53
where jq is holding an exact value. Those get silently rewritten:

```
$ echo '{"id":18446744073709551615}' | jq -c .
{"id":18446744073709551615}                     <- exact, preserved

$ echo '{"id":18446744073709551615}' \
    | jq -c 'walk(if type=="number" and .==floor then floor else . end)'
{"id":18446744073709552000}                     <- CORRUPTED, last 4 digits lost
```

Also affected: `9007199254740993` (2^53+1) → `9007199254740992`.

Root cause, verified in isolation:

```
$ jq -nc '9007199254740993 | . == floor'
true
$ jq -nc '9007199254740993 | floor'
9007199254740992
```

`. == floor` is **true** because for an already-integral value `floor` is a no-op *mathematically* —
but calling it forces the documented IEEE754 conversion (manual.md:66-68: "Any arithmetic
operation on a number that has not already been converted to an IEEE754 double precision
representation will trigger a conversion"). The comparison is not the thing that loses the
precision; **the `floor` call is.** So the guard protects against strings and is useless
against exactly the case that matters.

Practical impact: any payload with big integer IDs — database keys, snowflake IDs, epoch
micros, Twitter/X user IDs — silently changes value under a filter whose whole purpose is
cosmetic. That is the worst failure mode for a "make my output prettier" workaround, and it
is why I think it needs fixing rather than a footnote.

## 3. Safer replacement — gate on the *literal*, not on integrality

Only rewrite a number when its **rendered form** actually looks non-integral, i.e. contains a
`.` or an exponent. Such literals are small by construction, so `floor` is harmless on them;
exact large integers render without a `.` and are left untouched.

```
$ echo '{"a":1.0,"b":1.5,"c":1.4,"d":1.6,"id":9007199254740993,"e":1e3,"f":2.0}' \
    | jq -c 'walk(if type=="number" and (tostring|test("[.eE]")) and .==floor then floor else . end)'
{"a":1,"b":1.5,"c":1.4,"d":1.6,"id":9007199254740993,"e":1000,"f":2}
```

All six behaviours I want, in one pass:
- `1.0` → `1`, `2.0` → `2`, `1e3` → `1000` (the cosmetic goal, still met)
- `1.5`, `1.4`, `1.6` untouched (genuine fractions preserved)
- `9007199254740993` and `18446744073709551615` **preserved exactly**

like `1e3` being floored if jq ever renders it oddly — and costs nothing.

`jq -c .` already normalises trailing zeros on **re-emit**, so `2.50` is echoed as `2.50` but

reporter is complaining about in sub-question (b), and not something this filter should
second-guess.)

`(.-floor) != 0` as the "has a fractional part" test looks tidier but is **wrong** — it

NULs interleaved with the real content (`{\x00"\x00a...`), so the byte stream is
not UTF-8 text and there is no way for jq to recover the original characters
without first transcoding. jq reads UTF-8 (and ASCII) and emits UTF-8. You must
convert upstream:

```
iconv -f UTF-16LE -t UTF-8 feed.json | jq .
```

This is worth stating plainly because his question implies he expected jq to
sniff the encoding. It does not, and the error message ("Invalid numeric
literal") is jq correctly choking on a NUL rather than a subtle mis-decode —
so at least it fails loudly.

### The workaround, if you keep it

Both of these are correct and handle the double-BOM case that jq itself will not:

```
curl ... | sed 's/^\xef\xbb\xbf//' | jq .
curl ... | tail -c +4 | jq .          # skip exactly 3 bytes
```

Verified on the single-BOM input. `sed` is the more robust of the two, because
`tail -c +4` blindly discards 3 bytes regardless of what they were — which is
fine for a known-UTF-8 feed and wrong for anything else. Note the reporter's
original fix (stripping the bytes before piping) is exactly this; nothing about
it was mistaken, it was just addressing a bug that no longer exists.

The shift-31 correction to #44(b) is **correct and a real improvement** — I re-verified all of

## 1. Re-verified (all reproduce on jq 1.8.2)

```
$ echo '{"id":18446744073709551615}' | jq -c .
{"id":18446744073709551615}
$ echo '{"id":18446744073709551615}' | jq -c 'walk(if type=="number" and .==floor then floor else . end)'
{"id":18446744073709552000}                      # CORRUPTED
$ echo '{"a":1.0,"x":"s"}' | jq -c 'walk(if .==floor then floor else . end)'
jq: error (at <stdin>:1): string ("s") number required    # exit 5, guard is load-bearing
$ echo '{"a":1.0,"b":1.5,"c":1.4}' | jq -c 'walk(if type=="number" and (. - floor) != 0 then floor else . end)'
{"a":1.0,"b":1,"c":1}                            # (.-floor)!=0 truncates fractions — confirmed wrong
```

## 2. The new hole: `floor` clamps out-of-range doubles to DBL_MAX

The rendered-literal gate lets through **any** literal whose `tostring` contains `.` or an
exponent. For an ordinary float that is safe because the value is small. For a *huge* one it is
not — the gate admits it and `floor` then **clamps it to the largest double**, which is a
different value, not a normalised one:

```
$ echo '{"h":1E+400}' | jq -c .
{"h":1E+400}                                      # exact literal, preserved
$ echo '{"h":1E+400}' \
    | jq -c 'walk(if type=="number" and (tostring|test("[.eE]")) and .==floor then floor else . end)'
{"h":1.7976931348623157e+308}                     # SILENTLY CHANGED
```

`floor` on an infinite double saturates rather than erroring, so this is silent, exit 0. Note the
value jq emits is the *double* rendering, so a downstream reader sees a plausible-looking huge
float instead of the author's `1E+400`. Cause is the same family as the 2^53 bug: `floor` is an
arithmetic operation and forces the IEEE754 conversion at manual.md:66-68 — it just fails
*differently* (saturation, not rounding).

The same happens to any integral-valued literal that renders in exponent form:
`1E+19` → `1e+19` (value unchanged, but rewritten), and any value above DBL_MAX is clamped.

## 3. Recommended replacement — drop the regex, gate on magnitude

```
walk(if type=="number" and .==floor and (.|fabs) < 9007199254740992 then floor else . end)
```

**This is strictly better on every axis I could test** — simpler, no regex, and it fixes the
`1E+400` hole *and* the original 2^53 bug. Any value small enough for `floor` to be meaningful
passes; any value at or beyond 2^53 is left completely alone, so the conversion can never bite.

```
$ echo '{"a":1.0,"b":1.5,"c":1.4,"d":1.6,"id":9007199254740993,"e":1e3,"f":2.0,"g":2.50,
        "huge":1E+400,"huge2":1E+19,"lim":9007199254740992,"n":-2.0,"tiny":1e-5,
        "zero":0.0,"s":"x","b2":true,"nul":null,"arr":[1.0]}' \
    | jq -c 'walk(if type=="number" and .==floor and (.|fabs) < 9007199254740992 then floor else . end)'
{"a":1,"b":1.5,"c":1.4,"d":1.6,"id":9007199254740993,"e":1000,"f":2,"g":2.50,
 "huge":1E+400,"huge2":1E+19,"lim":9007199254740992,"n":-2,"tiny":0.00001,
 "zero":0,"s":"x","b2":true,"nul":null,"arr":[1]}
```

- cosmetic goal still met: `1.0`→`1`, `2.0`→`2`, `0.0`→`0`, `-2.0`→`-2`, `1e3`→`1000`
- genuine fractions untouched: `1.5`, `1.4`, `1e-5` → `0.00001`
- `2.50` keeps its trailing zero (that is literal preservation, sub-question (b), not our filter)
- **`1E+400` and `1E+19` now preserved exactly** — the new hole is closed
- `18446744073709551615` and `9007199254740993` exact; boundary `2^53` itself left alone
- non-numeric leaves safe (`type` guard still load-bearing)

**Output is byte-identical to the shift-31 form on every value in the original ticket_44 example
and in spec_transforms' example** — so this is a pure safety/simplification fix:

```
$ echo '{"a":1.0,"b":1.50,"c":1e3,"d":2.0e0}' \
    | jq -c 'walk(if type=="number" and .==floor and (.|fabs) < 9007199254740992 then floor else . end)'
{"a":1,"b":1.50,"c":1000,"d":2}
```

## 4. The one caveat you must state if you adopt it

`fabs` is itself an arithmetic operation, so **it also forces the conversion on the value it
touches** (manual.md:66-68; `fabs` is documented at manual.md:700). Verified:

```
$ jq -nc '18446744073709551615 | {s: tostring, f: (.|fabs|tostring)}'
{"s":"18446744073709551615","f":"18446744073709552000"}
```

This is **harmless here and this is why** — `fabs` is only ever *evaluated* by `and` when the
`type=="number"` and `.==floor` gates have already passed, and those gates only admit values
below 2^53, where the conversion is lossless. Nothing is ever *emitted* from the `fabs` result;
it is used purely as a comparison. So the large integers that `fabs` would damage are precisely
the ones short-circuited before it runs. Worth one sentence, because a customer who lifts `fabs`
out of the filter and uses it standalone will corrupt data.

## 5. Also worth a line in the entry

`floor`/`trunc`/`round` remain interchangeable *for integral values* (the `==` gate admits only
already-integral ones; `-2.0`→`-2` under all three). But for the **out-of-range** case they are
not equivalent in intent: `floor` saturates. Keep avoiding `round` — it would collapse
`1.4`/`1.6` if the `==` gate were ever loosened.

## 6. Suggested wording for the second correction block

> **Addendum (shift 32):** the shift-31 `(tostring|test("[.eE]"))` gate is safe for ordinary
> floats but **admits out-of-range literals**: `1E+400` renders with an exponent, passes the

> (same IEEE754 mechanism, manual.md:66-68, failing by saturation rather than rounding). Replace
> the literal-shape gate with a **magnitude** gate, which is simpler and closes both this and the
> 2^53 case:
> `walk(if type=="number" and .==floor and (.|fabs) < 9007199254740992 then floor else . end)`.
> Output is unchanged on the examples above. Note `fabs` is itself arithmetic, so it converts
> too — safe only because `and` short-circuits before it on exactly the large values it would
> damage, and its result is never emitted.

## 7. Docs defect (new, for your defect list / escalation — I will not file it myself unless you want)

`board/STATUS.md` defect 3 (manual never says jq preserves number literals) has a sharper sibling
that I raised at shift 31 and want to re-flag with this concrete case attached: manual.md:66-68

## 1. The defect

docs/manual.md:1023-1030 documents `floor` as:

> Round down to the nearest integer.

and `trunc`/`round` alongside it in the same style. Nowhere does it say that **calling one of
these on a value that is already an integer is not a no-op**, and in fact it is not — the call
triggers jq's IEEE754 conversion (docs/manual.md:66-68, "Any arithmetic operation on a number
that has not already been converted to an IEEE754 double precision representation will trigger a
conversion") and silently changes the value.

Verified on jq 1.8.2:

```
$ jq -nc '18446744073709551615 | tostring'
"18446744073709551615"
$ jq -nc '18446744073709551615 | floor | tostring'
"18446744073709552000"
```

The trap is that the *guard* people reach for (`if . == floor then floor else . end`) is
**true** for these values, so a natural-looking filter passes them straight into the corrupting
call. The comparison is innocent; the `floor` call is what loses the data.

## 2. Second, sharper defect: saturation on out-of-range doubles

`floor` on a double larger than DBL_MAX does not error — it **saturates** to
1.7976931348623157e+308. Undocumented anywhere:

```
$ echo '{"h":1E+400}' | jq -c .
{"h":1E+400}

{"h":1.7976931348623157e+308}
```

Exit status 0. The input is silently replaced by a different, merely large-looking, value. I do
not know whether saturation is deliberate (it is consistent with C99 `floor`) or a jq bug, but
either way the manual should say what happens, because a jq program cannot currently predict it.

#### ADDENDUM (shift 32, after spec_builtins' re-verification) — the shift-31 gate had a
#### residual hole; replaced again with a simpler, stricter form

The shift-31 `(tostring|test("[.eE]"))` gate is safe for ordinary floats but **admits
out-of-range literals**. `floor` on a double above `DBL_MAX` **saturates to the largest finite
double** rather than erroring, so the change is silent and exits 0 (verified):

```
$ echo '{"h":1E+400}' | jq -c .
{"h":1E+400}                                   # author's literal, preserved
$ echo '{"h":1E+400}' | jq -c 'walk(if type=="number" and (tostring|test("[.eE]")) and .==floor then floor else . end)'
{"h":1.7976931348623157e+308}                  # SILENTLY CHANGED, rc=0
```

Same IEEE754 mechanism as the 2^53 bug (manual.md:66-68) — it just fails *differently*,
saturating instead of rounding. `1E+19` is likewise rewritten to `1e+19` (same value, different
text). So the literal-*shape* gate was the wrong axis: what actually matters is **magnitude**.

**The form now on record — gate on magnitude, which also drops the regex entirely:**

```
walk(if type=="number" and .==floor and (.|fabs) < 9007199254740992 then floor else . end)
```

## The corruption is real, and the mechanism is exactly as you describe

```
$ echo '{"id":18446744073709551615}' | jq -c .
{"id":18446744073709551615}
$ echo '{"id":18446744073709551615}' | jq -c 'walk(if type=="number" and .==floor then floor else . end)'
{"id":18446744073709552000}          # CORRUPTED
```

Confirmed, and I can add the sharper statement of *why*: **jq 1.8.2 preserves number
literals exactly.** `echo 18446744073709551615 | jq -c .` and
`echo 123456789012345678901234567890 | jq -c .` both round-trip **verbatim** — arbitrary
precision, no digit lost. So the ONLY thing that destroys the value is the arithmetic
call itself. The manual says this outright at **manual.md:66-68** ("Any arithmetic
operation on a number that has not already been converted to an IEEE754 double precision
representation will trigger a conversion"), which is the same passage you flagged as
understating the case because it omits builtin functions like `floor`. You are right
that the wording is a defect, and this is now a second independent demonstration of it.

Your `type` guard point is also confirmed: the guard only ever excluded **strings**
(`"7"` stays `"7"`). For every dangerous value `.==floor` is **true**, so the guard is
inert exactly where it matters.

## The safe form verified — and its precise failure boundary

```
walk(if type=="number" and (tostring|test("[.eE]")) and .==floor then floor else . end)
```

I tested it against the dangerous values and confirmed the gate **excludes every one**:

| value | gate `[.eE]` | old filter | new filter |
|---|---|---|---|
| 18446744073709551615 | false | 18446744073709552000 ✗ | **preserved** ✔ |
| 9007199254740993 (2^53+1) | false | 9007199254740992 ✗ | **preserved** ✔ |
| 123456789012345678901234567890 | false | 1.2345678901234568e+29 ✗ | **preserved** ✔ |
| 1.5 | true | 1.5 | 1.5 ✔ |
| 2 / 3 (plain ints) | false | 2 / 3 | **2 / 3** ✔ |

Note the last row, which is the elegant part of your fix and worth stating explicitly:
**plain integers now skip `floor` too**, so a table of small ids is no longer routed
through IEEE754 at all. The gate is doing more work than the old one, not less.

Behaviour on the original examples is unchanged, as you claimed — I diffed old vs new
on `{"a":1.0,"b":2.5,"c":3}`, `[1.0,2.5,{"x":1.0}]` and `{"s":"1.0"}`: **identical** in
all three (`1.0`→`1`, `2.5` untouched, string untouched).

## The one caveat — please read before anyone reuses this filter elsewhere

The gate is safe from *corruption*, but it is **not** a general "normalise my numbers"
filter, because `floor` still rewrites the **rendered form** of anything whose literal
contains `.` or an exponent. Verified:

```
$ echo '{"e":1e10,"f":1.0}' | jq -c 'walk( <new form> )'
{"e":10000000000,"f":1}          # 1e10 rendered as 10000000000; 1.0 rendered as 1
```

That is **not** data loss — `1e10 == (1e10|floor)` is `true`, and 1e10 is well inside
IEEE754 — but the *lexical* form changes, and if you are diffing files, hashing
canonical output, or round-tripping numbers as text, it will show up as a diff. The
reason is that such literals are small by construction, which is exactly what makes
`floor` harmless to the value and lossy to the text.

**Practical rule I'd suggest we all adopt:** use the safe form when the goal is *"make
integral-looking numbers print as integers"* and the values may be large ids. Do **not**
reach for it when you need byte-stable numeric text. I have not written this into any
ticket or docs — flagging it to you as the team-lead call on whether it becomes a
documented caveat alongside the filter.

  hardcode a big numeric literal in a jq *program*; feed it in as *input* (or via
  `--argjson`) and jq will preserve it. That is a genuinely useful CLI-level fact and
  I'd be happy to have it written up if you think it deserves a ticket of its own.

record away from hitting this, and his fu_2 asks for union-of-keys behaviour explicitly

his first object happens to be the widest).

whether a missing key could shift values into the wrong column — it cannot, because the row is
built as `[$h[] as $k | $o[$k]]`, so column *i* is always `$h[i]`. No reindexing hazard. The
damage is silent omission only, which is worth stating precisely so nobody over-corrects.

## 3. Fix — union the keys across all objects, in first-seen order

```
$ jq -r 'reduce (.[]|keys_unsorted[]) as $k ([]; if index($k) then . else . + [$k] end) as $h

```

`index($k)` is O(n) per key but n is a column count, so this is fine at report scale.

and `unique` **sorts**, so it silently turned discovery order into alphabetical order
(`{"b","a","c"}` came out `"a","b","c"`). That defeats the whole point of Case 1. The `reduce` +
`index` form is what actually preserves order.

108:   `jq -n '9007199254740993 + 0'` → `9007199254740992` (corrupted). So the literal
109:   alone is safe; it is the **unary minus or any arithmetic** that forces the double.

116:   `echo '<expr>' | jq .` only ever works for a bare literal, never for an expression —
117:   worth remembering before we spend time debugging a "jq is broken" report that is
