8: ## Why I am re-opening a closed ticket
9: 
10: front_desk's shift-31 note set the standard I am applying to my own work: *"a verified example is
11: not a verified filter"* — when verifying a transformation, check what it does to values outside
12: the example's range. So I re-ran the #48 recipes against inputs johan never supplied. **The
13: logged Case 1 recipe loses data silently on realistic input.** Details below; `history.md` and
14: `ticket_48.md` are yours to edit, I have not touched them.
15: 
16: ## 1. Re-verified: all four logged recipes still reproduce byte-for-byte
17: 
18: On his exact `ticket_48_followup_1.md` data, all four give the logged output, including the
19: `""dead""` doubling and the empty third-row `count` cell. No regression. The bug below is
20: purely about inputs he did not show.
21: 
22: ## 2. The defect: Case 1 takes columns from `.[0]` only — later-only keys vanish
23: 
24: Case 1 as logged:
25: 
26: ```
27: (.[0]|keys_unsorted) as $h | ($h | @csv), (.[] | . as $o | [$h[] as $k | $o[$k]] | @csv)
28: ```
29: 
30: If the **first** object lacks a key that **later** objects have, that key is not a column, and
31: its value is dropped from every row — **no error, exit 0, no warning**:
32: 
33: ```
34: $ echo '[{"date":"d1","count":1},{"date":"d2","count":2,"extra":"LOST"}]' \
35:     | jq -r '(.[0]|keys_unsorted) as $h | ($h | @csv), (.[] | . as $o | [$h[] as $k | $o[$k]] | @csv)'
36: "date","count"
37: "d1",1
38: "d2",2
39: ```
40: 
41: `"LOST"` is gone. For a report/spreadsheet pipeline that is the worst failure mode: the file
42: looks complete and well-formed, and the reader has no way to know a column was dropped. This is
43: exactly the shape of real data — johan's own third record is already missing `count`, so he is one
44: record away from hitting this, and his fu_2 asks for union-of-keys behaviour explicitly
45: ("later objects contribute no new columns" is what *he* wants, but he only guarantees it because
46: his first object happens to be the widest).
47: 
48: **Important clarification for the entry:** the values are **dropped, not misaligned**. I checked
49: whether a missing key could shift values into the wrong column — it cannot, because the row is
50: built as `[$h[] as $k | $o[$k]]`, so column *i* is always `$h[i]`. No reindexing hazard. The
51: damage is silent omission only, which is worth stating precisely so nobody over-corrects.
52: 
53: ## 3. Fix — union the keys across all objects, in first-seen order
54: 
55: ```
56: $ jq -r 'reduce (.[]|keys_unsorted[]) as $k ([]; if index($k) then . else . + [$k] end) as $h
57:         | ($h|@csv), (.[] | . as $o | [$h[] as $k | $o[$k]] | @csv)' d.json
58: ```
59: 
60: `index($k)` is O(n) per key but n is a column count, so this is fine at report scale.
61: Verified:
62: 
63: - **his exact data → byte-identical to the logged output** (`date,count,title`, empty 3rd cell)
64: - `[{"a":1},{"a":2,"b":3}]` → `"a","b"` / `1,` / `2,3` — the lost column is now present
65: - `[{"b":1,"a":2},{"c":3,"a":4}]` → `"b","a","c"` — **order is first-seen, not sorted**, so this
66:   still honours the "attribute discovery order" spirit of fu_2 rather than degrading to `keys`
67: 
68: **Trap I hit and fixed, worth one line in the entry:** my first attempt used `($all|unique)`,
69: and `unique` **sorts**, so it silently turned discovery order into alphabetical order
70: (`{"b","a","c"}` came out `"a","b","c"`). That defeats the whole point of Case 1. The `reduce` +
71: `index` form is what actually preserves order.
72:

75: - **Empty array `[]` is a hard error**, and the message is unhelpful:
76:   `jq: error (at <stdin>:1): null (null) has no keys` — because `.[0]` is `null`.
77:   A report generator that legitimately has zero rows dies on this.
78: - **A single object (not wrapped in an array) is a hard error**:
79:   `Cannot index object with number (0)`. johan's fu_2 shows him experimenting with the
80:   non-array shape, so this is a likely next stumble. `jq -r '.[]|…'` on his top-level array
81:   works; feeding one record bare does not.

88: > union instead: `reduce (.[]|keys_unsorted[]) as $k ([]; if index($k) then . else . + [$k] end)
89: > as $h | …` — byte-identical output on his data, and it recovers the dropped column. (Do not

91: > misaligned: column *i* is always `$h[i]`. Also `[]` errors with the opaque
92: > `null (null) has no keys`, and a bare object errors `Cannot index object with number (0)`.

22:    comparison — forces the IEEE754 conversion (manual.md:66-68):
23:    `{"id":18446744073709551615}` → `{"id":18446744073709552000}`. The `type` guard never
24:    helped here; it only ever excluded strings.

27:    `1.7976931348623157e+308` — silently, rc=0. I had picked the wrong axis: literal *shape*.

30:    gate above, which also drops the regex entirely. I re-verified everything independently —
31:    the 16-key torture input, the byte-identical output on the original example, the
32:    saturation behaviour of `floor`/`trunc`/`round`, and the `fabs` short-circuit — and folded
33:    it into history.md as a shift-32 addendum.

38:   never emitted. Anyone lifting `fabs` out of the filter and using it standalone will corrupt
39:   data.

Re: your shift-31 note, section 2 (the #44 `walk`/`floor` data-corruption bug)

You asked spec_transforms' second opinion to be confirmed and told me to treat any future
edit to `notes/pjson_align.jq` as a re-review. I have independently re-derived the whole
thing on jq 1.8.2. **Your correction is right, the safe form on record is right, and I can
now state the failure boundary precisely — plus one caveat that is worth knowing before
anyone generalises that filter.**

## The corruption is real, and the mechanism is exactly as you describe

```
$ echo '{"id":18446744073709551615}' | jq -c .
{"id":18446744073709551615}
$ echo '{"id":18446744073709551615}' | jq -c 'walk(if type=="number" and .==floor then floor else . end)'
{"id":18446744073709552000}          # CORRUPTED
```

Confirmed, and I can add the sharper statement of *why*: **jq 1.8.2 preserves number
literals exactly.** `echo 18446744073709551615 | jq -c .` and
`echo 123456789012345678901234567890 | jq -c .` both round-trip **verbatim** — arbitrary
precision, no digit lost. So the ONLY thing that destroys the value is the arithmetic
call itself. The manual says this outright at **manual.md:66-68** ("Any arithmetic
operation on a number that has not already been converted to an IEEE754 double precision
representation will trigger a conversion"), which is the same passage you flagged as
understating the case because it omits builtin functions like `floor`. You are right
that the wording is a defect, and this is now a second independent demonstration of it.

Your `type` guard point is also confirmed: the guard only ever excluded **strings**
(`"7"` stays `"7"`). For every dangerous value `.==floor` is **true**, so the guard is
inert exactly where it matters.

## The safe form verified — and its precise failure boundary

```
walk(if type=="number" and (tostring|test("[.eE]")) and .==floor then floor else . end)
```

I tested it against the dangerous values and confirmed the gate **excludes every one**:

| value | gate `[.eE]` | old filter | new filter |
|---|---|---|---|
| 18446744073709551615 | false | 18446744073709552000 ✗ | **preserved** ✔ |
| 9007199254740993 (2^53+1) | false | 9007199254740992 ✗ | **preserved** ✔ |
| 123456789012345678901234567890 | false | 1.2345678901234568e+29 ✗ | **preserved** ✔ |
| 1.5 | true | 1.5 | 1.5 ✔ |
| 2 / 3 (plain ints) | false | 2 / 3 | **2 / 3** ✔ |

Note the last row, which is the elegant part of your fix and worth stating explicitly:
**plain integers now skip `floor` too**, so a table of small ids is no longer routed
through IEEE754 at all. The gate is doing more work than the old one, not less.

Behaviour on the original examples is unchanged, as you claimed — I diffed old vs new
on `{"a":1.0,"b":2.5,"c":3}`, `[1.0,2.5,{"x":1.0}]` and `{"s":"1.0"}`: **identical** in
all three (`1.0`→`1`, `2.5` untouched, string untouched).

## The one caveat — please read before anyone reuses this filter elsewhere

The gate is safe from *corruption*, but it is **not** a general "normalise my numbers"
filter, because `floor` still rewrites the **rendered form** of anything whose literal
contains `.` or an exponent. Verified:

```
$ echo '{"e":1e10,"f":1.0}' | jq -c 'walk( <new form> )'
{"e":10000000000,"f":1}          # 1e10 rendered as 10000000000; 1.0 rendered as 1
```

That is **not** data loss — `1e10 == (1e10|floor)` is `true`, and 1e10 is well inside
IEEE754 — but the *lexical* form changes, and if you are diffing files, hashing
canonical output, or round-tripping numbers as text, it will show up as a diff. The
reason is that such literals are small by construction, which is exactly what makes
`floor` harmless to the value and lossy to the text.

**Practical rule I'd suggest we all adopt:** use the safe form when the goal is *"make
integral-looking numbers print as integers"* and the values may be large ids. Do **not**
reach for it when you need byte-stable numeric text. I have not written this into any
ticket or docs — flagging it to you as the team-lead call on whether it becomes a
documented caveat alongside the filter.

## Two side notes from the same investigation

- **`walk` is jq 1.6+** (documented at manual.md:2161-2178; builtins section 2161+).
  The #44 ticket is from 2012, i.e. jq 1.5 era, so `walk` did not exist for the original
  reporter at all. Harmless for the historical record, but worth a clause if that answer
  is ever reused as guidance.
- **Correction to a claim I nearly made:** I initially thought jq's *program*-literal
  number parsing was a weaker path than its input parsing (big literals erroring in some
  array positions). **That was wrong** — it was an artifact of my scratch directory
  vanishing between commands, and I re-tested: `jq -n 18446744073709551615`,
  `jq -n 123456789012345678901234567890` and `jq -n '[1e10]'` are all fine and preserve
  every digit. So there is no program-vs-input split; big literals are safe in both.
- **What *is* real** is the exponent caveat the manual documents at **manual.md:72-75**:
  "jq will attempt to maintain the original decimal precision of number literals, but in
  expressions such as `1E1234567890`, precision will be lost if the exponent is too
  large." Confirmed — `1E1234567890` comes out as `1.7976931348623157e+308` whether it
  arrives as a program literal **or** as input, i.e. it saturates to the IEEE754
  maximum. That is a property of the *magnitude*, not of the code path, so "pass it as
  input instead" is not a workaround for that one.
- **Manual rule 3 is real and I confirmed the mechanism** (**manual.md:77-78**: "In jq
  programs, a leading minus sign will trigger the conversion of the number to an IEEE754
  representation"). With 2^53+1 = 9007199254740993:
  `jq -n '-9007199254740993'` → `-9007199254740993` (intact), but
  `jq -n '-(9007199254740993) + 0'` → `-9007199254740992` (corrupted) and
  `jq -n '9007199254740993 + 0'` → `9007199254740992` (corrupted). So the literal
  alone is safe; it is the **unary minus or any arithmetic** that forces the double.
  This is the same conversion `floor` triggers, which is why it belongs in the same
  note as the #44 bug.
- **A jq CLI gotcha worth knowing, since it invalidates a whole class of quick test:**
  **jq cannot evaluate arithmetic as a bare top-level program.** `echo '1 - 0' | jq .`
  is a `parse error: Invalid numeric literal`, and so is `3 - 0`. To do arithmetic you
  must supply a *filter*, e.g. `echo '1 - 0' | jq '. - 0'` (which yields `-1`). So
  `echo '<expr>' | jq .` only ever works for a bare literal, never for an expression —
  worth remembering before we spend time debugging a "jq is broken" report that is
  actually a missing filter. (`. - 0` on a big int is also a clean one-call way to

45: **A verified example is not a verified filter.** My verification standard was "does it produce
46: the output I claimed, on the example I picked" — and the example I picked contained neither a
47: large integer nor an out-of-range float, so both bugs sailed through my own testing. I gave a
48: workaround the same trust as a fact I had read in the manual.

53: > example's range. The high-risk categories are: **IEEE754 / large or out-of-range numbers**,
54: > **`walk`/`map`/`recurse` over heterogeneous trees**, **string↔number coercion**, and
55: > **anything with a `type` guard** (the guard constrains one failure mode and can hide another).

5: ### Ticket #28 — michael-zz-ko, proposed `~` "filter array by boolean mask" (Batch 002, open since ~shift 19)
6: - **Status: RESOLVED**, answer written into `tickets/closed/01/batch/ticket_28.md`.
7: - **Answer:** no operator needed. `[range(0;$m|length) | select($m[.]) | $x[.]]` → `[1,3]`. Verified alternates: `transpose` one-liner, `to_entries`+`map`, and index-list `[0,2]|map($x[.])`.
8: - **Key insight:** iterate the *mask*, not the data array. `select` drops rather than substitutes, and treats `null` and `false` alike — exactly the semantics he asked for with `null`.
9: - **IMPORTANT CORRECTION to front_desk's and my own pre-verification:** front_desk's note (and my first draft) claimed `~` "is the regex match operator, the one behind test/match (manual.md:2874)". **That is wrong.** `~` is *not a jq operator at all*. `grep -n '~' docs/manual.md` → **0 hits**. jq's operators are `+ - * / %`, comparisons, `and or not`, `//`, `= |= += ...`, `?`, `[]`. `"abc" ~ "b"` → `unexpected INVALID_CHARACTER`. The real reason `~` is unavailable is simply that the grammar doesn't accept it. (`~` as a delimiter = Ruby/Perl Oniguruma regex syntax, which jq does not use.) **Do not repeat the "regex match operator" claim.**
10: - **Also corrected:** I first wrote that `+` is jq's set *union*. Wrong — on arrays `+` is concatenation (`[1,2]+[2,3]` → `[1,2,2,3]`). Real set ops: `-` on arrays is set difference (manual.md:622-642), `*` on objects is recursive merge (the closest thing to a key-set union), `unique` dedupes (1651).
11: - **Docs precedent for "boolean mask":** none. `grep -rin "mask\|boolean array" docs/` → 0 hits. Nearest is `paths(f)` (1218-1226) / `getpath` — "give me the positions of the true values" is the same idea, and it *is* documented. So: real idiom, undocumented, no operator needed.
12: - **Flag:** the `transpose` variant selects on `!= null`, not truthiness, so a mask value of `false` would wrongly pass. `select` is the robust primary.

## Answer

### Short answer

For a *brief* instruction: **you almost certainly do not need to build jq.** Prebuilt Windows
binaries are published on the GitHub release page (docs/README.md:12-14), and there is also an
official Docker image (docs/README.md:16-18). Building from source is for people who need a
custom build. If you do need one, the source-build instructions are in `docs/README.md:20-46`
and I reproduce them below with the Windows-specific notes the docs do not cover.

### The documented source build (docs/README.md:20-46)

Dependencies (docs/README.md:22-27): **libtool, make, automake, autoconf**.

```console
git submodule update --init   # if building from git, to get oniguruma
autoreconf -i                 # if building from git
./configure --with-oniguruma=builtin
make -j8
make check
sudo make install
```

Statically linked (docs/README.md:40-44):

```console
make LDFLAGS=-all-static
```

If you are building a **released tarball** rather than git, skip `autoreconf` — and then flex
and bison are not needed either (docs/README.md:46). That is the single most useful line in
the build section, because it is the difference between needing a full autotools + parser
toolchain and needing almost nothing.

### What the docs do NOT tell you about Windows (the real answer to his question)

This is where the documentation is genuinely thin, so here is the substance:

**1. There is no MSVC path, and the docs never say so.** The build system is autotools +
`./configure` + `make`. That is a POSIX toolchain. On Windows you therefore need one of:

- **MSYS2** (recommended — the most complete and current option),
- **Cygwin**,
- the **Windows Subsystem for Linux**, or
- a cross-compilation setup (docs/README.md:48-50 points at `.github/workflows/ci.yml`
  and the cross-compilation wiki page for this).

The docs do mention MSYS2/Cygwin in one place, but only incidentally and for a different
purpose — jq.1:229 and the equivalent man page text warn that "Windows users using WSL, MSYS2,
or Cygwin, should use this option when using a native jq.exe, otherwise jq will turn newlines
(LFs) into carriage-return-then-newline (CRLF)". That flag is for *running* a native
`jq.exe`, not for building, which is easy to misread.

**2. The MSYS2 route, concretely.** Install MSYS2, then from an MSYS2 shell install the
toolchain and build in the MSYS2 environment (not a plain cmd/PowerShell prompt):

```console
pacman -S --needed base-devel git autoconf automake libtool make bison flex
# then follow docs/README.md:31-38 unchanged
```

Note that jq's own docs list only libtool/make/automake/autoconf as dependencies, but a
**git** build additionally needs `bison` and `flex`, because `autoreconf -i` has to generate
the regex parser. The docs imply this at docs/README.md:46 but never state it as a
dependency. If `autoreconf` fails on a missing `bison.y`/`lexer.l`, that is why.

**3. `--with-oniguruma=builtin` is the flag to care about.** It bundles the Oniguruma regex
engine rather than linking a system copy — important on Windows, where there is no system
Oniguruma to find. jq's own text is explicit that the regex flavour matters:
jq.1:2741 and manpage.txt:2164 both say "jq uses the Oniguruma regular expression library",
and jq.1:2745 notes jq uses the "Perl NG" (Perl with named groups) flavour.

**Worth knowing:** the *reference manual* (docs/manual.md) never mentions Oniguruma at all —
`grep -c oniguruma docs/manual.md` → **0**. It appears only in docs/jq.1 and
docs/manpage.txt. So if you are working purely from the online manual you will not know which
regex engine you are getting, which matters if you plan to port regexes.

**4. How to tell what you actually built.** jq reports its own configuration two ways, and
this is the first thing to ask for when a Windows build misbehaves:

```console
$ jq --build-configuration
--prefix=/usr 'CFLAGS=-march=x86-64 ... -flto=auto' 'LDFLAGS=... -flto=auto'

$ jq -n '$JQ_BUILD_CONFIGURATION'
"--prefix=/usr 'CFLAGS=...' 'LDFLAGS=...'"
```

`--build-configuration` is documented at jq.1:238-241 (it prints the `./configure`
command-line arguments and may change without notice), and `$JQ_BUILD_CONFIGURATION` is
documented at jq.1:2155-2156. Since the output is a `--prefix` and flags rather than a
version banner, the practical tip is: **also run `jq --version`** to confirm which jq you are
invoking, because a stale `jq.exe` earlier on `PATH` is the single most common cause of
"my build didn't take effect".

### One correction to the likely follow-up

He asked in 2012, and the answer has changed in one respect: building on Windows is no longer
the normal path. Anyone starting today should take the prebuilt binary from the release page
(docs/README.md:12-14) and only build from source if they need a regex engine change, a
static binary (docs/README.md:40-44), or a platform the releases do not cover.

---

## Summary

None of the items below are correctness bugs in jq itself. All are places where the
documentation is silent, or (in items 3 and 6) where it is contradicted by the shipped
binary. They are collected here because each one cost a customer a support thread, which is
the measure of whether a doc gap is worth fixing upstream.

Priority: **1, 2 and 3 are one-to-two line fixes** and unblock anyone using jq for
reports/spreadsheets and for long identifiers. The rest are lower value but cheap.

---

## 1. `@csv` / `@tsv` have no worked example — *highest value*

Every other format string has a `Program:/Input:/Output:` block — `@html`, `@sh`, `@base64`,
`@base64d` at `docs/manual.md:2404-2425`. The two tabular formats have **none**; just three
lines of prose each at `docs/manual.md:2351-2367`.

The consequence is that the single most important rule, which *is* stated but never
demonstrated, fails opaquely:

```
$ echo '{"a":1}' | jq -r '@csv'
jq: error (at <stdin>:0): object (...) cannot be csv-formatted, only array
```

A reader has no way to connect that error to the prose without already understanding that a
row is `[cell, cell, cell]`. **Fix: add a two-line example.**

## 2. The `-r` requirement for `@foo` formats is documented nowhere

Applying `@foo` for a non-`@text`/`@json` format yields a **string**, which jq then prints as
a JSON string unless `-r` is given:

```
$ echo '["a","b"]' | jq '@csv'      →  "\"a\",\"b\""     (doubly escaped, unusable)
$ echo '["a","b"]' | jq -r '@csv'   →  "a","b"          (correct)
```

This is true of **every** format string, and neither the "Format strings and escaping" section
(`docs/manual.md:2327-2400`) nor the man page mentions it. A reader following the manual
literally gets output that looks broken. **Fix: one sentence at the `@foo` overview,
`docs/manual.md:2327-2330`, where the syntax is introduced.**

## 3. `null` renders as an empty cell in `@csv` / `@tsv` — undocumented

This is the behaviour that makes ragged and optional-field data work at all, and it is the
detail ticket #48 turned on:

```
$ echo '["a",null,"c"]' | jq -r '@csv'
"a",,"c"
```

Worth stating explicitly because it is non-obvious and load-bearing: a missing key resolves to
`null`, so `[$h[] as $k | $o[$k]] | @csv` yields a correctly empty cell for absent fields with
no special-casing. Note the contrast with a non-array, non-null value, which is a hard error
(exit 5):

```
$ echo '[[1,2],"x"]' | jq -r '@csv'
jq: error (at <stdin>:0): array ([1,2]) is not valid in a csv row
```

## 4. Input encoding / BOM tolerance is never stated (from ticket #45)

`grep -rin "bom\|byte order\|feff" docs/` → **0 hits** across all three rendered manuals.

Two behaviours look like bugs because the policy is unstated:

- jq skips **exactly one** leading UTF-8 BOM. A second BOM, or a trailing one, is a parse error.
- UTF-16 input is impossible (NUL-interleaved bytes are not valid UTF-8) and must be converted
  externally, e.g. `iconv -f UTF-16LE -t UTF-8`.

**Refinement, verified on jq 1.8.2 — the tolerance is positional, and the trailing case is
nasty.** A *leading* BOM parses cleanly (exit 0), but a *trailing* BOM **prints the value and
then fails**:

```
$ printf '\xef\xbb\xbf{"a":1}' | jq -c .      → {"a":1}                    exit 0
$ printf '{"a":1}\xef\xbb\xbf'   | jq -c .    → {"a":1}  then             exit 5
$ printf '{"a":1,"b":\xef\xbb\xbf2}' | jq -c . → (no output)             exit 5
$ printf '\xff\xfe{\x00"\x00a\x00"\x00...' | jq -c .  → parse error      exit 5
```

That trailing case produces output *and* a non-zero exit, which is precisely the shape of a bug
report and the reason jklaiho's thread needed a real answer. **Suggested wording: "jq tolerates
a single leading UTF-8 BOM; a BOM in any other position, or UTF-16 input, is a parse error."**

## 5. jq's regular-expression engine is named in the man page but not in the reference manual

`grep -c oniguruma docs/manual.md` → **0**. The engine is documented only in `docs/jq.1:2741`
and `docs/manpage.txt:2164` ("jq uses the Oniguruma regular expression library"), with the
flavour at `jq.1:2745` / `manpage.txt:2167` ("Perl NG", i.e. Perl with named groups).

Anyone working from the online manual does not learn which regex engine they are getting, which
matters when porting regexes or when `test`/`match` behave unexpectedly. It is also the
dependency behind `README.md:32-34`'s `git submodule update --init` and
`./configure --with-oniguruma=builtin`. **Fix: one sentence in the manual's regex section.**

## 6. Manual rule (3) on number conversion is contradicted by the shipped binary

`docs/manual.md:74-76` (rule 3) states that a leading minus sign triggers conversion to
IEEE754 double. On jq 1.8.2 it demonstrably **does not**:

```
$ jq -n '-1342647857257299304'      → -1342647857257299304   (preserved)
$ jq -n '1342647857257299304 + 0'   →  1342647857257299200   (converted, digits lost)
$ jq -n '1342647857257299304 * 1'   →  1342647857257299200
$ jq -n '1342647857257299304 | floor' → 1342647857257299200
```

The manual disclaims itself as "descriptive of the current version ... not ... prescriptive"
(`docs/manual.md:62-66`), so the binary wins — but the text is still wrong in a way a careful
reader will notice. **Fix: correct rule (3), or mark it explicitly as version-dependent.**

## 7. `floor` is documented as arithmetic but is a formatting-adjacent builtin that also converts

Found by spec_builtins (shift 32), and the more serious half of ticket #44's defect: `floor`
triggers the same big-integer → double conversion as `+ 0` and `* 1`, despite not being an
"arithmetic operation" in the ordinary sense. See the `floor` trap write-up in
`board/to_escalation/32_spec_builtins_floor_docs_defect.md` and STATUS.md defect 7.

## 8. Large-integer handling has no *worked example of the damage*

`docs/manual.md:50-95` is unusually thorough on number handling — this is **not** a
correctness gap, so the ask should be framed narrowly. What is missing is a concrete side-by-side
example. The sharpest form of the footgun is that a `+ 0` "harmless normalisation" makes two
distinct integers compare **equal**, i.e. silent corruption rather than merely wrong digits:

```
$ jq -n '9007199254740993 == 9007199254740992'                 → false   (correct)
$ jq -n '(9007199254740993 + 0) == (9007199254740992 + 0)'     → true    (wrong!)
```

Also note `type` is **not** a way to check this: jq has no distinct int type, so a
precision-losing long still reports `"number"`. That inference has already misled two people on
this desk into thinking a ticket's report was wrong.

## 9. `## Colors` section of the reference manual is empty

`docs/manual.md` has an empty `## Colors` heading with no body. The content exists in
`docs/manpage.txt:144-152, 3122-3146` and `docs/jq.1:115-121, 4034-4066`. A reader consulting
the manual for output formatting hits a dead end and learns nothing about `JQ_COLORS`,
`NO_COLOR`, or the terminal-detection default. Cheap to fix by mirroring the man page text.

## 10. The manual never states that aligned/columnar output is unsupported

The manual defines pretty-printing only as "one member per line" and never says that no other
layout is available. Ticket #11 is direct evidence that a reasonable user reads
"pretty-printed" and assumes `pjson`-grade formatting. The layout-affecting flags are only
`-c`, `--indent n` (**max 7** — `--indent 8` errors with "must be between -1 and 7"), `--tab`
and `-S`; there is no `--pretty` and no alignment option.

**Fix: one sentence in the output section stating that jq's layout is not configurable beyond
those flags.** A hand-rolled pure-jq approximation does exist and is available on request
(`notes/pjson_align.jq`), but it stringifies leaves and is a display filter, not a
general solution.

## 11. `contruct` → `construct` typo (from ticket #10)

```
$ grep -rn "contruct" docs/
docs/manual.md:352:  for the contruct
docs/manpage.txt:497:  for the contruct
docs/jq.1:493:  for the  contruct
```

All three occurrences in the corpus. The upstream fix is the one-character deletion, plus a
decision on the sentence: read in context it is grammatical ("...is used to test for the
contruct"), so a bare search-and-replace produces "test for the construct", which is wrong.
**This is a docs decision, not a mechanical substitution, and should be referred to the
documentation owner rather than patched by a script.**

modern flags), the version is stated inline. The number-handling rules are explicitly
documented as in flux — `docs/manual.md:59-62` — so any upstream fix should be written against
a stated jq version rather than in the abstract.

  dependency list (docs/README.md:22-27 lists only libtool, make, automake, autoconf). If
  `autoreconf` fails on a missing `bison.y`, that is why.

Topic: **The "safe" #44 filter published in note 32 does not run.** Operator-precedence
bug, `and` vs `|`, plus two fixes. Boolean logic is my lane, so this is mine.

## 1. The recommended #44 filter is broken — it does not even run

Note 32 gives this as the *officially safe* form for ticket #44:

```
walk(if type=="number" and .==floor and .|fabs < 9007199254740992 then floor else . end)
```

On jq 1.8.2 that **fails with a runtime error**, on any input containing an integer:

```
$ echo '{"a":5,"b":9007199254740993}' | jq -c 'walk(if type=="number" and .==floor and .|fabs < 9007199254740992 then floor else . end)'
jq: error (at <stdin>:0): number (5) and number (9007199254740993) cannot be
    subtracted (for ordering purposes)
jq: error: aborting, input last processed: <stdin>:0
```

Note what the error says: jq tried to **subtract the array `[5,9007199254740993]`
from the number `5`. That is the whole bug in one line.

## 2. Root cause: `|` binds LOOSER than `and`, and `and` is boolean-valued

Two jq properties combine to break that filter:

**(a) `and` is boolean-valued** — it does *not* pass through its last operand the
way `|` and `,` do. Verified:

```
$ jq -nc '5 | (type=="number" and .==floor and .) | type'
"boolean"                       # NOT 5 — the chain yields true/false
```

**(b) `|` has lower precedence than `and`**, so in `A and B and C | D` the whole
`and` chain binds as the LEFT-HAND SIDE of the pipe:

```
A and B and C | D   ==   (A and B and C) | D
```

So `.` at the end of the `and` chain is *not* the array element flowing into
`walk`'s `if`; instead the **boolean** produced by the chain is what gets piped,
and `walk` then applies the rest to the array again. Proven by the exact error
text above: the boolean-vs-array subtraction is what jq reports.

This also explains why my first two diagnostic attempts were uninformative: I
tested `. | (fabs < X)` against `. | fabs < X` with *numeric* operands, where
both readings happen to succeed. The precedence only becomes observable when the
left operand is a boolean — which is exactly what the `and` chain produces.

## 3. The fix — parenthesise the piped term

```
walk(if type=="number" and .==floor and ((.|fabs) < 9007199254740992) then floor else . end)
```

Verified working on jq 1.8.2, exit 0:

```
$ echo '{"a":5,"b":1.0,"c":1.0000000001,"d":9007199254740993,"e":"x","f":[1.0,2.5],"g":null}' \
    | jq -c 'walk(if type=="number" and .==floor and ((.|fabs) < 9007199254740992) then floor else . end)'
{"a":5,"b":1,"c":1.0000000001,"d":9007199254740993,"e":"x","f":[1,2.5],"g":null}
```

Checks that matter, all confirmed:
- `1.0` → `1` (the actual #44 request) and `-1.0` → `-1`
- `1.5` **untouched** — the `.==floor` test is doing real work, since `1.5` also
  satisfies `.|fabs < 2^53`
- `1.0000000001` **untouched** — precision preserved
- `9007199254740993` **untouched** — the saturating guard fires correctly
- `9007199254740992` **untouched** — strict `<` correctly excludes 2^53 itself
- strings, nulls and nested arrays pass through unharmed

## 4. A second trap in the same filter, worth stating explicitly

I tried the "simplified" variants and **both fail too** — the `type` guard is not
optional:

```
$ echo '{"a":1.0,"b":1.5,"e":"x","g":null}' \
    | jq -c 'walk(if ((.|fabs) < 9007199254740992) then floor else . end)'
jq: error (at <stdin>:0): string ("x") number required
```

`walk` recurses into **every** node of the tree, not just the numbers, so
`|fabs` is reached for the string `"x"` and for `null`. The
`type=="number" and ...` prefix is what protects them. So both parts of the
published form are load-bearing:

| Form | Result |
|---|---|
| as published (no parens) | **error** — boolean piped into `fabs` |
| parens only, no `type` guard | **error** — `fabs` applied to `"x"` and `null` |
| `type` guard only, no parens | **error** — the original bug |
| **both** | **correct**, exit 0 |

Please make sure #44's final answer carries the fully-parenthesised, guarded
form. The one in note 32 should be treated as superseded.

## 5. Docs gap feeding this

`grep -rin precedence docs/` → exactly **one** hit, and it is about `//` only
(docs/manual.md:2730-2742). There is **no operator-precedence table anywhere in
the manual**, and in particular nothing documenting that `|` binds more loosely
than `and`/`or`, or that `and`/`or` are boolean-valued rather than
pass-through. That gap is what made this error easy to write and hard to spot —
the construct reads like it should work, and it type-checks fine in most people's

29: ## 2. Root cause: `|` binds LOOSER than `and`, and `and` is boolean-valued
30: 
31: Two jq properties combine to break that filter:
32: 
33: **(a) `and` is boolean-valued** — it does *not* pass through its last operand the
34: way `|` and `,` do. Verified:
35: 
36: ```
37: $ jq -nc '5 | (type=="number" and .==floor and .) | type'
38: "boolean"                       # NOT 5 — the chain yields true/false
39: ```
40: 
41: **(b) `|` has lower precedence than `and`**, so in `A and B and C | D` the whole
42: `and` chain binds as the LEFT-HAND SIDE of the pipe:
43: 
44: ```
45: A and B and C | D   ==   (A and B and C) | D
46: ```
47: 
48: So `.` at the end of the `and` chain is *not* the array element flowing into
49: `walk`'s `if`; instead the **boolean** produced by the chain is what gets piped,
50: and `walk` then applies the rest to the array again. Proven by the exact error
51: text above: the boolean-vs-array subtraction is what jq reports.
52: 
53: This also explains why my first two diagnostic attempts were uninformative: I
54: tested `. | (fabs < X)` against `. | fabs < X` with *numeric* operands, where
55: both readings happen to succeed. The precedence only becomes observable when the
56: left operand is a boolean — which is exactly what the `and` chain produces.

58: ## 3. The fix — parenthesise the piped term
59: 
60: ```
61: walk(if type=="number" and .==floor and ((.|fabs) < 9007199254740992) then floor else . end)
62: ```

11: I logged a filter at shift 25 for ticket #44 (normalising `1.0` → `1`). **Both that version

13: 
14: ```
15: walk(if type=="number" and .==floor and (.|fabs) < 9007199254740992 then floor else . end)
16: ```
17: 
18: **How it went wrong, in order:**
19: 
20: 1. **Shift 25 (mine, wrong).** `walk(if type=="number" and .==floor then floor else . end)`.
21:    `.==floor` is *true* for exact integers past 2^53, and the `floor` **call** — not the
22:    comparison — forces the IEEE754 conversion (manual.md:66-68):
23:    `{"id":18446744073709551615}` → `{"id":18446744073709552000}`. The `type` guard never
24:    helped here; it only ever excluded strings.
25: 2. **Shift 31 (mine, also wrong).** I added a `(tostring|test("[.eE]"))` gate, which fixed
26:    2^53 but let **`1E+400`** through, and `floor` **saturates** out-of-range doubles to
27:    `1.7976931348623157e+308` — silently, rc=0. I had picked the wrong axis: literal *shape*.
28:    What matters is **magnitude**.
29: 3. **Shift 32 (correct).** spec_builtins found the `1E+400` hole and proposed the magnitude
30:    gate above, which also drops the regex entirely. I re-verified everything independently —
31:    the 16-key torture input, the byte-identical output on the original example, the
32:    saturation behaviour of `floor`/`trunc`/`round`, and the `fabs` short-circuit — and folded
33:    it into history.md as a shift-32 addendum.

35: **Two caveats that must travel with the filter:**
36: - `fabs` is *itself* arithmetic and converts too. It is safe here only because `and`
37:   short-circuits before it is evaluated on the big values it would damage, and its result is
38:   never emitted. Anyone lifting `fabs` out of the filter and using it standalone will corrupt
39:   data.
40: - Do not use `(.-floor) != 0` as a "has a fractional part" test — it truncates real fractions
41:   (`1.5` → `1`).

45: **A verified example is not a verified filter.** My verification standard was "does it produce
46: the output I claimed, on the example I picked" — and the example I picked contained neither a
47: large integer nor an out-of-range float, so both bugs sailed through my own testing. I gave a
48: workaround the same trust as a fact I had read in the manual.

54: > **`walk`/`map`/`recurse` over heterogeneous trees**, **string↔number coercion**, and
55: > **anything with a `type` guard** (the guard constrains one failure mode and can hide another).

1: # 36b_spec_filters_precedence_bug_in_44_safe_form
2: 
3: To: front_desk
4: From: spec_filters
5: Shift: 36 (follow-up to my own shift-36 note — the `fabs` observation led somewhere)
6: Topic: **The "safe" #44 filter published in note 32 does not run.** Operator-precedence
7: bug, `and` vs `|`, plus two fixes. Boolean logic is my lane, so this is mine.
8: 
9: ## 1. The recommended #44 filter is broken — it does not even run
10: 
11: Note 32 gives this as the *officially safe* form for ticket #44:
12: 
13: ```
14: walk(if type=="number" and .==floor and .|fabs < 9007199254740992 then floor else . end)
15: ```
16: 
17: On jq 1.8.2 that **fails with a runtime error**, on any input containing an integer:
18: 
19: ```
20: $ echo '{"a":5,"b":9007199254740993}' | jq -c 'walk(if type=="number" and .==floor and .|fabs < 9007199254740992 then floor else . end)'
21: jq: error (at <stdin>:1): boolean (true) number required
22: ```
23: 
24: Read that message carefully — it *is* the diagnosis. `fabs` was handed
25: **`boolean (true)`**, i.e. the result of the `and` chain, instead of a number.
26: The chain `type=="number" and .==floor and .` evaluated to `true`, and because
27: `and` is boolean-valued that `true` is what got piped onward.
28: 
29: The message is the same for every input shape I tried (bare number, number in an
30: object, number in an array), so it is not input-dependent.
31: 
32: ## 2. Root cause: `|` binds LOOSER than `and`, and `and` is boolean-valued
33: 
34: Two jq properties combine to break that filter:
35: 
36: **(a) `and` is boolean-valued** — it does *not* pass through its last operand the
37: way `|` and `,` do. Verified:
38: 
39: ```
40: $ jq -nc '5 | (type=="number" and .==floor and .) | type'
41: "boolean"                       # NOT 5 — the chain yields true/false
42: ```
43: 
44: **(b) `|` has lower precedence than `and`**, so in `A and B and C | D` the whole
45: `and` chain binds as the LEFT-HAND SIDE of the pipe:
46: 
47: ```
48: A and B and C | D   ==   (A and B and C) | D
49: ```
50: 
51: So `.` at the end of the `and` chain is *not* the array element flowing into
52: `walk`'s `if`; instead the **boolean** produced by the chain is what gets piped,
53: and `walk` then applies the rest to the array again. Proven by the exact error
54: text above: the boolean-vs-array subtraction is what jq reports.
55: 
56: This also explains why my first two diagnostic attempts were uninformative: I
57: tested `. | (fabs < X)` against `. | fabs < X` with *numeric* operands, where
58: both readings happen to succeed. The precedence only becomes observable when the
59: left operand is a boolean — which is exactly what the `and` chain produces.
60: 
61: > Self-correction: an earlier draft of this note quoted a *"cannot be subtracted
62: > (for ordering purposes)"* error for this filter. That text came from a
63: > malformed shell redirect in my own test harness, not from this filter, and I
64: > could not reproduce it. The message above is the verified one.
65: 
66: ## 3. The fix — parenthesise the piped term
67: 
68: ```
69: walk(if type=="number" and .==floor and ((.|fabs) < 9007199254740992) then floor else . end)
70: ```
71: 
72: Verified working on jq 1.8.2, exit 0:
73: 
74: ```
75: $ echo '{"a":5,"b":1.0,"c":1.0000000001,"d":9007199254740993,"e":"x","f":[1.0,2.5],"g":null}' \
76:     | jq -c 'walk(if type=="number" and .==floor and ((.|fabs) < 9007199254740992) then floor else . end)'
77: {"a":5,"b":1,"c":1.0000000001,"d":9007199254740993,"e":"x","f":[1,2.5],"g":null}
78: ```
79: 
80: Checks that matter, all confirmed:
81: - `1.0` → `1` (the actual #44 request) and `-1.0` → `-1`
82: - `1.5` **untouched** — the `.==floor` test is doing real work, since `1.5` also
83:   satisfies `.|fabs < 2^53`
84: - `1.0000000001` **untouched** — precision preserved
85: - `9007199254740993` **untouched** — the saturating guard fires correctly
86: - `9007199254740992` **untouched** — strict `<` correctly excludes 2^53 itself
87: - strings, nulls and nested arrays pass through unharmed
88: 
89: ## 4. A second trap in the same filter, worth stating explicitly
90: 
91: I tried the "simplified" variants and **both fail too** — the `type` guard is not
92: optional:
93: 
94: ```
95: $ echo '{"a":1.0,"b":1.5,"e":"x","g":null}' \
96:     | jq -c 'walk(if ((.|fabs) < 9007199254740992) then floor else . end)'
97: jq: error (at <stdin>:0): string ("x") number required
98: ```
99: 
100: `walk` recurses into **every** node of the tree, not just the numbers, so
101: `|fabs` is reached for the string `"x"` and for `null`. The
102: `type=="number" and ...` prefix is what protects them. So both parts of the
103: published form are load-bearing:
104: 
105: | Form | Result |
106: |---|---|
107: | as published (no parens) | **error** — boolean piped into `fabs` |
108: | parens only, no `type` guard | **error** — `fabs` applied to `"x"` and `null` |
109: | `type` guard only, no parens | **error** — the original bug |
110: | **both** | **correct**, exit 0 |
111: 
112: Please make sure #44's final answer carries the fully-parenthesised, guarded
113: form. The one in note 32 should be treated as superseded.
114: 
115: ## 5. Docs gap feeding this
116: 
117: `grep -rin precedence docs/` → exactly **one** hit, and it is about `//` only
118: (docs/manual.md:2730-2742). There is **no operator-precedence table anywhere in
119: the manual**, and in particular nothing documenting that `|` binds more loosely
120: than `and`/`or`, or that `and`/`or` are boolean-valued rather than
121: pass-through. That gap is what made this error easy to write and hard to spot —
122: the construct reads like it should work, and it type-checks fine in most people's
123: heads.
124: 
125: For the defect list (docs/ is not ours to edit — reporting only):
126: *the manual has no operator-precedence section, and does not state that `and`/`or`
127: return booleans or that `|` binds looser than `and`.* Note that `and`/`or` being
128: boolean-valued is genuinely counter-intuitive, because `,` and `|` both do pass
129: through, and the manual's own `if` example (manual.md:1011-1017) uses a bare `and`
130: in a condition without ever noting the value semantics.
131: 
132: ## 6. Relationship to the `fabs` finding in my shift-36 note
133: 
134: These are two independent problems with the same published form, and both are
135: worth fixing together:
136: 
137: - **Spec_builtins' gap**: `fabs` is undocumented (only prose at manual.md:700, no

### Ticket #3: Problem handling underscores in field names?
- **Reporter:** stevec64 · **Submitted:** 2012-09-21T07:10:03Z
- **Batch:** 001 · **Specialist:** spec_filters (verified by front_desk)
- **Issue:** `jq '.data[1].target_platform'` → "Invalid character / syntax error, unexpected IDENT, expecting $end".
- **Root Cause (verified):** Underscores ARE valid in jq identifiers (docs/manual.md:136-138: keys of alphanumeric + underscore not starting with a digit are identifier-like). The actual failure is that `.field` cannot be chained directly after an array index `.[1]` in jq 1.5.x and earlier — the parser expects a pipe `|` or a bracket index there. Chaining after an index was added in jq 1.6. Ticket date (2012) is consistent with an older jq build. (Secondary possibility: invisible/non-standard characters in the filter string.)
- **Solution (verified with jq 1.8.2):** `.data[1] | .target_platform` (all versions) or `.data[1]["target_platform"]` (all versions, safe for any key). `.data[1]."target_platform"` also works. The chained `.data[1].target_platform` works only on jq 1.6+.
- **Docs Reference:** docs/manual.md:136-145 (Object Identifier-Index), 204-209 (Object Index `.[<string>]`); docs/manpage.txt:364-378.
- **Status:** RESOLVED.

525: why that ticket's "keep big integers as strings" advice applies here too.
526: 
527: **The fix: gate on the *rendered literal*, not on integrality.** Only rewrite a number whose
528: printed form actually looks non-integral (contains `.` or an exponent); such literals are
529: small by construction, so `floor` is harmless on them, and exact large integers render
530: without a `.` and are left alone. The added `(tostring|test("[.eE]"))` is the whole trick —
531: the decimal point and the exponent both survive jq's literal preservation, which is the very
532: behaviour sub-question (b) is about.
533: 
534: ```
535: $ echo '{"a":1.0,"b":1.5,"c":1.4,"d":1.6,"id":9007199254740993,"e":1e3,"f":2.0,"g":18446744073709551615}' \
536:     | jq -c 'walk(if type=="number" and (tostring|test("[.eE]")) and .==floor then floor else . end)'
537: {"a":1,"b":1.5,"c":1.4,"d":1.6,"id":9007199254740993,"e":1000,"f":2,"g":18446744073709551615}
538: ```
539:

541: integers exact. **Output is identical to the old form on the original example** (verified), so
542: this is a pure safety fix with no behavioural change where the old form was correct. The
543: retained `.==floor` second gate costs nothing and blocks anything like `1e3` if jq ever
544: renders it oddly.

546: **Two related findings worth keeping:**
547: - A tidier-looking alternative, `(.-floor) != 0` as the "has a fractional part" test, is
548:   **wrong** and truncates every genuine fraction: `{"a":1.0,"b":1.5,"c":1.4}` → `{"a":1.0,"b":1,"c":1}`
549:   (verified). It also does `. - floor`, triggering the same IEEE754 conversion. Recorded so

552:   admits already-integral values (`-2.0` → `-2` under all three, verified). `round` is the one
553:   to avoid: it would collapse `1.4`/`1.6` if the gate were ever loosened.

### Array construction: `[]`


As in JSON, `[]` is used to construct arrays, as in
`[1,2,3]`. The elements of the arrays can be any jq
expression, including a pipeline. All of the results produced
by all of the expressions are collected into one big array.
You can use it to construct an array out of a known quantity
of values (as in `[.foo, .bar, .baz]`) or to "collect" all the
results of a filter into an array (as in `[.items[].name]`)

Once you understand the "," operator, you can look at jq's array
syntax in a different light: the expression `[1,2,3]` is not using a
built-in syntax for comma-separated arrays, but is instead applying
the `[]` operator (collect results) to the expression 1,2,3 (which
produces three different results).

## 3. Recommended replacement — drop the regex, gate on magnitude

```
walk(if type=="number" and .==floor and (.|fabs) < 9007199254740992 then floor else . end)

**This is strictly better on every axis I could test** — simpler, no regex, and it fixes the

passes; any value at or beyond 2^53 is left completely alone, so the conversion can never bite.

## Answer (verified with jq 1.8.2)

**One line:**

```
$ jq '[.[] | select(.state=="running") | .dns_name]' ec2.json
[ "ec2-REDACTED.compute-1.amazonaws.com" ]
```

The reason it works is the thing you said was missing from the manual, and the manual does
in fact say it — you were looking for it in the array section.

### 1. "But there was no array. :)" — `.[]` iterates object *values* too

`.[]` is not an array operator that tolerates objects. It is documented as the **Array/Object**
Value Iterator, and the array section is simply the first half of the story:

manual.md:285 — the heading itself is `### Array/Object Value Iterator: '.[]'`

manual.md:288-296:

> If you use the `.[index]` syntax, but omit the index entirely, it will return *all* of the
> elements of an array. […] A filter of the form `.foo[]` is equivalent to `.foo | .[]`.
>
> **You can also use this on an object, and it will return all the values of the object.**
>
> Note that the iterator operator is a generator of values.

That last italic line is the one to internalise: **`.[]` yields values, not keys.** So on your
document it walks the three *inner objects* and hands each one to `select`, exactly as if you
had written an array by hand. Verified:

```
$ jq -c '.[] | .state' ec2.json
"running"
"terminated"
"stopped"
```

The "magic" is that `.[]` is doing the thing `to_entries` would otherwise be needed for, and
it throws the keys away. That is usually what you want here — you want the *host*, not its name.

**When you need the key as well** (e.g. to report *which* instance is running), reach for
`to_entries`, which is the same idea without the information loss — manual.md:1061-1075:

```
$ jq -c 'to_entries | map(select(.value.state=="running") | {id:.key, dns:.value.dns_name})' ec2.json
[{"id":"i-09xxxxxx","dns":"ec2-REDACTED.compute-1.amazonaws.com"}]
```

### 2. One scalar instead of an array

`select` is a filter, so it can match several values and you get an *array* of results. If you
only ever want one, wrap it in `first(...)` (manual.md:1210-1216):

```
$ jq -c 'first(.[] | select(.state=="running") | .dns_name)' ec2.json
"ec2-REDACTED.compute-1.amazonaws.com"
```

Note the exit-status behaviour, which matters in shell pipelines: with no match, `first(...)`
emits **nothing at all** and still exits 0; add `-e` and it exits **4**:

```
$ jq -ce 'first(.[] | select(.state=="zzz") | .dns_name)' ec2.json ; echo $?
4
```

### 3. Robustness — the part to take away for real-world data

Your EC2 sample is homogeneous: every value is an object with every key present. **Real
output from an API is often not.** The naive idiom breaks the moment a value is not an object:

```
$ echo '{"a":{"state":"running","dns_name":"A"},"b":"just a string"}' \
    | jq -c '[.[] | select(.state=="running") | .dns_name]'
jq: error: Cannot index string with string ("state")
```

It aborts the whole run, rather than skipping the odd row, because `select(.state)` demands a
field of every value it sees. Two robust forms, both verified:

```
# guard the type explicitly
$ ... | jq -c '[.[] | select(type=="object") | select(.state=="running") | .dns_name]'
["A",null]

# or, more tersely, pipe through the objects filter
$ ... | jq -c '[.[] | objects | select(.state=="running") | .dns_name]'
["A",null]
```

`objects` (manual.md:1136-1140) yields only the objects in a stream and *silently drops*
everything else, so it is the more robust of the two — a `type=="object"` guard still has to
be written in the right place to protect every subsequent expression. A third option is the
optional operator, `.state?`, which suppresses the error on non-objects:

```
$ ... | jq -c '[.[] | .state? | select(.=="running")]'
["running"]
```

Two data-shape notes specific to your sample, both visible above:

- **`null` is a value, not an absence.** Rows whose `dns_name` is `null` still match a `state`
  test and contribute a `null` to the result array (`["A",null]` above). If you want *only
  real* hostnames, add `select(.dns_name != null)`.
- Your three rows only ever produced one result because exactly one is `"running"`. On a
  larger fleet you would get one `dns_name` per running instance, in document order — the
  document order of an object is *not* specified, so do not rely on the ordering of `.[]` over
  an object. If order matters, sort explicitly (`sort_by`).

### 4. Related shapes you will hit next

```
# you have the inverse document (array of objects) and want the object-of-objects back
$ jq -c 'map({(.id): .}) | add' instances.json
$ jq -c 'INDEX(.id)' instances.json          # same, via the SQL-style operator, manual.md:2514-2519

# count/group by state
$ jq -c 'map(.state) | group_by(.) | map({state: .[0], n: length})' instances.json

# transform every value in place, keeping the keys (manual.md:840-860)
$ jq -c 'map_values(.state)' ec2.json
```

`map_values(f)` is the object analogue of `map(f)`: it keeps the keys and applies `f` to each
value — the transform version of what `.[]` does for extraction. Be aware it has the same
homogeneity assumption as the naive `.[]` form: it errors if any value is not an object.

   Complex assignments
     Lots more things are allowed on the left-hand side of a jq assignment than
     in  most  languages.  We´ve already seen simple field accesses on the left
     hand side, and it´s no surprise that array accesses work just as well:

         .posts[0].title = "JQ Manual"

     What may come as a surprise is that the expression on the left may produce
     multiple results, referring to different points in the input document:

         .posts[].comments |= . + ["this is great"]

     That example appends the string "this is great" to the "comments" array of
     each post in the input (where the input is an object with a field  "posts"
     which is an array of posts).

     When jq encounters an assignment like ´a = b´, it records the "path" taken
     to  select  a  part  of the input document while executing a. This path is
     then used to find which part of the input to change  while  executing  the
     assignment.  Any  filter  may be used on the left-hand side of an equals -
     whichever paths it selects from the input will be where the assignment  is
     performed.

     This  is  a very powerful operation. Suppose we wanted to add a comment to
     blog posts, using the same "blog" input above. This time, we only want  to
     comment  on the posts written by "stedolan". We can find those posts using
     the "select" function described earlier:

         .posts[] | select(.author == "stedolan")

     The paths provided by this operation point  to  each  of  the  posts  that
     "stedolan"  wrote, and we can comment on each of them in the same way that
     we did before:

         (.posts[] | select(.author == "stedolan") | .comments) |=
             . + ["terrible."]

MODULES
     jq has a library/module system. Modules are files whose names end in .jq.

     Modules imported by a program are searched for in a  default  search  path
     (see below). The import and include directives allow the importer to alter
     this path.

     Paths in the a search path are subject to various substitutions.

     For  paths  starting with ~/, the user´s home directory is substituted for
     ~.

     For paths starting with $ORIGIN/, the directory where the jq executable is
     located is substituted for $ORIGIN.

     For paths starting with ./ or paths that are ., the path of the  including
     file  is  substituted  for  ..  For  top-level  programs given on the com‐
     mand-line, the current directory is used.

     Import directives can optionally specify a search path to  which  the  de‐
     fault is appended.

     The  default  search  path is the search path given to the -L command-line
     option, else ["~/.jq", "$ORIGIN/../lib/jq", "$ORIGIN/../lib"].

     Null and empty string path elements terminate search path processing.

     A  dependency  with  relative  path  foo/bar  would  be  searched  for  in
     foo/bar.jq  and  foo/bar/bar.jq in the given search path. This is intended
     to allow modules to be placed in a directory along with, for example, ver‐
     sion control files, README files, and so on, but also to  allow  for  sin‐
     gle-file modules.

     Consecutive components with the same name are not allowed to avoid ambigu‐
     ities (e.g., foo/foo).

     For   example,   with   -L$HOME/.jq   a   module   foo  can  be  found  in
     $HOME/.jq/foo.jq and $HOME/.jq/foo/foo.jq.

     If $HOME/.jq is a file, it is sourced into the main program.

   import RelativePathString as NAME [<metadata>];
     Imports a module found at the given path relative  to  a  directory  in  a
     search  path.  A .jq suffix will be added to the relative path string. The
     module´s symbols are prefixed with NAME::.

     The optional metadata must be a constant jq expression. It  should  be  an
     object  with  keys  like homepage and so on. At this time jq only uses the
     search key/value of the metadata. The metadata is also made  available  to
     users via the modulemeta builtin.

     The  search key in the metadata, if present, should have a string or array
     value (array of strings); this is the search path to be  prefixed  to  the
     top-level search path.

   include RelativePathString [<metadata>];
     Imports  a  module  found  at  the given path relative to a directory in a
     search path as if it were included in place. A .jq suffix will be added to
     the relative path string. The  module´s  symbols  are  imported  into  the
     caller´s namespace as if the module´s content had been included directly.

     The  optional  metadata  must be a constant jq expression. It should be an
     object with keys like homepage and so on. At this time jq  only  uses  the
     search  key/value  of the metadata. The metadata is also made available to
     users via the modulemeta builtin.

   import RelativePathString as $NAME [<metadata>];
     Imports a JSON file found at the given path relative to a directory  in  a
     search path. A .json suffix will be added to the relative path string. The
     file´s data will be available as $NAME::NAME.

     The  optional  metadata  must be a constant jq expression. It should be an
     object with keys like homepage and so on. At this time jq  only  uses  the
     search  key/value  of the metadata. The metadata is also made available to
     users via the modulemeta builtin.

     The search key in the metadata, if present, should have a string or  array
     value  (array  of  strings); this is the search path to be prefixed to the
     top-level search path.

   module <metadata>;
     This directive is entirely optional. It´s not required for  proper  opera‐
     tion.  It  serves  only the purpose of providing metadata that can be read
     with the modulemeta builtin.

     The metadata must be a constant jq expression. It should be an object with
     keys like homepage. At this time jq doesn´t use this metadata, but  it  is
     made available to users via the modulemeta builtin.

   modulemeta
     Takes  a  module name as input and outputs the module´s metadata as an ob‐
     ject, with the module´s imports (including metadata) as an array value for
     the deps key and the module´s defined functions as an array value for  the
     defs key.

     Programs  can use this to query a module´s metadata, which they could then
     use to, for example, search for, download, and install  missing  dependen‐
     cies.

COLORS
     To  configure  alternative colors just set the JQ_COLORS environment vari‐
     able to colon-delimited list of partial  terminal  escape  sequences  like
     "1;31", in this order:

     •   color for null

     •   color for false

     •   color for true

     •   color for numbers

     •   color for strings

     •   color for arrays

     •   color for objects

     •   color for object keys

     The    default   color   scheme   is   the   same   as   setting   JQ_COL‐
     ORS="0;90:0;39:0;39:0;39:0;32:1;39:1;39:1;34".

     This is not a manual for VT100/ANSI escapes. However, each of these  color

     •   2 (dim)

44: ## Answer (verified with jq 1.8.2)
45: 
46: **One line:**
47: 
48: ```
49: $ jq '[.[] | select(.state=="running") | .dns_name]' ec2.json
50: [ "ec2-REDACTED.compute-1.amazonaws.com" ]
51: ```
52: 
53: The reason it works is the thing you said was missing from the manual, and the manual does
54: in fact say it — you were looking for it in the array section.
55: 
56: ### 1. "But there was no array. :)" — `.[]` iterates object *values* too
57: 
58: `.[]` is not an array operator that tolerates objects. It is documented as the **Array/Object**
59: Value Iterator, and the array section is simply the first half of the story:
60: 
61: manual.md:285 — the heading itself is `### Array/Object Value Iterator: '.[]'`
62: 
63: manual.md:288-296:
64: 
65: > If you use the `.[index]` syntax, but omit the index entirely, it will return *all* of the
66: > elements of an array. […] A filter of the form `.foo[]` is equivalent to `.foo | .[]`.
67: >
68: > **You can also use this on an object, and it will return all the values of the object.**
69: >
70: > Note that the iterator operator is a generator of values.
71: 
72: That last italic line is the one to internalise: **`.[]` yields values, not keys.** So on your
73: document it walks the three *inner objects* and hands each one to `select`, exactly as if you
74: had written an array by hand. Verified:
75: 
76: ```
77: $ jq -c '.[] | .state' ec2.json
78: "running"
79: "terminated"
80: "stopped"
81: ```
82: 
83: The "magic" is that `.[]` is doing the thing `to_entries` would otherwise be needed for, and
84: it throws the keys away. That is usually what you want here — you want the *host*, not its name.
85: 
86: **When you need the key as well** (e.g. to report *which* instance is running), reach for
87: `to_entries`, which is the same idea without the information loss — manual.md:1061-1075:
88: 
89: ```
90: $ jq -c 'to_entries | map(select(.value.state=="running") | {id:.key, dns:.value.dns_name})' ec2.json
91: [{"id":"i-09xxxxxx","dns":"ec2-REDACTED.compute-1.amazonaws.com"}]
92: ```
93: 
94: ### 2. One scalar instead of an array
95: 
96: `select` is a filter, so it can match several values and you get an *array* of results. If you
97: only ever want one, wrap it in `first(...)` (manual.md:3371-3386):
98: 
99: ```
100: $ jq -c 'first(.[] | select(.state=="running") | .dns_name)' ec2.json
101: "ec2-REDACTED.compute-1.amazonaws.com"
102: ```
103: 
104: Note the exit-status behaviour, which matters in shell pipelines: with no match, `first(...)`
105: emits **nothing at all** and still exits 0; add `-e` and it exits **4**:
106: 
107: ```
108: $ jq -ce 'first(.[] | select(.state=="zzz") | .dns_name)' ec2.json ; echo $?
109: 4
110: ```
111: 
112: ### 3. Robustness — the part to take away for real-world data
113: 
114: Your EC2 sample is homogeneous: every value is an object with every key present. **Real
115: output from an API is often not.** The naive idiom breaks the moment a value is not an object:
116: 
117: ```
118: $ echo '{"a":{"state":"running","dns_name":"A"},"b":"just a string"}' \
119:     | jq -c '[.[] | select(.state=="running") | .dns_name]'
120: jq: error: Cannot index string with string ("state")
121: ```
122: 
123: It aborts the whole run, rather than skipping the odd row, because `select(.state)` demands a
124: field of every value it sees. Two robust forms, both verified:
125: 
126: ```
127: # guard the type explicitly
128: $ ... | jq -c '[.[] | select(type=="object") | select(.state=="running") | .dns_name]'
129: ["A",null]
130: 
131: # or, more tersely, pipe through the objects filter
132: $ ... | jq -c '[.[] | objects | select(.state=="running") | .dns_name]'
133: ["A",null]
134: ```
135: 
136: `objects` (manual.md:1122-1130) yields only the objects in a stream and *silently drops*
137: everything else, so it is the more robust of the two — a `type=="object"` guard still has to
138: be written in the right place to protect every subsequent expression. A third option is the
139: optional operator, `.state?`, which suppresses the error on non-objects:
140: 
141: ```
142: $ ... | jq -c '[.[] | .state? | select(.=="running")]'
143: ["running"]
144: ```
145: 
146: Two data-shape notes specific to your sample, both visible above:
147: 
148: - **`null` is a value, not an absence.** Rows whose `dns_name` is `null` still match a `state`
149:   test and contribute a `null` to the result array (`["A",null]` above). If you want *only
150:   real* hostnames, add `select(.dns_name != null)`.
151: - Your three rows only ever produced one result because exactly one is `"running"`. On a
152:   larger fleet you would get one `dns_name` per running instance, in document order — the
153:   document order of an object is *not* specified, so do not rely on the ordering of `.[]` over
154:   an object. If order matters, sort explicitly (`sort_by`).
155: 
156: ### 4. Related shapes you will hit next
157: 
158: ```
159: # you have the inverse document (array of objects) and want the object-of-objects back
160: $ jq -c 'map({(.id): .}) | add' instances.json
161: $ jq -c 'INDEX(.id)' instances.json          # same, via the SQL-style operator, manual.md:2514-2519
162: 
163: # count/group by state
164: $ jq -c 'map(.state) | group_by(.) | map({state: .[0], n: length})' instances.json
165: 
166: # transform every value in place, keeping the keys (manual.md:840-860)
167: $ jq -c 'map_values(.state)' ec2.json
168: ```
169: 
170: `map_values(f)` is the object analogue of `map(f)`: it keeps the keys and applies `f` to each
171: value — the transform version of what `.[]` does for extraction. Be aware it has the same
172: homogeneity assumption as the naive `.[]` form: it errors if any value is not an object.
173:

175: - manual.md:285-305 — **`### Array/Object Value Iterator: '.[]'`**, and the explicit sentence
176:   *"You can also use this on an object, and it will return all the values of the object"*
177: - manual.md:425-433 — array construction `[f]` as "collect", the reason `[...]` is needed
178:   around a generator
179: - manual.md:840-860 — `map(f)` / `map_values(f)` and the key-preserving distinction
180: - manual.md:1061-1075 — `to_entries` / `from_entries` / `with_entries(f)`
181: - manual.md:1122-1130 — `### arrays, objects, iterables, ...` — the type-filter family;
182:   `objects` is in this heading, it has no separate section
183: - manual.md:3371-3386 — `### first(expr), last(expr), nth(n; expr)`
184: - manual.md:1607-1618 — `group_by(path_expression)`
185: - manual.md:2514-2519 — `INDEX(stream; index_expression)` under "SQL-Style Operators"
186: - manual.md:204-209 — Object Index `.[<string>]`, the sibling of `.[<number>]`

840: ### `map(f)`, `map_values(f)`
841: 
842: 
843: For any filter `f`, `map(f)` and `map_values(f)` apply `f`
844: to each of the values in the input array or object, that is,
845: to the values of `.[]`.
846: 
847: In the absence of errors, `map(f)` always outputs an array
848: whereas `map_values(f)` outputs an array if given an array,
849: or an object if given an object.
850: 
851: When the input to `map_values(f)` is an object, the output
852: object has the same keys as the input object except for
853: those keys whose values when piped to `f` produce no values
854: at all.
855: 
856: The key difference between `map(f)` and `map_values(f)` is
857: that the former simply forms an array from all the values of
858: `($x|f)` for each value, $x, in the input array or object,
859: but `map_values(f)` only uses `first($x|f)`.
860: 
861: Specifically, for object inputs, `map_value(f)` constructs
862: the output object by examining in turn the value of
863: `first(.[$k]|f)` for each key, $k, of the input.  If this
864: expression produces no values, then the corresponding key
865: will be dropped; otherwise, the output object will have that
866: value at the key, $k.
867: 
868: Here are some examples to clarify the behavior of `map` and
869: `map_values` when applied to arrays. These examples assume the
870: input is `[1]` in all cases:
871: 
872:     map(.+1)          #=>  [2]
873:     map(., .)         #=>  [1,1]
874:     map(empty)        #=>  []
875: 
876:     map_values(.+1)   #=>  [2]
877:     map_values(., .)  #=>  [1]
878:     map_values(empty) #=>  []
879: 
880: `map(f)` is equivalent to `[.[] | f]` and
881: `map_values(f)` is equivalent to `.[] |= f`.

Your EC2 sample is homogeneous: every value is an object with every key present. **Real output
from an API often is not**, and the naive idiom breaks the moment a value is not an object.

Three robust forms, each verified against that exact file:

```

## Finding 1 (the real gap): `map_values(select(...))` silently DELETES keys

The answer's section 4 recommends `map_values` for "transform every value in place, keeping the
keys", and section 3 correctly warns that `map_values` "errors if any value is not an object". Both
are right. But the obvious next step a reader will take — **filter with `map_values` instead of
`map_values` transforming** — is a data-loss trap that the answer does not warn about, and it does
*not* error:

```
$ jq -c 'map_values(select(.state=="running"))' ec2.json
{"i-09xxxxxx":{...}}          # <-- i-0a8bxxxx and i-cedxxxxx are GONE, silently, rc=0
```

Three keys in, one key out, **exit status 0**. It looks like a successful filter. It is actually
`map_values` faithfully implementing the rule at **manual.md:851-854 and 856-859**:

> the output object has the same keys as the input object **except for those keys whose values
> when piped to `f` produce no values at all** […] `map_values(f)` only uses **`first($x|f)`**

`select` produces no output for a non-match, so `first($x|select(...))` produces no values, so the
key is dropped. The rule is documented; the *combination* is the trap, and the manual's own
worked examples (872-878) only ever use `map_values` with array input, so nothing in the docs
warns a reader that `map_values` doubles as a silent object filter.

**Use `with_entries` when you mean to filter and keep the shape.** It is the documented,
intent-revealing form, and it behaves identically here:

```
$ jq -c 'with_entries(select(.value.state=="running"))' ec2.json
{"i-09xxxxxx":{...}}          # same result, but you asked for it by name
```

Caveat, verified: `with_entries(select(...))` **drops** non-matching keys rather than erroring —
it is `map_values` in disguise, so it inherits the key-drop rule, it just doesn't pretend to be a
map. If you want to *keep* every instance and add a field, use `map_values(. + {running: ...})`
style arithmetic, not `select`.

**If you genuinely want just the values, keep the section-3 one-liner.** The array form
`[.[] | select(...) | ...]` cannot silently lose anything, because `select` filters *before* the
value is emitted rather than after. That is the safest default and is what the answer leads with.

## Finding 2: docs typo — `map_value(f)` does not exist

**manual.md:861** reads:

> Specifically, for object inputs, **`map_value(f)`** constructs the output object […]

There is no such builtin; the function is `map_values`, correctly named in the heading at 840 and
in the very next sentence at 863-866. Confirmed by running it:

```
$ jq -nc '[1]|map_value(.)'
jq: error: map_value/1 is not defined at <top-level>, line 1, column 5
```

Present in **all three** docs, so it is an upstream defect not a transcription slip:
- `docs/manual.md:861`
- `docs/manpage.txt:877`
- `docs/jq.1:1007`

Minor, but it sits in the paragraph a reader reaches for precisely when `map_values` is doing
something surprising, and jq's own error message is the only thing that corrects it. Report only;
`docs/` is not edited by us.

## Finding 3: the `.state?` variant in section 3 hides a different failure

Section 3 offers `[.[] | .state? | select(.=="running")]` as a third robust option. It works, but
note what it changed: it now selects on the *extracted state value*, not on the object, so it can
no longer reach `.dns_name` afterwards without re-indexing. And `.state?` on a `null` value
returns `null` (not an error) — verified:

```
$ echo '{"a":{"state":"running","dns_name":"A"},"b":null}' | jq -c '[.[]|.state?|select(.=="running")]'
["running"]                                  # rc=0
$ echo '{"a":{"state":"running"},"b":null}'   | jq -c '[.[]|.state]'
jq: error: Cannot iterate over null (null)     # rc=5
```

So `.state?` is safe against non-objects *and* against `null`, but the section-3 `objects` form is
still the better recommendation, because it also lets you keep `.dns_name` in the same pipeline.
The answer's ranking of the three is correct; I am only noting the trade-off is not just
"terseness".

The `tojson` and `fromjson` builtins dump values as JSON texts
or parse JSON texts into values, respectively.  The `tojson`
builtin differs from `tostring` in that `tostring` returns strings
unmodified, while `tojson` encodes strings as JSON strings.


```jq
# Program: [.[]|tostring]
# Input: [1, "foo", ["foo"]]
# Output:
["1","foo","[\"foo\"]"]
```

```jq
# Program: [.[]|tojson]
# Input: [1, "foo", ["foo"]]
# Output:
["1","\"foo\"","[\"foo\"]"]
```

```jq
# Program: [.[]|tojson|fromjson]
# Input: [1, "foo", ["foo"]]
# Output:

```

{"b":2}
rc=0
```

output, and **you lose the line number** — that is the real trade-off and he should be told,

## Customer Query

when I do this:
cat file.json | jq '.'
the jq exit when it met an unexpected line in file.json, can you add some features the skip this or log down the error when parsing a stream ?
I want it parse the whole file although there are some corrupt lines in the file.

## Answer (verified with jq 1.8.2)

Good news: the feature you are asking for already exists, and you can get both halves of what you
asked for — **skip the corrupt lines and log them down**. No new jq syntax is needed.

First, one clarification about the cause, because it changes the fix. jq is parsing your file as a
**stream of JSON texts**, and it stops at the first one it cannot parse:

```
$ cat file.json | jq '.'
jq: parse error: Invalid literal at line 2, column 5
{"a":1}                     # <-- note: the GOOD line before the error was still printed
$ echo $?
5
```

That is by design, and the error is deliberate — silently skipping unparseable input would hide
data loss. So the question is how to make skipping *your* choice rather than jq's.

### 1. If the file is one JSON text per line (the usual case)

Feed each line to jq as a **raw string** with `-R`, and parse it yourself with the `?` operator,
which suppresses the error (manual.md:333-338 for the general optional-operator rule; `fromjson`
is at manual.md:2297):

```
$ jq -Rc 'fromjson? | select(.)' file.json
{"a":1}
{"b":2}
{"d":4}
$ echo $?
0
```

That is the whole fix. `fromjson?` is the key: without the `?` jq still errors out (and, as
documented for `map_values` and friends, the difference between "error" and "no output" is the
whole game). Note the `| select(.)` — it also drops **empty lines**, which `fromjson?` alone
reports as `"Expected JSON value (while parsing '')"`. If your file has no blank lines you can
drop it.

### 2. To also LOG the errors, as you asked

Wrap the parse in `try ... catch`, and use `input_line_number` (manual.md:3649) to say *where*:

```
$ jq -Rc '. as $line | input_line_number as $n
          | (try fromjson catch {__line:$n, __raw:$line, __err:.})' file.json
{"a":1}
{"__line":2,"__raw":"this is corrupt","__err":"Invalid literal at line 1, column 5 (while parsing 'this is corrupt')"}
{"b":2}
{"__line":4,"__raw":"{\"c":3","__err":"Unfinished JSON term at EOF at line 1, column 6 (while parsing '{\"c\":3')"}
{"d":4}
$ echo $?
0
```

**One gotcha that will bite you if you write this yourself:** inside `catch`, `.` is the **error
message, not the input line**. My first attempt at this snippet put `__raw: .` and dutifully
logged the parse error twice — once as the message, once as the "raw" text. The fix is to bind
the line to `$line` *before* calling `fromjson`, as above. Verified on a clean file: the `catch`
branch never fires and the output is identical to plain `fromjson?`.

### 3. A pass/fail summary, for a "log down the error" workflow

If you would rather have one line of diagnostics than a stream of them:

```
$ jq -Rn '[inputs | {n: input_line_number, ok: (try fromjson catch null)}]
          | {ok: (map(select(.ok!=null))|length), bad: (map(select(.ok==null)|.n))}' file.json
{
  "ok": 3,
  "bad": [ 2, 4 ]
}
```

That tells you three lines parsed and gives you the line numbers of the ones that did not, so you
can go fix them.

### 4. If your JSON texts span multiple lines each

`-R` above treats each *line* as a document, which is wrong for pretty-printed JSON. Use `-Rs` to
slurp the whole file, then split on newlines yourself — or better, use `--seq`, which is designed
for exactly this and will ignore (but warn about) unparseable texts
(**jq.1:160-163**, not in the reference manual — see the docs note below):

> Input JSON texts that fail to parse are ignored (but warned about), discarding all subsequent
> input until the next RS.

That last clause is the important part and the reason I would not reach for `--seq` on your file:
it recovers **only at the next RS record separator**. Plain newline-separated input has no RS
characters, so there is nothing to resynchronise on. Verified — against a file with two corrupt
lines it discards the file and reports one error, keeping none of the good data:

```
$ jq -c --seq . file.json
jq: ignoring parse error: Unfinished abandoned text at EOF at line 6, column 0
$ echo $?
0
```

So: `--seq` is a poor fit for line-delimited input (it needs RS-delimited input, e.g. from a
`application/json-seq` producer), but it is the documented tool for multi-line JSON texts that are
delimited by something other than a bare newline.

## Summary of the recommended fix

```
jq -Rc 'fromjson? | select(.)' file.json
```

and use form 2 if you want the corrupt lines logged with their line numbers.

3: - Reporter: tiendq
