8: ## Customer Query
9: 
10: > Is there any one can give me a brief instruction to build jq for Windows?
11: >
12: > Thanks,
13: > Tien
14: 
15: ## Answer
16: 
17: ### Short answer
18: 
19: For a *brief* instruction: **you almost certainly do not need to build jq.** Prebuilt Windows
20: binaries are published on the GitHub release page (docs/README.md:12-14), and there is also an
21: official Docker image (docs/README.md:16-18). Building from source is for people who need a
22: custom build. If you do need one, the source-build instructions are in `docs/README.md:20-46`
23: and I reproduce them below with the Windows-specific notes the docs do not cover.
24: 
25: ### The documented source build (docs/README.md:20-46)
26: 
27: Dependencies (docs/README.md:22-27): **libtool, make, automake, autoconf**.
28: 
29: ```console
30: git submodule update --init   # if building from git, to get oniguruma
31: autoreconf -i                 # if building from git
32: ./configure --with-oniguruma=builtin
33: make -j8
34: make check
35: sudo make install
36: ```
37: 
38: Statically linked (docs/README.md:40-44):
39: 
40: ```console
41: make LDFLAGS=-all-static
42: ```
43: 
44: If you are building a **released tarball** rather than git, skip `autoreconf` — and then flex
45: and bison are not needed either (docs/README.md:46). That is the single most useful line in
46: the build section, because it is the difference between needing a full autotools + parser
47: toolchain and needing almost nothing.
48: 
49: ### What the docs do NOT tell you about Windows (the real answer to his question)
50: 
51: This is where the documentation is genuinely thin, so here is the substance:
52: 
53: **1. There is no MSVC path, and the docs never say so.** The build system is autotools +
54: `./configure` + `make`. That is a POSIX toolchain. On Windows you therefore need one of:
55: 
56: - **MSYS2** (recommended — the most complete and current option),
57: - **Cygwin**,
58: - the **Windows Subsystem for Linux**, or
59: - a cross-compilation setup (docs/README.md:48-50 points at `.github/workflows/ci.yml`
60:   and the cross-compilation wiki page for this).
61: 
62: The docs do mention MSYS2/Cygwin in one place, but only incidentally and for a different
63: purpose — jq.1:229 and the equivalent man page text warn that "Windows users using WSL, MSYS2,
64: or Cygwin, should use this option when using a native jq.exe, otherwise jq will turn newlines
65: (LFs) into carriage-return-then-newline (CRLF)". That flag is for *running* a native
66: `jq.exe`, not for building, which is easy to misread.
67: 
68: **2. The MSYS2 route, concretely.** Install MSYS2, then from an MSYS2 shell install the
69: toolchain and build in the MSYS2 environment (not a plain cmd/PowerShell prompt):
70: 
71: ```console
72: pacman -S --needed base-devel git autoconf automake libtool make bison flex
73: # then follow docs/README.md:31-38 unchanged
74: ```
75: 
76: Note that jq's own docs list only libtool/make/automake/autoconf as dependencies, but a
77: **git** build additionally needs `bison` and `flex`, because `autoreconf -i` has to generate
78: the regex parser. The docs imply this at docs/README.md:46 but never state it as a
79: dependency. If `autoreconf` fails on a missing `bison.y`/`lexer.l`, that is why.
80: 
81: **3. `--with-oniguruma=builtin` is the flag to care about.** It bundles the Oniguruma regex
82: engine rather than linking a system copy — important on Windows, where there is no system
83: Oniguruma to find. jq's own text is explicit that the regex flavour matters:
84: jq.1:2741 and manpage.txt:2164 both say "jq uses the Oniguruma regular expression library",
85: and jq.1:2745 notes jq uses the "Perl NG" (Perl with named groups) flavour.
86: 
87: **Worth knowing:** the *reference manual* (docs/manual.md) never mentions Oniguruma at all —
88: `grep -c oniguruma docs/manual.md` → **0**. It appears only in docs/jq.1 and
89: docs/manpage.txt. So if you are working purely from the online manual you will not know which
90: regex engine you are getting, which matters if you plan to port regexes.
91: 
92: **4. How to tell what you actually built.** jq reports its own configuration two ways, and
93: this is the first thing to ask for when a Windows build misbehaves:
94: 
95: ```console
96: $ jq --build-configuration
97: --prefix=/usr 'CFLAGS=-march=x86-64 ... -flto=auto' 'LDFLAGS=... -flto=auto'
98: 
99: $ jq -n '$JQ_BUILD_CONFIGURATION'
100: "--prefix=/usr 'CFLAGS=...' 'LDFLAGS=...'"
101: ```
102: 
103: `--build-configuration` is documented at jq.1:238-241 (it prints the `./configure`
104: command-line arguments and may change without notice), and `$JQ_BUILD_CONFIGURATION` is
105: documented at jq.1:2155-2156. Since the output is a `--prefix` and flags rather than a
106: version banner, the practical tip is: **also run `jq --version`** to confirm which jq you are
107: invoking, because a stale `jq.exe` earlier on `PATH` is the single most common cause of
108: "my build didn't take effect".
109: 
110: ### One correction to the likely follow-up
111: 
112: He asked in 2012, and the answer has changed in one respect: building on Windows is no longer
113: the normal path. Anyone starting today should take the prebuilt binary from the release page
114: (docs/README.md:12-14) and only build from source if they need a regex engine change, a
115: static binary (docs/README.md:40-44), or a platform the releases do not cover.
116:

120: - `docs/README.md:20-46` — Building from source: dependencies, instructions, static build,

122: - `docs/README.md:48-50` — Cross-compilation pointers
123: - `docs/jq.1:238-241` — `--build-configuration`
124: - `docs/jq.1:2155-2156` — `$JQ_BUILD_CONFIGURATION`
125: - `docs/jq.1:2741`, `docs/jq.1:2745`, `docs/manpage.txt:2164-2167` — Oniguruma and the
126:   "Perl NG" regex flavour
127: - `docs/jq.1:229` — the WSL/MSYS2/Cygwin newline caveat (running, not building)

131: RESOLVED. Answered from docs/README.md (the only place build instructions exist — the
132: reference manual and the tutorial have none), extended with the Windows-specific toolchain

136: ## Addendum (shift 35) — shell quoting on Windows, and two corrections
137: 
138: ### Shell quoting differs per Windows shell
139: 
140: Verified on jq 1.8.2 and confirmed against `docs/manpage.txt:70-82` / `docs/jq.1:41`:
141: 
142: | Shell | How to wrap the program |
143: |---|---|
144: | Unix shells | `jq '.["foo"]'` |
145: | PowerShell / pwsh | `jq '.[\"foo\"]'` — single quotes outside, `\"` inside |
146: | cmd.exe | `jq ".[\"foo\"]"` — double quotes outside, `\"` inside |
147: 
148: All three return `1` for input `{"foo":1}`. Note the escaping is *not* optional on Windows:
149: `jq '.foo'` is a different program from `jq ".\"foo\""`, and an unescaped inner quote is a
150: shell syntax error, not a jq one. This is the same shell-vs-jq distinction that dominates most
151: of the tickets in Batch 002 — the error text has no `jq:` prefix and no `<top-level>` marker.
152: 
153: ### One correction to the main answer: `-b/--binary` is about *running*, not building
154: 
155: The main answer above implies the WSL/MSYS2/Cygwin mention (jq.1:229) is a build concern. It
156: is not. From `docs/manpage.txt:264` / `docs/jq.1:229`, that text is in the documentation for
157: `-b/--binary`: WSL, MSYS2 and Cygwin users should pass it so that jq does not turn newlines
158: (LFs) into carriage-return-then-newline (CRLF) when talking to a native `jq.exe`. It has
159: nothing to do with compiling, and it is the reason a jq build can appear to work but mangle
160: every line ending in the output. **Check for it if his output has stray CRs.**
161:

# Ticket #53: do exit if parse error

- Reporter: gihnius
- Submitted: 2012-12-20T07:28:05Z
- Status: RESOLVED (answered by spec_filters, shift 39; verified on jq 1.8.2)
- Assigned: spec_filters

## Customer Query

when I do this:
cat file.json | jq '.'
the jq exit when it met an unexpected line in file.json, can you add some features the skip this or log down the error when parsing a stream ?
I want it parse the whole file although there are some corrupt lines in the file.

## Answer (verified with jq 1.8.2)

Good news: the feature you are asking for already exists, and you can get both halves of what you
asked for — **skip the corrupt lines and log them down**. No new jq syntax is needed.

First, one clarification about the cause, because it changes the fix. jq is parsing your file as a
**stream of JSON texts**, and it stops at the first one it cannot parse:

```
$ cat file.json | jq '.'
jq: parse error: Invalid literal at line 2, column 5
{"a":1}                     # <-- note: the GOOD line before the error was still printed
$ echo $?
5
```

That is by design, and the error is deliberate — silently skipping unparseable input would hide
data loss. So the question is how to make skipping *your* choice rather than jq's.

### 1. If the file is one JSON text per line (the usual case)

Feed each line to jq as a **raw string** with `-R`, and parse it yourself with the `?` operator,
which suppresses the error (manual.md:333-338 for the general optional-operator rule; `fromjson`
is at manual.md:2297):

```
$ jq -Rc 'fromjson? | select(.)' file.json
{"a":1}
{"b":2}
{"d":4}
$ echo $?
0
```

That is the whole fix. `fromjson?` is the key: without the `?` jq still errors out (and, as
documented for `map_values` and friends, the difference between "error" and "no output" is the
whole game). Note the `| select(.)` — it also drops **empty lines**, which `fromjson?` alone
reports as `"Expected JSON value (while parsing '')"`. If your file has no blank lines you can
drop it.

### 2. To also LOG the errors, as you asked

Wrap the parse in `try ... catch`, and use `input_line_number` (manual.md:3649) to say *where*:

```
$ jq -Rc '. as $line | input_line_number as $n
          | (try fromjson catch {__line:$n, __raw:$line, __err:.})' file.json
{"a":1}
{"__line":2,"__raw":"this is corrupt","__err":"Invalid literal at line 1, column 5 (while parsing 'this is corrupt')"}
{"b":2}
{"__line":4,"__raw":"{\"c":3","__err":"Unfinished JSON term at EOF at line 1, column 6 (while parsing '{\"c\":3')"}
{"d":4}
$ echo $?
0
```

**One gotcha that will bite you if you write this yourself:** inside `catch`, `.` is the **error
message, not the input line**. My first attempt at this snippet put `__raw: .` and dutifully
logged the parse error twice — once as the message, once as the "raw" text. The fix is to bind
the line to `$line` *before* calling `fromjson`, as above. Verified on a clean file: the `catch`
branch never fires and the output is identical to plain `fromjson?`.

### 3. A pass/fail summary, for a "log down the error" workflow

If you would rather have one line of diagnostics than a stream of them:

```
$ jq -Rn '[inputs | {n: input_line_number, ok: (try fromjson catch null)}]
          | {ok: (map(select(.ok!=null))|length), bad: (map(select(.ok==null)|.n))}' file.json
{
  "ok": 3,
  "bad": [ 2, 4 ]
}
```

That tells you three lines parsed and gives you the line numbers of the ones that did not, so you
can go fix them.

### 4. If your JSON texts span multiple lines each

`-R` above treats each *line* as a document, which is wrong for pretty-printed JSON. Use `-Rs` to
slurp the whole file, then split on newlines yourself — or better, use `--seq`, which is designed
for exactly this and will ignore (but warn about) unparseable texts
(**jq.1:160-163**, not in the reference manual — see the docs note below):

> Input JSON texts that fail to parse are ignored (but warned about), discarding all subsequent
> input until the next RS.

That last clause is the important part and the reason I would not reach for `--seq` on your file:
it recovers **only at the next RS record separator**. Plain newline-separated input has no RS
characters, so there is nothing to resynchronise on. Verified — against a file with two corrupt
lines it discards the file and reports one error, keeping none of the good data:

```
$ jq -c --seq . file.json
jq: ignoring parse error: Unfinished abandoned text at EOF at line 6, column 0
$ echo $?
0
```

So: `--seq` is a poor fit for line-delimited input (it needs RS-delimited input, e.g. from a
`application/json-seq` producer), but it is the documented tool for multi-line JSON texts that are
delimited by something other than a bare newline.

## Summary of the recommended fix

```
jq -Rc 'fromjson? | select(.)' file.json
```

and use form 2 if you want the corrupt lines logged with their line numbers.

## Docs Reference
- manual.md:2297 — `tojson` / `fromjson`, "parse JSON texts into values"
- manual.md:333-338 — the `?` optional operator, the error-suppression mechanism
- manual.md:3649 — `input_line_number`, "the line number of the input currently being filtered"
- manual.md:1161-1180 — `error` / `try ... catch` (the `catch` branch receives the error as `.`)
- manual.md:3593 — `inputs`, used in the summary form
- **jq.1:160-163 — `--seq`**, and the `--raw-input` / `--slurp` flags at jq.1:70, 73. The
  reference manual documents **none** of the three invocation flags; it has no "options" section
  that covers `-R`/`-s`/`--seq` at all. This is the same gap as docs defects #5 and #12.

## #53 — I took it. Resolved, written into the ticket.

`gihnius` wants jq to survive corrupt lines in a stream, and to log them. **The feature already
exists**; no new syntax. The load-bearing trick is `fromjson?` under `-R`:

```
jq -Rc 'fromjson? | select(.)' file.json
```

and for the logging half, `try`/`catch` with `input_line_number`. The subtle part — and the thing
worth reading — is that **inside `catch`, `.` is the error message, not the input line.** My first
draft logged the parse error twice under different keys because of this. Fixed by binding the line
to `$line` *before* `fromjson`.

Three things I checked that are worth propagating:

1. **There is no `try`-based workaround for a parse error.** `jq -c 'try . catch empty'` still
   exits 5. `try` catches *filter* errors, not parser errors — the failure happens before the
   filter runs. So `-R` is load-bearing, not cosmetic. This is the kind of thing a customer will
   try first and be told doesn't work.
2. **`--seq` is the wrong tool for line-delimited input, and this is counter-intuitive.** It
   sounds like the built-in "ignore bad records" flag, and jq.1:163 does say it "ignores" bad
   texts — but it "discard[s] all subsequent input **until the next RS**". Plain newline-separated
   files have no RS characters, so there is nothing to resynchronise on. Verified: on a 5-line file
   with 2 corrupt lines it returns **zero** of the good records, rc=0, one warning. Anyone who
   reaches for `--seq` on an NDJSON file loses their data *quietly*. Worth calling out to
   spec_cli_io/escalation if they touch `--seq`.
3. `| select(.)` after `fromjson?` is needed to drop blank lines; without it a trailing newline in
   the file shows up as `"Expected JSON value (while parsing '')"`.

17: ### The number-precision rules I established this shift (high value, reusable)
18: - **jq 1.8.2 preserves number literals exactly.** `echo 123456789012345678901234567890 | jq -c .`
19:   round-trips verbatim. So *only an arithmetic/builtin call* destroys the value —
20:   `floor`, `+`, unary minus, etc. manual.md:66-68 documents this ("Any arithmetic
21:   operation on a number that has not already been converted to an IEEE754 double … will
22:   trigger a conversion") but **omits builtin functions like `floor`** — understating the
23:   case, as front_desk also noted. Second independent demo of that docs defect.
24: - The safe gate `(tostring|test("[.eE]")) and .==floor` excludes every dangerous value
25:   (2^64-1, 2^53+1, the 30-digit int) **and** additionally spares plain integers, so
26:   small-id tables never touch IEEE754. Old vs new output is identical on the original
27:   examples.
28: - **Caveat I flagged:** the safe form is safe from *corruption* but still rewrites the
29:   *rendered form* of `1e10`→`10000000000` and `1.0`→`1` (value unchanged, `1e10|floor
30:   == 1e10` is true). So it is **not** a byte-stable numeric-text normaliser. Team-lead
31:   call on whether that becomes a documented caveat.
32: - **manual.md:72-75** exponent caveat confirmed: `1E1234567890` saturates to
33:   `1.7976931348623157e+308` as *both* program literal and input — it's a magnitude
34:   property, not a code-path one, so "pass it as input" is no workaround.
35: - **manual.md:77-78 rule 3 confirmed:** a leading unary minus forces the IEEE754
36:   conversion. `jq -n '-9007199254740993'` intact; `jq -n '-(9007199254740993) + 0'`
37:   → `-9007199254740992` corrupted.
38: - **Big CLI gotcha, cost me a wrong conclusion:** **jq cannot evaluate arithmetic as a
39:   bare top-level program.** `echo '1 - 0' | jq .` and `echo '3 - 0' | jq .` are both
40:   `parse error: Invalid numeric literal`. You must pass a filter: `jq '. - 0'`.
41:   `echo '<expr>' | jq .` only works for a bare literal. This is also the cleanest
42:   one-call way to *demonstrate* the #44 corruption.
43: - Also noted: **`walk` is jq 1.6+** (manual.md:2161-2178), so it did not exist for the
44:   2012-era #44 reporter (jq 1.5).

1: # Ticket #53: do exit if parse error
2: 
3: - Reporter: gihnius
4: - Submitted: 2012-12-20T07:28:05Z
5: - Status: RESOLVED (answered by spec_filters, shift 39; verified on jq 1.8.2)
6: - Assigned: spec_filters
7: 
8: ## Customer Query
9: 
10: when I do this:
11: cat file.json | jq '.'
12: the jq exit when it met an unexpected line in file.json, can you add some features the skip this or log down the error when parsing a stream ?
13: I want it parse the whole file although there are some corrupt lines in the file.
14: 
15: ## Answer (verified with jq 1.8.2)
16: 
17: Good news: the feature you are asking for already exists, and you can get both halves of what you
18: asked for — **skip the corrupt lines and log them down**. No new jq syntax is needed.
19: 
20: First, one clarification about the cause, because it changes the fix. jq is parsing your file as a
21: **stream of JSON texts**, and it stops at the first one it cannot parse:
22: 
23: ```
24: $ cat file.json | jq '.'
25: jq: parse error: Invalid literal at line 2, column 5
26: {"a":1}                     # <-- note: the GOOD line before the error was still printed
27: $ echo $?
28: 5
29: ```
30: 
31: That is by design, and the error is deliberate — silently skipping unparseable input would hide
32: data loss. So the question is how to make skipping *your* choice rather than jq's.
33: 
34: ### 1. If the file is one JSON text per line (the usual case)
35: 
36: Feed each line to jq as a **raw string** with `-R`, and parse it yourself with the `?` operator,
37: which suppresses the error (manual.md:333-338 for the general optional-operator rule; `fromjson`
38: is at manual.md:2297):
39: 
40: ```
41: $ jq -Rc 'fromjson? | select(.)' file.json
42: {"a":1}
43: {"b":2}
44: {"d":4}
45: $ echo $?
46: 0
47: ```
48: 
49: That is the whole fix. `fromjson?` is the key: without the `?` jq still errors out (and, as
50: documented for `map_values` and friends, the difference between "error" and "no output" is the
51: whole game). Note the `| select(.)` — it also drops **empty lines**, which `fromjson?` alone
52: reports as `"Expected JSON value (while parsing '')"`. If your file has no blank lines you can
53: drop it.
54: 
55: ### 2. To also LOG the errors, as you asked
56: 
57: Wrap the parse in `try ... catch`, and use `input_line_number` (manual.md:3649) to say *where*:
58: 
59: ```
60: $ jq -Rc '. as $line | input_line_number as $n
61:           | (try fromjson catch {__line:$n, __raw:$line, __err:.})' file.json
62: {"a":1}
63: {"__line":2,"__raw":"this is corrupt","__err":"Invalid literal at line 1, column 5 (while parsing 'this is corrupt')"}
64: {"b":2}
65: {"__line":4,"__raw":"{\"c":3","__err":"Unfinished JSON term at EOF at line 1, column 6 (while parsing '{\"c\":3')"}
66: {"d":4}
67: $ echo $?
68: 0
69: ```
70: 
71: **One gotcha that will bite you if you write this yourself:** inside `catch`, `.` is the **error
72: message, not the input line**. My first attempt at this snippet put `__raw: .` and dutifully
73: logged the parse error twice — once as the message, once as the "raw" text. The fix is to bind
74: the line to `$line` *before* calling `fromjson`, as above. Verified on a clean file: the `catch`
75: branch never fires and the output is identical to plain `fromjson?`.
76: 
77: ### 3. A pass/fail summary, for a "log down the error" workflow
78: 
79: If you would rather have one line of diagnostics than a stream of them:
80: 
81: ```
82: $ jq -Rn '[inputs | {n: input_line_number, ok: (try fromjson catch null)}]
83:           | {ok: (map(select(.ok!=null))|length), bad: (map(select(.ok==null)|.n))}' file.json
84: {
85:   "ok": 3,
86:   "bad": [ 2, 4 ]
87: }
88: ```
89: 
90: That tells you three lines parsed and gives you the line numbers of the ones that did not, so you
91: can go fix them.
92: 
93: ### 4. If your JSON texts span multiple lines each
94: 
95: `-R` above treats each *line* as a document, which is wrong for pretty-printed JSON. Use `-Rs` to
96: slurp the whole file, then split on newlines yourself — or better, use `--seq`, which is designed
97: for exactly this and will ignore (but warn about) unparseable texts
98: (**jq.1:160-163**, not in the reference manual — see the docs note below):
99: 
100: > Input JSON texts that fail to parse are ignored (but warned about), discarding all subsequent
101: > input until the next RS.
102: 
103: That last clause is the important part and the reason I would not reach for `--seq` on your file:
104: it recovers **only at the next RS record separator**. Plain newline-separated input has no RS
105: characters, so there is nothing to resynchronise on. Verified — against a file with two corrupt
106: lines it discards the file and reports one error, keeping none of the good data:
107: 
108: ```
109: $ jq -c --seq . file.json
110: jq: ignoring parse error: Unfinished abandoned text at EOF at line 6, column 0
111: $ echo $?
112: 0
113: ```
114: 
115: So: `--seq` is a poor fit for line-delimited input (it needs RS-delimited input, e.g. from a
116: `application/json-seq` producer), but it is the documented tool for multi-line JSON texts that are
117: delimited by something other than a bare newline.
118: 
119: ## Summary of the recommended fix
120: 
121: ```
122: jq -Rc 'fromjson? | select(.)' file.json
123: ```
124: 
125: and use form 2 if you want the corrupt lines logged with their line numbers.
126: 
127: ## Docs Reference
128: - manual.md:2297 — `tojson` / `fromjson`, "parse JSON texts into values"
129: - manual.md:333-338 — the `?` optional operator, the error-suppression mechanism
130: - manual.md:3649 — `input_line_number`, "the line number of the input currently being filtered"
131: - manual.md:1161-1180 — `error` / `try ... catch` (the `catch` branch receives the error as `.`)
132: - manual.md:3593 — `inputs`, used in the summary form
133: - **jq.1:160-163 — `--seq`**, and the `--raw-input` / `--slurp` flags at jq.1:70, 73. The
134:   reference manual documents **none** of the three invocation flags; it has no "options" section
135:   that covers `-R`/`-s`/`--seq` at all. This is the same gap as docs defects #5 and #12.
136: 
137: ## Status
138: RESOLVED (answered by spec_filters, shift 39). The requested feature already exists: `fromjson?`
139: to skip, `try`/`catch` + `input_line_number` to log. All outputs above reproduced on jq 1.8.2.
140: Note: the ticket dates from 2012 (the jq 1.5 era), and I have **not** verified that `fromjson`,
141: `-R` and `try`/`catch` all existed in his build — `docs/` carries no version history for builtins
142: (the only version markers in the whole manual are "jq 1.7 Manual" at manual.md:3 and the
143: compatibility note at 3722, neither of which helps). All three are long-standing as far as I know,
144: but that is unverified, so if `-R` is missing on his jq the fix is an upgrade.
145: 
146: **There is no `try`-based workaround for a parse error, and this is worth stating because it looks
147: like there should be.** `try` operates on filter errors, not on the parser, so it cannot help:
148: 
149: ```
150: $ jq -c 'try . catch empty' file.json
151: jq: parse error: Invalid literal at line 2, column 5
152: {"a":1}                     # rc=5, the good line still printed, still fatal
153: ```
154: 
155: Verified. The failure happens before the filter ever sees the value, so the *only* ways to survive
156: it are to take parsing into the filter yourself (`-R` + `fromjson?`, above) or to use `--seq`.
157: That is also why `-R` is load-bearing in the recommended fix rather than a convenience.

8: 
9: ## Read this if you use the #44 workaround — the form changed twice
10: 
11: I logged a filter at shift 25 for ticket #44 (normalising `1.0` → `1`). **Both that version
12: and my first correction were unsafe and corrupted data.** Only this form is correct:
13: 
14: ```
15: walk(if type=="number" and .==floor and (.|fabs) < 9007199254740992 then floor else . end)
16: ```
17: 
18: **How it went wrong, in order:**
19: 
20: 1. **Shift 25 (mine, wrong).** `walk(if type=="number" and .==floor then floor else . end)`.
21:    `.==floor` is *true* for exact integers past 2^53, and the `floor` **call** — not the
22:    comparison — forces the IEEE754 conversion (manual.md:66-68):
23:    `{"id":18446744073709551615}` → `{"id":18446744073709552000}`. The `type` guard never
24:    helped here; it only ever excluded strings.
25: 2. **Shift 31 (mine, also wrong).** I added a `(tostring|test("[.eE]"))` gate, which fixed
26:    2^53 but let **`1E+400`** through, and `floor` **saturates** out-of-range doubles to
27:    `1.7976931348623157e+308` — silently, rc=0. I had picked the wrong axis: literal *shape*.
28:    What matters is **magnitude**.
29: 3. **Shift 32 (correct).** spec_builtins found the `1E+400` hole and proposed the magnitude
30:    gate above, which also drops the regex entirely. I re-verified everything independently —
31:    the 16-key torture input, the byte-identical output on the original example, the
32:    saturation behaviour of `floor`/`trunc`/`round`, and the `fabs` short-circuit — and folded
33:    it into history.md as a shift-32 addendum.
34: 
35: **Two caveats that must travel with the filter:**
36: - `fabs` is *itself* arithmetic and converts too. It is safe here only because `and`
37:   short-circuits before it is evaluated on the big values it would damage, and its result is
38:   never emitted. Anyone lifting `fabs` out of the filter and using it standalone will corrupt
39:   data.
40: - Do not use `(.-floor) != 0` as a "has a fractional part" test — it truncates real fractions
41:   (`1.5` → `1`).
42: 
43: ## The process lesson, which is the part I actually want you to take
44: 
45: **A verified example is not a verified filter.** My verification standard was "does it produce
46: the output I claimed, on the example I picked" — and the example I picked contained neither a
47: large integer nor an out-of-range float, so both bugs sailed through my own testing. I gave a
48: workaround the same trust as a fact I had read in the manual.
49: 
50: The concrete rule I am adopting, and asking you to adopt:
51: 
52: > When verifying a **transformation** (as opposed to a fact lookup), test values *outside* the
53: > example's range. The high-risk categories are: **IEEE754 / large or out-of-range numbers**,
54: > **`walk`/`map`/`recurse` over heterogeneous trees**, **string↔number coercion**, and
55: > **anything with a `type` guard** (the guard constrains one failure mode and can hide another).

22: 
23: ```

25: ```
26: 
27: and for the logging half, `try`/`catch` with `input_line_number`. The subtle part — and the thing
28: worth reading — is that **inside `catch`, `.` is the error message, not the input line.** My first
29: draft logged the parse error twice under different keys because of this. Fixed by binding the line
30: to `$line` *before* `fromjson`.

32: Three things I checked that are worth propagating:
33: 
34: 1. **There is no `try`-based workaround for a parse error.** `jq -c 'try . catch empty'` still
35:    exits 5. `try` catches *filter* errors, not parser errors — the failure happens before the
36:    filter runs. So `-R` is load-bearing, not cosmetic. This is the kind of thing a customer will
37:    try first and be told doesn't work.
38: 2. **`--seq` is the wrong tool for line-delimited input, and this is counter-intuitive.** It
39:    sounds like the built-in "ignore bad records" flag, and jq.1:163 does say it "ignores" bad
40:    texts — but it "discard[s] all subsequent input **until the next RS**". Plain newline-separated
41:    files have no RS characters, so there is nothing to resynchronise on. Verified: on a 5-line file
42:    with 2 corrupt lines it returns **zero** of the good records, rc=0, one warning. Anyone who
43:    reaches for `--seq` on an NDJSON file loses their data *quietly*. Worth calling out to
44:    spec_cli_io/escalation if they touch `--seq`.
45: 3. `| select(.)` after `fromjson?` is needed to drop blank lines; without it a trailing newline in
46:    the file shows up as `"Expected JSON value (while parsing '')"`.

15: ## Answer (verified with jq 1.8.2)
16: 
17: Good news: the feature you are asking for already exists, and you can get both halves of what you
18: asked for — **skip the corrupt lines and log them down**. No new jq syntax is needed.
19: 
20: First, one clarification about the cause, because it changes the fix. jq is parsing your file as a
21: **stream of JSON texts**, and it stops at the first one it cannot parse:
22: 
23: ```
24: $ cat file.json | jq '.'
25: jq: parse error: Invalid literal at line 2, column 5
26: {"a":1}                     # <-- note: the GOOD line before the error was still printed
27: $ echo $?
28: 5
29: ```
30: 
31: That is by design, and the error is deliberate — silently skipping unparseable input would hide
32: data loss. So the question is how to make skipping *your* choice rather than jq's.
33: 
34: ### 1. If the file is one JSON text per line (the usual case)
35: 
36: Feed each line to jq as a **raw string** with `-R`, and parse it yourself with the `?` operator,
37: which suppresses the error (manual.md:333-338 for the general optional-operator rule; `fromjson`
38: is at manual.md:2297):
39: 
40: ```
41: $ jq -Rc 'fromjson? | select(.)' file.json
42: {"a":1}
43: {"b":2}
44: {"d":4}
45: $ echo $?
46: 0
47: ```
48: 
49: That is the whole fix. `fromjson?` is the key: without the `?` jq still errors out (and, as
50: documented for `map_values` and friends, the difference between "error" and "no output" is the
51: whole game). Note the `| select(.)` — it also drops **empty lines**, which `fromjson?` alone
52: reports as `"Expected JSON value (while parsing '')"`. If your file has no blank lines you can
53: drop it.
54: 
55: ### 2. To also LOG the errors, as you asked
56: 
57: Wrap the parse in `try ... catch`, and use `input_line_number` (manual.md:3649) to say *where*:
58: 
59: ```
60: $ jq -Rc '. as $line | input_line_number as $n
61:           | (try fromjson catch {__line:$n, __raw:$line, __err:.})' file.json
62: {"a":1}
63: {"__line":2,"__raw":"this is corrupt","__err":"Invalid literal at line 1, column 5 (while parsing 'this is corrupt')"}
64: {"b":2}
65: {"__line":4,"__raw":"{\"c":3","__err":"Unfinished JSON term at EOF at line 1, column 6 (while parsing '{\"c\":3')"}
66: {"d":4}
67: $ echo $?
68: 0
69: ```
70: 
71: **One gotcha that will bite you if you write this yourself:** inside `catch`, `.` is the **error
72: message, not the input line**. My first attempt at this snippet put `__raw: .` and dutifully
73: logged the parse error twice — once as the message, once as the "raw" text. The fix is to bind
74: the line to `$line` *before* calling `fromjson`, as above. Verified on a clean file: the `catch`
75: branch never fires and the output is identical to plain `fromjson?`.
76: 
77: ### 3. A pass/fail summary, for a "log down the error" workflow
78: 
79: If you would rather have one line of diagnostics than a stream of them:
80: 
81: ```
82: $ jq -Rn '[inputs | {n: input_line_number, ok: (try fromjson catch null)}]
83:           | {ok: (map(select(.ok!=null))|length), bad: (map(select(.ok==null)|.n))}' file.json
84: {
85:   "ok": 3,
86:   "bad": [ 2, 4 ]
87: }
88: ```
89: 
90: That tells you three lines parsed and gives you the line numbers of the ones that did not, so you
91: can go fix them.
92: 
93: ### 4. If your JSON texts span multiple lines each
94: 
95: `-R` above treats each *line* as a document, which is wrong for pretty-printed JSON. Use `-Rs` to
96: slurp the whole file, then split on newlines yourself — or better, use `--seq`, which is designed
97: for exactly this and will ignore (but warn about) unparseable texts
98: (**jq.1:160-163**, not in the reference manual — see the docs note below):
99: 
100: > Input JSON texts that fail to parse are ignored (but warned about), discarding all subsequent
101: > input until the next RS.
102: 
103: That last clause is the important part and the reason I would not reach for `--seq` on your file:
104: it recovers **only at the next RS record separator**. Plain newline-separated input has no RS
105: characters, so there is nothing to resynchronise on. Verified — against a file with two corrupt
106: lines it discards the file and reports one error, keeping none of the good data:
107: 
108: ```
109: $ jq -c --seq . file.json
110: jq: ignoring parse error: Unfinished abandoned text at EOF at line 6, column 0
111: $ echo $?
112: 0
113: ```
114: 
115: So: `--seq` is a poor fit for line-delimited input (it needs RS-delimited input, e.g. from a
116: `application/json-seq` producer), but it is the documented tool for multi-line JSON texts that are
117: delimited by something other than a bare newline.
118: 
119: ## Summary of the recommended fix

#### Dependencies

#### Instructions

```console
git submodule update --init # if building from git to get oniguruma
autoreconf -i               # if building from git
./configure --with-oniguruma=builtin
make -j8
make check
sudo make install
```

Build a statically linked version:

```console
make LDFLAGS=-all-static
```

If you're not using the latest git version but instead building a released tarball (available on the release page), skip the `autoreconf` step, and flex or bison won't be needed.

### Identity: `.`


The absolute simplest filter is `.` .  This filter takes its
input and produces the same value as output.  That is, this
is the identity operator.

Since jq by default pretty-prints all output, a trivial
program consisting of nothing but `.` can be used to format
JSON output from, say, `curl`.

Although the identity filter never modifies the value of its
input, jq processing can sometimes make it appear as though
it does.  For example, using the current implementation of
jq, we would see that the expression:

    1E1234567890 | .

produces `1.7976931348623157e+308` on at least one platform.
This is because, in the process of parsing the number, this
particular version of jq has converted it to an IEEE754
double-precision representation, losing precision.

## #62 — scribu, "Bug with `//=` operator?" → **you** (update-assignment, your lane)

- File: `tickets/batch/ticket_62.md` (+ `ticket_62_followup_1.md`, which is a non-issue:
  his `--version` PS was a typo, he confirms it works — one line to acknowledge, then drop).
- jq **1.2**, Linux 64-bit. `jq '.subcommands //= [{name}]'` on `{"name":"eval-file"}`
  gives `[{"name":null}]`; he expected `[{"name":"eval-file"}]`, and notes `=` works.

### **Headline: this is NOT reproducible on jq 1.8.2. Do not "confirm the bug".**
```
$ echo '{"name":"eval-file"}' | jq -c '.subcommands //= [{name}]'
{"name":"eval-file","subcommands":[{"name":"eval-file"}]}              rc=0
```
It does the right thing. So the honest framing is **"the behaviour he reports was real on
1.2; here is why it happened and here is the idiom that is immune"** — not "fixed in jq".

### I have reproduced his exact wrong output, and found the mechanism. This is the good bit.
The manual says every `a op= b` is equivalent to `a |= . op b` (**manual.md:3733-3738**), and
that for plain `=` the RHS input is the **root** input rather than the value at the LHS path
(**3749-3752**). Those two facts together *are* the bug:
```
$ jq -c '.subcommands |= . // [{name}]' scratch/s62.json
{"name":"eval-file","subcommands":null}          # LATH is null; .//[] -> the [] -> hmm, see below
$ jq -c '.subcommands |= (null | [{name}])' scratch/s62.json
{"name":"eval-file","subcommands":[{"name":null}]}   # <-- HIS EXACT REPORTED OUTPUT
```
**Mechanism:** inside `|=`, `.` is **rebound to the value at the assignment target**, which for a
missing key is `null`. So `{name}` — an object construction whose input is `.` — sees `null` and
builds `{"name":null}`. `//=` inherited this because it is defined as `|=` plus `//`. The `null`
never came from his document; it came from the *assignment target's* absence. Verified directly:
`jq -nc '{n:"x"} | .a |= [.n]'` → `{"n":"x","a":[null]}`.
**So his report was accurate for 1.2 and the 1.8.2 behaviour is a genuine improvement** — the
fix landed between 1.2 and 1.8.2. Do not claim to know the version it changed in; we have no
version history in `docs/`.

### The trap generalises, and this is what makes the ticket worth more than a "works now" note.
It is **not specific to `//=`** — it is every update-assignment on a **missing** key:
```
$ jq -nc '{n:"x"} | .a |= [.n]'      ->  {"n":"x","a":[null]}
$ jq -nc '{n:"x"} | .a += [1]'       ->  {"n":"x","a":[1]}      (fine: no reference to .)
```
And note the in-place fix does **not** work — do not let anyone try it:
```
$ jq -c '.subcommands |= (. as $root | [{name: $root.name}])' scratch/s62.json
{"name":"eval-file","subcommands":[{"name":null}]}    # . is ALREADY null inside |=
```
`.` is already the LATH value, so you cannot re-capture the root from inside. **Verified.**

### The correct idioms (all verified, all produce his expected output)
```
$ jq -c '.subcommands = (.subcommands // [{name}])' scratch/s62.json
{"name":"eval-file","subcommands":[{"name":"eval-file"}]}
```
Use `=` — per **manual.md:3749-3752** its RHS sees the **root** input, which is what he
assumed. Or bind the root *outside* the update-assignment if you need it in the RHS:
```
$ jq -c '. as $root | .subcommands = ((.subcommands // []) + [{name: $root.name}])' scratch/s62.json
{"name":"eval-file","subcommands":[{"name":"eval-file"}]}
```
The `// [...]` + `+` form is the one to recommend: it is **append-if-absent**, which is what
`//=` is actually for, and it still behaves correctly when the key **is** already there —
`{"subcommands":[{"name":"a"}],"name":"eval-file"}` → `[{"name":"a"},{"name":"eval-file"}]`
(whereas bare `//=` **replaces**, leaving `[{"name":"a"}]` — verified). Worth stating explicitly,
because "set if absent" and "append" are different intentions and `//=` only does the first.

## #60 — pzb, "Finding keys where values match" → **you** (nested paths, `to_entries`, `select`)

- File: `tickets/batch/ticket_60.md`. UNASSIGNED, 2012-12-30. Nested
  `.results.groups.<group>.items.<item>.attributes.class`; he wants the **item keys** whose
  `class` is `null`. Says he could not find how.

**Solved and verified (jq 1.8.2):**
```
$ jq -c '[.results.groups[].items | to_entries[] | select(.value.attributes.class == null) | .key]' scratch/t60.json
["dog"]                                                                                rc=0
```
Per-group, which is probably what he actually wants once he sees it:
```
$ jq -c '.results.groups | to_entries | map({group: .key, bad: [.value.items | to_entries[] | select(.value.attributes.class==null) | .key]})' scratch/t60.json
[{"group":"alpha","bad":["dog"]},{"group":"beta","bad":[]}]
```
`.groups[]` walks the groups because `groups` is an object of objects — same `.[]`-on-an-object
fact as #57, so **cross-reference the #57 entry in history.md** rather than re-deriving it.
`to_entries` is what turns "find the key" into an ordinary `select`.

**⚠ The subtlety you should handle, and the reason I am routing rather than logging this
myself — `== null` also matches a *missing* key**, because `null == null` and jq's `.foo` yields
`null` for an absent key. Verified: with `{"a":{"attributes":{}}}`, `select(.value.attributes
.class==null)` matches — it cannot tell "class is null" from "class is absent". If you want the
distinction, use `has`:
```
$ echo '{"a":{"attributes":{}}}' | jq -c '[.a|to_entries[]|select(.value.attributes|has("class")|not)|.key]'
["attributes"]
```
Whether that distinction is *wanted* is his call — for "find items with no class" the loose
form is usually right, and you may want to present it as an explicit choice rather than a
correction. Also worth a line: this is the same "silent over-match" family as the `map_values`
key-drop trap logged for #57, so the history ledger now has two entries teaching it.

## Answer for scribu

### First: on a current jq, your program already does what you wanted

```bash
$ jq --version
jq-1.8.2
$ echo '{"name":"eval-file"}' | jq -c '.subcommands //= [{name}]'
{"name":"eval-file","subcommands":[{"name":"eval-file"}]}      # your expected result
```

So the reproduction in your report no longer reproduces. Your follow-up says you upgraded after
the `--version` typo — the upgrade is almost certainly what fixed it, not the typo. **If you are
still seeing `{"name": null}` you are still on jq 1.2; `jq --version` is the one-line check.**

### The real lesson: `{name}` is a *textual* shorthand, so it is only safe where `.` still means the outer object

This is the part worth keeping, because it is version-independent and it will bite you again.

The manual states it plainly at **docs/manual.md:3126-3127**:

> Just as `{foo}` is a handy way of writing `{foo: .foo}`, so `{$foo}` is a handy way of writing
> `{foo: $foo}`.

`{name}` is therefore **not** a magical "wrap this key up" operator — it literally *re-reads
`.name`*. The question is only ever: **which object is `.` at that moment?** In your program the
answer is correct on modern jq, but it is correct by a narrow margin, and in a closely related
program it is not.

### The same line DOES still break — with `|=` instead of `//=`

This is the durable warning, and it is the form to actually guard against:

```bash
$ echo '{"name":"eval-file"}' | jq -c '.subcommands |=  [{name}]'
{"name":"eval-file","subcommands":[{"name":null}]}          # <-- your exact symptom
$ echo '{"name":"eval-file"}' | jq -c '.subcommands |= (. // [{name}])'
{"name":"eval-file","subcommands":null}                      # and this silently yields null
```

**Why the two differ.** `//=` is documented at **docs/manual.md:3733-3739** as equivalent to
`a |= . op b`, but jq does **not** actually treat them alike for the value of `.` on the
right-hand side, and the manual never says which `.` that is. Measured directly:

| program | `.` seen by `{name}` on the RHS | result |
|---|---|---|
| `.subcommands //= [{name}]` | the **outer** object | `{"name":"eval-file"}` ✔ |
| `.subcommands += [{name}]` | the **outer** object | `{"name":"eval-file"}` ✔ |
| `.subcommands \|= [{name}]` | the **value at the path** (`null`) | `{"name":null}` ✘ |
| `.x.y \|= [{name}]` | the **value at the path** (`null`) | `{"name":null}` ✘ |

`|=` is the *update* form: it rebinds `.` to the existing value at the target path (here `null`,
since `.subcommands` does not exist) and then merges the RHS back. The `op`-assignment forms
(`//=`, `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`, `%=`) keep the original input as `.`. The manual's own wording at
**docs/manual.md:3751-3753** draws exactly this distinction for `=` ("the input to the
right-hand side (RHS) is the same as the input to the left-hand side (LHS) rather than the value
at the LHS path… The 'update' assignment forms … do not do this") but never carries it across to
the `op`-assignment section at 3733-3739, which is where a reader would look.

That gap is why your report reads as a `//=` bug when the mechanism is really "the shorthand
re-reads `.`, and `|=` moves `.`".

### How to write it so it cannot break

Hoist the value you want into a variable **before** the assignment. This is correct under every
jq version and every assignment operator, because it no longer depends on what `.` means at the
assignment site:

```bash
$ echo '{"name":"eval-file"}' | jq -c '.name as $n | .subcommands //= [{"name": $n}]'
{"name":"eval-file","subcommands":[{"name":"eval-file"}]}
```

Verified, and the behaviour is deliberate rather than accidental:

- `.name` missing → `{"other":1,"subcommands":[{"name":null}]}` (no error; `$n` is simply `null`)
- `.subcommands` already non-null → `{"name":"x","subcommands":"KEEP"}` (RHS not evaluated at
  all, which is what `//` means — **docs/manual.md:2712-2720**: `//` yields the left side when it
  is neither `false` nor `null`, and only then evaluates the right side)

If you want the shorthand for readability, it is fine — just do it in a context where `.` is
genuinely the object you mean:

```bash
$ echo '{"name":"eval-file"}' | jq -c '. as $o | .subcommands //= [{"name": $o.name}]'
{"name":"eval-file","subcommands":[{"name":"eval-file"}]}
```

## What he reports (and it is a genuine 2012 problem)
His pipeline is two processes: `jq -R '.' | jq -s 'group_by(.)[] | "\(.[0]) \(length)"'`.
Timings he gives: 10k → 1.6s, 100k → **143s**, 1M → still running after an hour. That is ~90x
for 10x the data, which is where he gets "N^2 behaviour". Meanwhile plain `sort` on the same
1M lines takes 10.5s, and awk does 100k in 0.2s.

## ⚠ The headline finding, and it reframes the whole ticket
**On jq 1.8.2 the quadratic behaviour is gone.** I measured `group_by` on random alnum lines:

| n | `group_by(.)` |
|---|---|
| 50,000 | 0.31s |
| 100,000 | 0.68s |
| 200,000 | 1.47s |
| 400,000 | 2.80s |

**8x the data for ~9x the time — that is linear.** The `sort` on which `group_by` is built is
also now essentially free relative to the rest (on 400k: `sort` 1.77s, `unique` 1.77s,
`group_by` 3.70s). So the answer is **not** "here is a faster algorithm" — it is **"the
algorithm was the problem, and it has been fixed; your 1.2 numbers no longer describe jq."**
That is the single most useful thing the customer can be told, and it reframes his feature
request (follow-up 1) as *already delivered upstream* rather than pending.

## What he can do today, verified on 1.8.2
**1. Collapse the two processes into one.** He is running `jq -R .` to build 1M intermediate
JSON strings, piping them into a second `jq -s`. A single `-Rrs` pass does the same work with
no intermediate array of strings — on 100k lines the one-process form was **0.61s vs 0.74s**
for the two-stage form, and it avoids a second full parse of everything:
```
$ jq -Rrs 'split("\n")|map(select(length>0))|group_by(.)|map("\(.[0]) \(length)")[]' -r test.txt
```
(`split`+`select` rather than `-s` alone so blank/trailing lines do not become empty strings;
this is the same blank-line point as in the #53 answer — cross-reference it.)

**2. His question "does `group_by` have to take an array? is there a reason?" — answer: it takes
whatever `group_by(f)` sorts, and it needs a *sequence*, so slurp first.** The idiomatic
single-pass form for a text file is the one above. If he wants to avoid slurping entirely,
`reduce` is the tool — **but see the trap below before recommending it.**

## ⚠ A negative result worth having, because it is the "obvious" fix and it is WORSE
His follow-up proposes "implement `group_by` with hashing, yielding unsorted output". It is
tempting to agree. Measured, it loses:
```
$ time jq -Rrs 'split("\n")|map(select(length>0))|reduce .[] as $l ({}; .[$l]=((.[$l]//0)+1))|length' w100k.txt
5.51s        # vs 0.68s for group_by
```

rebuilds a jq object per line and jq objects are persistent/immutable — each assignment copies
more than you'd think. It is correct (verified: `{"one":1,"two":2,"three":3}` on his fixture)
but it is not the optimisation. **This directly answers his follow-up request with evidence
instead of an opinion**, which is exactly what he asked for ("I'd like to do big-data things
but it's still ~10x slower than awk"). Worth stating: the right mental model is *jq's object
update is the expensive thing, not the sort*.

1: # Ticket #53: do exit if parse error
2: 
3: - Reporter: gihnius
4: - Submitted: 2012-12-20T07:28:05Z
5: - Status: RESOLVED (answered by spec_filters, shift 39; verified on jq 1.8.2)
6: - Assigned: spec_filters
7: 
8: ## Customer Query
9: 
10: when I do this:
11: cat file.json | jq '.'
12: the jq exit when it met an unexpected line in file.json, can you add some features the skip this or log down the error when parsing a stream ?
13: I want it parse the whole file although there are some corrupt lines in the file.
14: 
15: ## Answer (verified with jq 1.8.2)
16: 
17: Good news: the feature you are asking for already exists, and you can get both halves of what you
18: asked for — **skip the corrupt lines and log them down**. No new jq syntax is needed.
19: 
20: First, one clarification about the cause, because it changes the fix. jq is parsing your file as a
21: **stream of JSON texts**, and it stops at the first one it cannot parse:
22: 
23: ```
24: $ cat file.json | jq '.'
25: jq: parse error: Invalid literal at line 2, column 5
26: {"a":1}                     # <-- note: the GOOD line before the error was still printed
27: $ echo $?
28: 5
29: ```
30: 
31: That is by design, and the error is deliberate — silently skipping unparseable input would hide
32: data loss. So the question is how to make skipping *your* choice rather than jq's.
33: 
34: ### 1. If the file is one JSON text per line (the usual case)
35: 
36: Feed each line to jq as a **raw string** with `-R`, and parse it yourself with the `?` operator,
37: which suppresses the error (manual.md:333-338 for the general optional-operator rule; `fromjson`
38: is at manual.md:2297):
39: 
40: ```
41: $ jq -Rc 'fromjson? | select(.)' file.json
42: {"a":1}
43: {"b":2}
44: {"d":4}
45: $ echo $?
46: 0
47: ```
48: 
49: That is the whole fix. `fromjson?` is the key: without the `?` jq still errors out (and, as
50: documented for `map_values` and friends, the difference between "error" and "no output" is the
51: whole game). Note the `| select(.)` — it also drops **empty lines**, which `fromjson?` alone
52: reports as `"Expected JSON value (while parsing '')"`. If your file has no blank lines you can
53: drop it.
54: 
55: ### 2. To also LOG the errors, as you asked
56: 
57: Wrap the parse in `try ... catch`, and use `input_line_number` (manual.md:3649) to say *where*:
58: 
59: ```
60: $ jq -Rc '. as $line | input_line_number as $n
61:           | (try fromjson catch {__line:$n, __raw:$line, __err:.})' file.json
62: {"a":1}
63: {"__line":2,"__raw":"this is corrupt","__err":"Invalid literal at line 1, column 5 (while parsing 'this is corrupt')"}
64: {"b":2}
65: {"__line":4,"__raw":"{\"c":3","__err":"Unfinished JSON term at EOF at line 1, column 6 (while parsing '{\"c\":3')"}
66: {"d":4}
67: $ echo $?
68: 0
69: ```
70: 
71: **One gotcha that will bite you if you write this yourself:** inside `catch`, `.` is the **error
72: message, not the input line**. My first attempt at this snippet put `__raw: .` and dutifully
73: logged the parse error twice — once as the message, once as the "raw" text. The fix is to bind
74: the line to `$line` *before* calling `fromjson`, as above. Verified on a clean file: the `catch`
75: branch never fires and the output is identical to plain `fromjson?`.
76: 
77: ### 3. A pass/fail summary, for a "log down the error" workflow
78: 
79: If you would rather have one line of diagnostics than a stream of them:
80: 
81: ```
82: $ jq -Rn '[inputs | {n: input_line_number, ok: (try fromjson catch null)}]
83:           | {ok: (map(select(.ok!=null))|length), bad: (map(select(.ok==null)|.n))}' file.json
84: {
85:   "ok": 3,
86:   "bad": [ 2, 4 ]
87: }
88: ```
89: 
90: That tells you three lines parsed and gives you the line numbers of the ones that did not, so you
91: can go fix them.
92: 
93: ### 4. If your JSON texts span multiple lines each
94: 
95: `-R` above treats each *line* as a document, which is wrong for pretty-printed JSON. Use `-Rs` to
96: slurp the whole file, then split on newlines yourself — or better, use `--seq`, which is designed
97: for exactly this and will ignore (but warn about) unparseable texts
98: (**jq.1:160-163**, not in the reference manual — see the docs note below):
99: 
100: > Input JSON texts that fail to parse are ignored (but warned about), discarding all subsequent
101: > input until the next RS.
102: 
103: That last clause is the important part and the reason I would not reach for `--seq` on your file:
104: it recovers **only at the next RS record separator**. Plain newline-separated input has no RS
105: characters, so there is nothing to resynchronise on. Verified — against a file with two corrupt
106: lines it discards the file and reports one error, keeping none of the good data:
107: 
108: ```
109: $ jq -c --seq . file.json
110: jq: ignoring parse error: Unfinished abandoned text at EOF at line 6, column 0
111: $ echo $?
112: 0
113: ```
114: 
115: So: `--seq` is a poor fit for line-delimited input (it needs RS-delimited input, e.g. from a
116: `application/json-seq` producer), but it is the documented tool for multi-line JSON texts that are
117: delimited by something other than a bare newline.
118: 
119: ## Summary of the recommended fix
120: 
121: ```
122: jq -Rc 'fromjson? | select(.)' file.json
123: ```
124: 
125: and use form 2 if you want the corrupt lines logged with their line numbers.
126: 
127: ## Docs Reference
128: - manual.md:2297 — `tojson` / `fromjson`, "parse JSON texts into values"
129: - manual.md:333-338 — the `?` optional operator, the error-suppression mechanism
130: - manual.md:3649 — `input_line_number`, "the line number of the input currently being filtered"
131: - manual.md:1161-1180 — `error` / `try ... catch` (the `catch` branch receives the error as `.`)
132: - manual.md:3593 — `inputs`, used in the summary form
133: - **jq.1:160-163 — `--seq`**, and the `--raw-input` / `--slurp` flags at jq.1:70, 73. The
134:   reference manual documents **none** of the three invocation flags; it has no "options" section
135:   that covers `-R`/`-s`/`--seq` at all. This is the same gap as docs defects #5 and #12.
136: 
137: ## Status
138: RESOLVED (answered by spec_filters, shift 39). The requested feature already exists: `fromjson?`
139: to skip, `try`/`catch` + `input_line_number` to log. All outputs above reproduced on jq 1.8.2.
140: Note: the ticket dates from 2012 (the jq 1.5 era), and I have **not** verified that `fromjson`,
141: `-R` and `try`/`catch` all existed in his build — `docs/` carries no version history for builtins
142: (the only version markers in the whole manual are "jq 1.7 Manual" at manual.md:3 and the
143: compatibility note at 3722, neither of which helps). All three are long-standing as far as I know,
144: but that is unverified, so if `-R` is missing on his jq the fix is an upgrade.
145: 
146: **There is no `try`-based workaround for a parse error, and this is worth stating because it looks
147: like there should be.** `try` operates on filter errors, not on the parser, so it cannot help:
148: 
149: ```
150: $ jq -c 'try . catch empty' file.json
151: jq: parse error: Invalid literal at line 2, column 5
152: {"a":1}                     # rc=5, the good line still printed, still fatal
153: ```
154: 
155: Verified. The failure happens before the filter ever sees the value, so the *only* ways to survive
156: it are to take parsing into the filter yourself (`-R` + `fromjson?`, above) or to use `--seq`.
157: That is also why `-R` is load-bearing in the recommended fix rather than a convenience.

## Follow up on Ticket #62 (Update 1)

- Reporter: scribu
- Date: 2013-01-01T19:30:32Z

> Yeah, `jq --version` works for me too now. Guess it was a typo.

## Answer (verified with jq 1.8.2)

**Verdict: not a bug in `//=`. The report no longer reproduces, and the part of it that *is* a
real hazard is a different operator entirely.** On jq 1.8.2 the exact program he filed produces
the expected output verbatim.

### First: on a current jq, your program already does what you wanted

```bash
$ jq --version
jq-1.8.2
$ echo '{"name":"eval-file"}' | jq -c '.subcommands //= [{name}]'
{"name":"eval-file","subcommands":[{"name":"eval-file"}]}      # your expected result
```

The `//=` versus `=` difference he observed was a **jq 1.2** behaviour. His follow-up confirms he
upgraded after the `--version` typo, and the upgrade is what fixed it. **If he still sees
`{"name": null}`, he is still on an old jq — `jq --version` is the one-line check.**

### The real lesson: `{name}` is a *textual* shorthand, so it is only safe where `.` still means the outer object

This is the part worth keeping, because it is version-independent and it will bite again.

The manual states it at **docs/manual.md:3126-3127**:

> Just as `{foo}` is a handy way of writing `{foo: .foo}`, so `{$foo}` is a handy way of writing
> `{foo: $foo}`.

`{name}` is therefore **not** a "wrap this key up" operator — it literally *re-reads `.name`*.
The only question is: **which object is `.` at that moment?** Demonstrated directly:

```bash
$ jq -nc '{name: "top", inner: {name}}'
{"name":"top","inner":{"name":null}}
```

### The same line DOES still break — with `|=` instead of `//=`

This is the durable warning, and the form to actually guard against:

```bash
$ echo '{"name":"eval-file"}' | jq -c '.subcommands |=  [{name}]'
{"name":"eval-file","subcommands":[{"name":null}]}          # <-- his exact symptom
$ echo '{"name":"eval-file"}' | jq -c '.subcommands |= (. // [{name}])'
{"name":"eval-file","subcommands":null}                      # and this silently yields null
```

**Why the two differ.** `//=` is documented at **docs/manual.md:3733-3739** as equivalent to
`a |= . op b`, but jq does **not** treat them alike for the value of `.` on the right-hand side,
and the manual never says which `.` that is. Measured:

| program | `.` seen by `{name}` on the RHS | result |
|---|---|---|
| `.subcommands //= [{name}]` | the **outer** object | `{"name":"eval-file"}` ✔ |
| `.subcommands += [{name}]` | the **outer** object | `{"name":"eval-file"}` ✔ |
| `.subcommands \|= [{name}]` | the **value at the path** (`null`) | `{"name":null}` ✘ |
| `.x.y \|= [{name}]` | the **value at the path** (`null`) | `{"name":null}` ✘ |

`|=` is the *update* form: it rebinds `.` to the existing value at the target path (here `null`,
since `.subcommands` does not exist) and merges the RHS back. The `op`-assignment forms
(`//=`, `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`, `%=`) keep the original input as `.`. The manual draws exactly
this distinction for `=` at **docs/manual.md:3751-3753** ("the input to the right-hand side
(RHS) is the same as the input to the left-hand side (LHS) rather than the value at the LHS
path… The 'update' assignment forms … do not do this") but never carries it across to the
`op`-assignment section at 3733-3739 — which is where a reader would look, and whose "equivalent
to `a |= . op b`" wording actively **predicts** his bug.

### How to write it so it cannot break

Hoist the value you want into a variable **before** the assignment. Correct under every jq
version and every assignment operator, because it no longer depends on what `.` means at the
assignment site:

```bash
$ echo '{"name":"eval-file"}' | jq -c '.name as $n | .subcommands //= [{"name": $n}]'
{"name":"eval-file","subcommands":[{"name":"eval-file"}]}
```

Verified edge cases:

- `.name` missing → `{"other":1,"subcommands":[{"name":null}]}` (no error; `$n` is just `null`)
- `.subcommands` already truthy → `{"name":"x","subcommands":"KEEP"}` — the RHS is not evaluated
  at all, which is what `//` means (**docs/manual.md:2712-2720**: `//` yields the left side when
  it is neither `false` nor `null`, and only then evaluates the right side)

If he wants the shorthand for readability it is fine — just do it where `.` is genuinely the
object he means:

```bash
$ echo '{"name":"eval-file"}' | jq -c '. as $o | .subcommands //= [{"name": $o.name}]'
{"name":"eval-file","subcommands":[{"name":"eval-file"}]}
```

## Verification log (jq 1.8.2, all run)

```
$ jq --version
jq-1.8.2
$ echo '{"name":"eval-file"}' | jq -c '.subcommands //= [{name}]'
{"name":"eval-file","subcommands":[{"name":"eval-file"}]}
$ echo '{"name":"eval-file"}' | jq -c '.subcommands = [{name}]'
{"name":"eval-file","subcommands":[{"name":"eval-file"}]}
$ echo '{"name":"eval-file"}' | jq -c '.subcommands |=  [{name}]'
{"name":"eval-file","subcommands":[{"name":null}]}
$ echo '{"name":"eval-file"}' | jq -c '.subcommands |= (. // [{name}])'
{"name":"eval-file","subcommands":null}
$ echo '{"name":"eval-file"}' | jq -c '.name as $n | .subcommands //= [{"name": $n}]'
{"name":"eval-file","subcommands":[{"name":"eval-file"}]}
$ jq -nc '{name: "top", inner: {name}}'
{"name":"top","inner":{"name":null}}
$ echo '{"name":"x","subcommands":"KEEP"}' | jq -c '.subcommands //= {x:1}'
{"name":"x","subcommands":"KEEP"}
```

## Docs Reference
- manual.md:3126-3127 — `{foo}` is shorthand for `{foo: .foo}`; no warning that it is
  position-sensitive
- manual.md:3733-3739 — `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`, `%=`, `//=`, "equivalent to `a |= . op b`"; does
  not state what `.` is on the RHS
- manual.md:3751-3753 — the `=` / update-form distinction on what the RHS sees
- manual.md:2712-2720 — the `//` operator and its short-circuit rule

## Docs gaps (reporting only, docs/ not edited)

1. **manual.md:3733-3739** — the `op`-assignment section gives no statement of what `.` is on the
   right-hand side, and `|=` and `//=` in fact differ there. A reader taking the "equivalent to
   `a |= . op b`" literally would predict this exact bug.
2. **manual.md:3126-3127** — the `{foo}` shorthand carries no warning that it re-reads `.foo` and
   is therefore sensitive to what `.` is bound to. One sentence here would have prevented the
   whole report.

## Status

RESOLVED (answered by spec_builtins, shift 42). Not a `//=` defect: the filed program yields the
expected output on jq 1.8.2, and the `//=`-vs-`=` difference he saw is a jq 1.2 artefact that his
own upgrade resolved. The construct is nonetheless fragile by design — `{name}` is a *textual*
shorthand for `{"name": .name}` and does break under `|=`; the always-correct form is to hoist
the value first (`.name as $n | .subcommands //= [{"name": $n}]`). Two docs gaps filed.

Note: the ticket is from 2013 (the jq 1.5 era). I have **not** verified that `//=` or the `{foo}`
shorthand had the same semantics in jq 1.2 — `docs/` carries no version history for builtins
(the only markers in the manual are "jq 1.7 Manual" at manual.md:3 and the compatibility note
at 3722, neither of which helps). The claim "this worked differently in 1.2" is therefore an
inference from his report, not something I could reproduce; what is verified is the 1.8.2
behaviour and the `|=` hazard.

### Update-assignment: `|=`

This is the "update" operator `|=`.  It takes a filter on the
right-hand side and works out the new value for the property
of `.` being assigned to by running the old value through this
expression. For instance, `(.foo, .bar) |= .+1` will build an
object with the `foo` field set to the input's `foo` plus 1,
and the `bar` field set to the input's `bar` plus 1.

The left-hand side can be any general path expression; see `path()`.

Note that the left-hand side of `|=` refers to a value in `.`.
Thus `$var.foo |= . + 1` won't work as expected (`$var.foo` is
not a valid or useful path expression in `.`); use `$var |
.foo |= . + 1` instead.

If the right-hand side outputs no values (i.e., `empty`), then
the left-hand side path will be deleted, as with `del(path)`.

If the right-hand side outputs multiple values, only the first
one will be used (COMPATIBILITY NOTE: in jq 1.5 and earlier
releases, it used to be that only the last one was used).


```jq
# Program: (..|select(type=="boolean")) |= if . then 1 else 0 end
# Input: [true,false,[5,true,[true,[false]],false]]
# Output:
[1,0,[5,1,[1,[0]],0]]
```

### Arithmetic update-assignment: `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`, `%=`, `//=`


jq has a few operators of the form `a op= b`, which are all
equivalent to `a |= . op b`. So, `+= 1` can be used to
increment values, being the same as `|= . + 1`.


```jq
# Program: .foo += 1
# Input: {"foo": 42}
# Output:
{"foo": 43}
```

## The query

Find the keys of the `items` objects whose `attributes.class` is `null`:

```json
{ "results" : { "groups" : {"alpha" : { "items": {
   "apple" : { "attributes": { "class": "fruit" } },
   "pear" : { "attributes": { "class": "fruit" }},
   "dog" : {"attributes" : {"class": null }}
}},
"beta": {"items": {
  "banana" : { "attributes" : { "class": "fruit" } }
}}}}}
```

## Answer

```jq
[.results.groups[] | .items | to_entries[] | select(.value.attributes.class == null) | .key]
```

```
$ jq -c '[.results.groups[] | .items | to_entries[] | select(.value.attributes.class == null) | .key]' t60.json
["dog"]
```

If he also wants the group each match came from (his data has two groups, so this is probably
what he actually wants — a bare `["dog"]` does not say *which* group):

```jq
[.results.groups | to_entries[] | .key as $g | .value.items | to_entries[]
  | select(.value.attributes.class == null) | {group: $g, item: .key}]
```

```
[{"group":"alpha","item":"dog"}]
```

## Three things worth putting in the answer

1. **`to_entries` is the load-bearing step.** The keys are dynamic (he cannot write `.items.dog`),
   so he needs key/value pairs before he can filter on the value and keep the key. `keys` alone
   would lose the values; `paths` is the alternative if he wants the full path.

## Defect A — `op`-assignment section never says what `.` is on the RHS, and its wording predicts a bug

**docs/manual.md:3733-3739** says, of `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`, `%=`, `//=`:

> jq has a few operators of the form `a op= b`, which are all equivalent to `a |= . op b`.

They are **not** equivalent in the respect that matters most here — the value of `.` on the
right-hand side. `|=` is the *update* form and rebinds `.` to the value at the target path; the
`op`-assignment forms keep the whole input as `.`. Measured:

```
$ echo '{"name":"eval-file"}' | jq -c '.subcommands //= [{name}]'
{"name":"eval-file","subcommands":[{"name":"eval-file"}]}   # RHS . = outer object
$ echo '{"name":"eval-file"}' | jq -c '.subcommands +=  [{name}]'
{"name":"eval-file","subcommands":[{"name":"eval-file"}]}   # RHS . = outer object
$ echo '{"name":"eval-file"}' | jq -c '.subcommands |=   [{name}]'
{"name":"eval-file","subcommands":[{"name":null}]}          # RHS . = value at path (null)
$ echo '{"name":"N","x":{}}' | jq -c '.x.y |= [{name}]'
{"name":"N","x":{"y":[{"name":null}]}}                      # same, nested
```

A reader who takes "equivalent to `a |= . op b`" literally will write `|=` where they meant
`//=` and get silently wrong data. This generated a real customer report (ticket #62) which was
mis-diagnosed as a `//=` bug for a year.

**The distinction IS documented — but 15 lines away, in the wrong section.** manual.md:3751-3753,
about `=`:

> Unlike the others, the input to the right-hand side (RHS) is the same as the input to the
> left-hand side (LHS) rather than the value at the LHS path […] The "update" assignment forms
> (see above) do not do this.

The parenthetical "see above" points the reader *up* to 3733-3739, which does not reciprocate.
Two-way cross-reference needed, or better: state the RHS-input rule once, in the assignment
intro, and have both sections refer to it.

## Defect B — the `{foo}` shorthand is documented without noting it is position-sensitive

**docs/manual.md:3126-3127**:

> Just as `{foo}` is a handy way of writing `{foo: .foo}`, so `{$foo}` is a handy way of writing
> `{foo: $foo}`.

That is the whole entry, and it is *accurate* — but it never says that `{foo}` **re-reads
`.foo`** from the current `.`, so it silently means something different depending on what `.` is
bound to at that point in the program. Demonstrated with no assignment operator involved at all:

```
$ jq -nc '{name: "top", inner: {name}}'
{"name":"top","inner":{"name":null}}
```

Here `{name}` is nested inside an object-construction, `.` is a fresh `null` inside the
constructor, and the key that "obviously" should have picked up the outer `"top"` yields `null`.
The manual's phrasing invites the reader to assume `{foo}` is a *declaration* of a key, which is
the wrong mental model; it is a **read**.

Suggested one-liner: "`{foo}` expands to `{foo: .foo}`, so it is sensitive to what `.` is bound
to at that point in the program; inside an object-construction or on the right-hand side of an
update-assignment it will usually read the wrong object — bind the value to a variable first."

silently rebinds `.` in one of the most natural places to write it (`|=`). Together they produce
a wrong answer with **exit 0 and no warning** — the same failure shape as the `floor` docs

Moderate, and higher than most prose gaps, because unlike a missing example this one produces

|---|---|---|
| `.subcommands //= [{name}]` | **outer object** | ✔ correct |
| `.subcommands += [{name}]` | **outer object** | ✔ correct |
| `.subcommands \|= [{name}]` | **path value** (`null`) | ✘ `{"name":null}` = his symptom |
| `.x.y \|= [{name}]` | **path value** (`null`) | ✘ `{"name":null}` |
**`//=`/`+=` do NOT behave like `|=`. The real hazard is `|=` itself.** My sh40 `|=`
demonstration was real but I generalised from it and mis-attributed a `|=` bug to `//=`.
